[PUBLICATION ABSTRACT]
ai_rationale: Historical study of medieval Milan's water infrastructure, examining communal and private governance of competing uses of canal/river water including domestic supply.

authors: Loftus, Alexander J; McDonald, David A
title: Of Liquid Dreams: A Political Ecology of Water Privatization in Buenos Aires
abstract: The privatization of water & sanitation in Buenos Aires has been hailed by its neoliberal proponents as an unprecedented success. This paper takes a deeper & more critical look than many of these accounts. It looks at political & economic changes within Argentina in order to explain the troubling findings regarding the performance of Aguas Argentinas, the private company that won the concession for most of Buenos Aires. The paper begins with a brief overview of the political & economic context in Argentina before describing the process involved in the water privatization in Buenos Aires. It then discusses the outcomes, including changes in coverage & charges to end users as well as impacts on labor & the environment. The paper describes how the promised reduction in water tariffs did not materialize (in fact the opposite occurred) & how agreed-upon targets for expanding sewerage connections & sewage treatment were not met. It also describes how the national government intervened to support the water company in conflicts with the regulatory agency & even bypassed the regulatory agency when the water company wanted to renegotiate the contract. Finally, the role of international financial institutions in this process is discussed. 3 Tables, 1 Map. Adapted from the source document.
ai_rationale: Political-economic case study of water/sanitation privatization in Buenos Aires examining regulatory conflict, tariffs and connection targets.

title: The Fight for Water and Democracy: An Interview with Oscar Olivera
abstract: Republication of an interview in Multinational Monitor, June 2000. Olivera, a spokesperson for the coordinator for the Defense of Water & Life in Bolivia, describes how the Bolivian government privatized state-owned industries, particularly water services, in 1999. Privatization did not benefit the country or workers; when the price of water increased, the coordinator staged its first mass mobilization to protest the water laws & force the government to break the contract with the private water services company. The government's response, subsequent protests, & lessons learned from this social action are described. M. Pflum
ai_rationale: Republished interview account of Bolivia's Cochabamba water privatization, contract, protests and law reversal.

authors: Mookherjee, Harsha N; Riemer, Jeffrey W; George, Dennis B; Wells, M J M; Clark, Y R; Rollins, Sharon; Gilbert, Anne; O'Connell, Ann
title: Environmental Justice Issues Related to Inadequate Wastewater Treatment in Small Communities in Tennessee
abstract: The environmental justice movement is based on the belief that the environment should be safe & nurturing & any environmental problem should be shared by all citizens. Most of the research suggests, however, that the less powerful, the poor, & the disadvantaged face most environmental injustices. Most epidemiological research suggests that the poor, the disadvantaged, & minority group members have higher rates of illness & mortality. Some of this illness is due to environmental factors, with water & wastewater as chief carriers. Water can also spoil an environment by foul taste, odor, & color. The general objectives of this research were to identify environmental justice issues related to inadequate wastewater treatment facilities in small (under 10,000 population) communities in TN; & to develop a decision-making process model, including socioeconomic, political, environmental, & physical factors that cause or prolong environmental injustices. The resultant decision-making process model could then serve as a means to evaluate other small communities as to their possible environmental justice problems. The research design began with the entire state of TN & narrowed the community selection down to 22 communities that showed evidence of a combination of public health problems, water quality problems, & aesthetic problems. Demographic information was gathered & onsite visits were made to 12 of the 22 communities. Here, public health officials, community residents, water treatment plant representatives, & key informants were interviewed, & wastewater problem areas were observed. The resulting community profiles coupled with evidence of water quality problems, public health problems, onsite visits, & resident concerns allowed for the refinement of the elements in the decision-making process model. The developed model shows how other communities, like those studied, can be systematically approached & evaluated as to possible environmental injustices & how each community can have its own unique set of problems & possible solutions. 2 Figures, 19 References. Adapted from the source document.
ai_rationale: Study of environmental justice issues from inadequate wastewater treatment in small Tennessee communities, developing a decision-making model of socioeconomic/political/environmental causes.

title: Community identification moderating the impact of financial incentives in a natural social dilemma: Water conservation
abstract: The moderating role of community identifiication wa sinvestigated in the impact of different tariff systems on domestic water use. Over a 9-month interval, both consumption and survey data were collected in 278 households in the United Kingdom, 203 of which were on a variable tariff (i.e., charges related to use) and 75 on a fixed tariff (i.e., charges unrealted to use). Adopting a social dilemma approach, I expected a fixed tariff to be associated with greater use than a variable tariff, in particular when resources were valuable and people identified weakly with their community.
ai_rationale: Field study of UK households on variable vs fixed water tariffs and domestic water use.

title: Implications of Legal Pluralism for Natural Resource Management
abstract: This article illustrates the implications of legal pluralism for our understanding of natural resource management & policies toward resource tenure, using the example of water rights. There is widespread recognition that property rights play a fundamental role in shaping how people manage natural resources. But many conceptions of property rights have focused only on static definitions, usually as defined in statutory law. The legal anthropological perspective highlights the coexistence & interaction between multiple legal orders such as state, customary, religious, project & local laws, all of which provide bases for claiming property rights. These multiple legal frameworks also facilitate considerable flexibility for people to maneuver in their use of natural resources, thus helping to cope with uncertainty. In many parts of the world, water rights are dynamic, flexible, & subject to frequent negotiations because of uncertain water supply, damages to intake structures due to floods & landslides, & social, economic, & political changes. The article demonstrates how multiple, flexible, & dynamic legal orders are more responsive to these uncertainties & changes than a single, fixed legal system with a static property regime. 30 References. Adapted from the source document.
ai_rationale: Legal anthropology analysis of legal pluralism and its implications for water rights and resource management.

title: Integrated management of water resources in the National Capital Region-Delhi
abstract: Competing demands between various sectors of water users such as agriculture, industry, urban and domestic use have put enormous pressure on the fresh water availability in India. Some investigations have shown that the per capita availability of water has gone down drastically in the last few decades. Yet, there is a little evidence to show that measures are being drawn up either to augment fresh water resources or to manage existing resource equitably. The reasons usually cited for the decline of water availability are deforestation, intensive water use in agriculture, growing population etc. Remedies must therefore be addressed to all these issues. However, there is an urgent need to look at the opportunities available in a country which is said to have had a riverine civilization and one which has the blessings of intensive precipitation during the monsoon months. Thus, on the one hand there are enormous possibilities available in rationalising water use in the agriculture sector, recycling water for industrial use and harnessing monsoon precipitation through water harvesting on a very large scale.It is also necessary to look at some of the policy aspects, legal aspects and financial aspects of water management. For instance, it needs to be asked whether official policy of conjunctive use of surface and ground water is being followed adequately. Also it needs to be asked whether, given that water is a State subject, there is adequate coordination among the States in order to facilitate optimalities in water use. In this context, it may be useful to re-evaluate all the existing inter-State water agreements which were drawn up several decades ago. Further, it needs to be investigated whether the moneys being spent on different aspects of water management such as inter-basin transfers, dam and canal construction, ground water management etc. are being done in a manner that is economically justifiable. Simultaneously, the existing fiscal mechanism in relation to water use should also be reexamined to see the future scope of making water use economically viable.
ai_rationale: Discussion of legal, policy, and financial aspects of integrated water resources management in the Delhi National Capital Region.

title: Towards sustainable development in the water sector: A perspective from Palestine
abstract: The water sector in Palestine suffers from great damage and serious institutional fragmentation. The deterioration in the water services and the inadequate coverage at the different levels are two major weaknesses in the sector. Adding to that, the responsibilities are scattered among relevant institutions and unclear. Aiming at facing the challenges and obstacles, and in order to approach the achievement of sustainable development in the water sector, the Palestinian Authority (PA) had to take certain measures and actions. The elements of a 'National Water Policy' have been adopted that aim at sustaining the resource. However, a set of measures and regulations in line with the policies still has to be issued and enforced. A central independent authority, the Palestinian Authority, was established in order to execute the National Water Policy. The main aims of this authority as a regulator will be represented. This fairly new approach for managing water resources in Palestine is time consuming and requires a big change in the national culture. Public awareness and stakeholder participation are vital strategies to create incentives for public commitment and involvement.
ai_rationale: Examines institutional fragmentation and inadequate water service coverage in the Palestinian water sector.

title: Challenges to urban water management in Sri Lanka
abstract: Sri Lanka has an urban population of 22% of the national population living in 1% of its land area in 1985. Coastal lands in the wet zone are thickly populated and demand for water supply is increasing for pipe-borne safe drinking water. Surface drainage and shallow groundwater are purified and distributed for domestic connections and public standposts. Municipal Councils, the National Water Supply and Drainage Board and the Irrigation Department control water resources for the benefit of the residents. Annual new domestic connections are around 100 000 under new projects and the plan is for 100% completion by 2005. The institutional and funding issues are discussed in this paper.
ai_rationale: Examines institutional challenges (municipal councils, national water authority) to expanding urban water supply connections in Sri Lanka.

title: Experiences in the use of domestic and end user metering. Legal and technical problems relating to domestic end-user metering in Hungary
abstract: Since the first establishment of the water supply in Hungary (second half of the 19th century) connections to the water supply were established along with a water meter, while domestic end user metering was an unknown concept. In 1990, water charges suddenly increased 5-6-fold and following this domestic end-user meters were installed in huge numbers. In just 7 years, a total of 800,000 domestic end-user water meters were set up in Hungary. Because of wrong regulations a largely unregulated process began which produces almost puzzlingly heterogeneous practice even to this day. This statement is proved by the authors' national survey, in which the different replies given to individual questions illustrates that there are as many types of practice as there are supply companies. In Hungary the main meters are verified every 4 years, the end-user water meters at 6 years. Based on the 1997 survey of 37 Hungarian water supply companies (which together furnish 95% of Hungary's water), many legal and technical problems are summarised. In seeking to understand the behaviour of Hungary's water supply companies, Szekesfehervar (100,000 inhabitants) and Budapest (2 million inhabitants) are two good extreme examples. In Szekesfehervar the waterworks set up its end-user meter system for nearly all the flats in its supply area (96.7% of the total). Budapest Water Works Rt. on the other hand, took a passive stance on the installation of end-user meters and even today it still considers the main meter as its basis for billing. In the future, the company intends to treat end-user meters simply as a means to determine the proportion of the total main meter consumption. As a consequence of this policy, just 18-20% of flats in its service area are equipped with end-user meters.
ai_rationale: Hungarian survey documents legal/regulatory problems in domestic water metering and connection practices.

title: Watershed protection challenges in rapidly Urbanizing regions: The case of tegucigalpa, honduras
abstract: Rapidly urbanizing regions present watershed managers with a range of challenges, especially when drinking water sources and their watersheds are located within the margins of urban and suburban expansion. These challenges can be acute in those developing countries where land-use regulations and environmental protection laws are inadequate or poorly applied, the latter often a result of the lack of defined institutional responsibilities and coordination. The Los Laureles reservoir and Guacerique watershed that supply 30 percent of Tegucigalpa's drinking water provide a powerful case study of the kinds of natural resource pressures that may lead to water quality and reliability deterioration as urban growth continues. Sedimentation, high turbidity, and high pathogen counts have accompanied decisions to locate projects such as the construction of a major ring-road/highway expansion, military bases and hospitals, and a 10, 000 unit public worker housing complex in the watershed. These problems have been exacerbated by the development of private housing and poultry plants, and widespread firewood extraction from the remaining forest cover around the margins and upstream of the reservoir. For a variety of reasons, geographical and economic, watersheds like Gaucerique may frequently become neglected components of the water supply system and their protection receive much lower priority than efforts to expand and improve water supply coverage to consumers. In particular, by contributing little to revenue generation in the short term, watershed spending may be cut back from already low levels during water sector privatization as managers are forced to pay greater attention to balancing their budgets. © 2000, Taylor & Francis Group, LLC.
ai_rationale: Honduras case ties land-use/institutional regulation gaps to drinking water supply reliability/coverage.

title: Who gets clean water? Aid allocation to small water systems in Pennsylvania
abstract: Research on the condition of drinking water provision in the United States documents the inequitable financial impact of environmental regulations on small water systems (those serving 3,300 or fewer people). While a variety of federal and state financial assistance programs are available for water systems, few quantitative analyses have evaluated the success of these programs in alleviating the problems of small systems. A case study of the largest aid initiative for water supply infrastructure in Pennsylvania provides the empirical framework through which to analyze government funding opportunities for water systems. This study examines the allocation practices of the Pennsylvania Infrastructure Investment Authority (PENNVEST) to water systems of varying sizes. Utilizing data from PENNVEST applications and the Pennsylvania Department of Environmental Protection, the distribution of PENNVEST award recipients and denied applicants by size characteristics are compared. The study indicates that very small water systems (those serving 500 or fewer) do not apply for or receive funds with the same frequency as their larger counterparts. Understanding the allocation of awards from PENNVEST offers insight into the ability of small communities to access capital for water supply infrastructure.; Research on the condition of drinking water provision in the United States documents the inequitable financial impact of environmental regulations on small water systems (those serving 3,300 or fewer people). While a variety of federal and state financial assistance programs are available for water systems, few quantitative analyses have evaluated the success of these programs in alleviating the problems of small systems. A case study of the largest aid initiative for water supply infrastructure in Pennsylvania provides the empirical framework through which to analyze government funding opportunities for water systems. This study examines the allocation practices of the Pennsylvania Infrastructure Investment Authority (PENNVEST) to water systems of varying sizes. Utilizing data from PENNVEST applications and the Pennsylvania Department of Environmental Protection, the distribution of PENNVEST award recipients and denied applicants by size characteristics are compared. The study indicates that very small water systems (those serving 500 or fewer) do not apply for or receive funds with the same frequency as their larger counterparts. Understanding the allocation of awards from PENNVEST offers insight into the ability of small communities to access capital for water supply infrastructure.
ai_rationale: Empirical case study of regulatory/funding-program effects on small water systems' access to capital.

title: The public-private sector partnership approach to sustainable municipal solid waste management and improvement of social services delivery
abstract: Improvements in the human settlement situation in Nairobi and other Kenyan urban centres are constrained by: (a) lack of financing for the construction sector; (b) local authority by-laws, outdated building codes, and zoning laws that make housing very expensive and encourage construction of substandard housing; (c) lack of adequate infrastructure such as roads, and water and electricity supply to facilitate private sector involvement; (d) lack of suitable land, especially serviced land; (e) lack of comprehensive land-use and housing policy as well as limited community participation in planning; and (f) limited institutional capacity in both central government ministries and local authorities; inadequate coordination of actors often leads to duplication of efforts. Despite the above constraints, piped water is provided to 96.3 per cent of Nairobi, while only 50.3 per cent of residents are serviced by sewage mains. On the other hand, only 42.5 per cent of the city's population has a reliable electricity supply. Private sector involvement in solid waste management (SWM) requires that the above issues be taken into consideration. Planning for billing for services needs to take into account the fact that more people are serviced with piped water than electricity. Payment of services through water billing would certainly cost less to the private sector service providers if the management and administration of water bill collection is improved. The city council has privatized the water billing system in order to improve collection.
ai_rationale: Reports Nairobi water/sewerage coverage data tied to institutional capacity and regulatory constraints.

title: Dilemmas of urban water management; [A települési vízgazdálkodás intézményi dilemmái]
abstract: This study is a "thinking-experiment" on the institutional frames within which an average Hungarian village (Átlagéujfalu-Averagenewvillage) carries out its daily water management activities. The local governments have seven obligatory tasks, among which one is the provision of healthy drinking water to the population. Further 15 tasks are performed in function of the respective local decisions. Among these latter there are two tasks of water management: sewerage and sewage treatment and the collection and drainage of stormwater runoff. The external frames of the operation of the village are as follows: -Legal regulations: In the field of water management activities there are 23 laws, 16 governmental and ministerial decrees to be complied with. In addition there are a respectively high number of financial, taxation, subsidence etc. regulations that should be complied with. -Institutions of the state administration: Organisations and professional institutions, which assure the connection between the local- and central governments. Their number in the field of water management decision making is at least 20. -Budget relationships: In the four main groups of government subsidies there are more than 50 forms of support, rendered to various development policy objectives. Objectives and tools appear in more than hundred lines of the central budget. Overlapping, deco-ordination characterise them and the system of objectives and priorities are non-functional in many respect. -Regional relationships: There are the country level organisations along with a number of smaller-larger regional associations, federations, etc. The activity of central state organs (decrees and supervisory functions of the authorities) is dominated by administrative management rules and by the fiscal aspects. The organised, free-of-charge, professional advisory system of the state is missing. Regional relations are week. The resources of Averagenewvillage cannot cover the handling of extreme situations, such as the defence against local water damages and the village cannot make any important development without the reimbursable subsidence of the state. This system of subsidence may lead to development through large disproportionalities, only (There is no interconnection between the main objectives, such as water supply and sewerage). The result is a gap between water supply and sewage collection and treatment (termed the "public utility scissors" in Hungary). The desirable internal proportions of professional solutions are not warranted (see the disproportionality between sewage collection and treatment, that was formed at certain locations). There are many contradictions between the local- and regional water management activities. There are contradictions even in the field of the otherwise well organised flood defence (for example: how long and to what extent may the local government defend their "summer dikes"?). No guarantee is given for the water saving technological development in the field of public services. In the operation of public water utilities the compliance with the principles of cost-minimising is not a must. The system is not safe. Processes are difficult and obscure, ill-supervised, allowing the realisation of interests other than those of the public. Due to continuous changes (for example the ever growing number of firms operating the public utilities) the sustainability of the institutional system may be questioned. The most serious development dilemmas are as follows: There is no objective method for choosing from the priorities. There is no local financial resource for the development projects. Fund rising defines the procedure and financial liquidity can be secured but hardly. Situations violating the basic long term development aspects and of the rules of public purchases might be created.
ai_rationale: Hungarian village case analyzes legal/institutional framework's effect on water supply/sewerage service gaps.

title: Water Service Delivery In Indonesia: The Case Study of Greater Bandung
abstract: Greater Bandung Area in Indonesia have taken the lead in a City Development Strategy (CDS) exercise. This exercise is supported by the World Bank and the government of Japan, and is partly aimed to improve urban planning and management capabilities of the local governments to ensure more efficient utilization of available resources. The exercise has identified water service delivery as a focus sector, thus creating the setting and background for this thesis research.Various problems faced by the two water companies (the PDAMs) in providing water service delivery to Greater Bandung are common in most PDAMs in Indonesia, leading to weak performance in water provision. The elements of substandard performance include low level of service coverage, poor reliability, low water production and the inability to meet current and future demands.Underlying these problems is a variety of technical, structural and procedural problems. These include inadequate water resource management, operation and maintenance problems (i.e. water production and unaccounted for water), and weak financial and human resource management. This study also identifies a series of legal, institutional and political factors that affect the ability and incentive for PDAMs to perform well.The alternatives to improve water service delivery in Greater Bandung involve implementation of technical reforms, management reforms and capacity building, and institutional reforms. Technical reforms include reforms in water resource management and in operations and maintenance. Management reforms include financial and human resource capacity building. Institutional restructuring, political reforms, private sector participation and improving investment strategies, are among the most important institutional reforms. Design and implementation of these reforms must be consistent with the decentralization policy that is currently evolving in Indonesia, a focal point of the CDS exercise.
ai_rationale: Thesis identifying legal, institutional and political factors affecting water service delivery performance in Bandung, Indonesia.

title: Proposed rule invalidated, then reinstated
abstract: The Florida Waterworks Association (FWA) and Florida Water Services Corp. (FWSC) challenged a proposed rule that would authorize immediate imputation of only 50 percent of projected CIAC against margin reserves. FWA and FWSC maintained that the utilities' margin reserves should never be reduced to reflect CIAC that the utilities receive as part of the service availability fees they collect when connections are made. An administrative law judge invalidated the proposed rule.
ai_rationale: Administrative law ruling on utility margin reserve treatment of connection fee-related charges (CIAC) in Florida.

title: Economics of integrated surface and ground water use management in the Jakarta region, Indonesia
abstract: Rapid population growth, urban development and industrialization in the city of Jakarta have placed increasing pressures on the water resources of the region. Unfortunately, due to inadequate infrastructure, the Jakarta water utility, PAM Jaya, is unable to keep up with the growing demand. The current piped water supply reaches only 27% of the total population, while the rest of the population uses groundwater as their main water source. This occurs due to the lack of enforcement of state ownership, which implies that groundwater is treated as if it were an open access resource. The absence of incentives to conserve groundwater gives rise to externality problems, undervalues the potential economic benefits of conservation and encourages rapid depletion and deterioration of groundwater resources. This study investigates the degree of economic inefficiency of the current institutional arrangements for surface and ground water management in meeting the current and future urban water demand in the Jakarta region. It also assesses some alternative water management scenarios which could improve efficiency, and evaluates the problems of water pricing and the “privatization” of PAM Jaya, Jakarta's water utility. A model of integrated surface and ground water management is developed using an optimal control method. The model maximizes the present value of net social benefits from water consumption across all users over time, from 1999 to 2025. The model is used to examine four policy scenarios: the status quo, the social planner's solution and two groundwater pumping quota scenarios: the aggregate and partial groundwater pumping quota. In each policy scenario, two investment options for PAM Jaya infrastructure are considered: (1) A fixed investment option, representing a fixed annual investment to maintain capital stocks in water treatment and distribution facilities at the current levels, and (2) An optimal investment option, representing the economically optimal investment in both water facilities. Two economic growth assumptions and three real discount rates are assessed in this study. The empirical models are solved using GAMS (General Algebraic Modeling System) software. The empirical results demonstrate that, the status quo over the planning horizon, depending on the investment option, economic growth and the discount rate, results in a 7.4 to 47.8% economic inefficiency relative to the social planner's solution. The aggregate and partial quota scenarios result in lower economic inefficiency compared to the status quo. The partial quota is the most feasible, applicable and manageable scenario. Excluding the costs of monitoring and of enforcement of the groundwater quota, it results in a sizeable economic efficiency gain. The optimal investment option could increase the volume of piped water supply and reduce the cost of water production and raise PAM Jaya's revenues. However, it does not have a significant role in reducing the cumulative groundwater extraction to save the groundwater stock. Investment in water distribution facilities is more productive than investment in water treatment facilities. The volume of water delivery could increase by up to 156% but, this implies only a 35% increase in the surface raw water demands above the current level It is due to significant improvement in water distribution efficiency.
ai_rationale: Economic modeling study showing how lack of enforcement of state groundwater ownership and inadequate institutional arrangements leave only 27% of Jakarta's population with piped water access, forcing reliance on unregulated groundwater.

title: Performance of drinking water and wastewater assistance programs for the United States-Mexico border region
abstract: This study analyzes performance of assistance programs for water and wastewater infrastructure in the U.S.-Mexico border region—the area one hundred kilometers on each side of the international boundary. Since 1965, the region has experienced rapid industrialization and population growth, which have strained its existing water and sewer systems. The programs evaluated are the Economically Distressed Areas Program (EDAP, 1989 through 1998) and the 1995 through 1998 joint activities of the Border Environment Cooperation Commission (BECC) and the North American Development Bank (NADBank). Data was gathered through interviews and reviews of documents and databases. EDAP provides subsidies to water and sewer service providers for construction of systems serving Texas “colonias”—unincorporated subdivisions that lack adequate sewage collection and/or water distribution. EDAP effectively committed grants for projects, but funded projects often failed to improve colonia residents' access to service because many households did not connect to constructed systems and some projects were slow to reach completion. I generate hypotheses linking the performance of individual projects to the incentives and project management capabilities of their service providers. BECC and NADBank, which were created to fulfill promises in the environmental side accord of the North American Free Trade Agreement, provide assistance in developing water and wastewater infrastructure projects in the border region. BECC oversees and certifies the development of projects, while NADBank produces project financing packages. BECC and NADBank have successfully assisted only a few Mexican projects because the institutional framework of water and wastewater projects in Mexico creates obstacles to their development. In contrast, the institutional framework in the U.S. is supportive of BECC and NADBank's activities and has contributed to the certification and financing of projects. EDAP, BECC, and NADBank illustrate differences in how organizations administering programs respond to problems affecting program performance. A program's contribution to the survival of the organization administering it and the organization's core tasks determines the organization's response to problems affecting program performance. The service providers undertaking program-assisted projects, the institutional framework of the programs, and the organizations administering the program together explain variations in program and project performances.
ai_rationale: Empirical evaluation of U.S.-Mexico border drinking water/wastewater assistance programs (EDAP, BECC/NADBank), finding many funded projects failed to improve colonia residents' actual connection to constructed water/sewer systems.

title: The voluntary sector in urban service provision and planning in Nairobi City, Kenya
abstract: Rapid population growth combined with poor planning, weak institutional, financial, and administrative conditions in many Third World cities has undermined many municipal governments' urban management capacity, especially the provision of basic services such as potable water and sanitation. Most of the urban residents with inadequate access to basic public services live in slum and squatter settlements. Traditionally, these residents have relied on informal sector services, which while affordable to many low-income people, are actually costly to the very poor, who constitute a growing segment of the population in slum and squatter settlements. The failure of municipal governments and the informal and/or the private sector to meet poor people's service needs has compelled them to turn to a third alternative—the voluntary sector, i.e., non-governmental and community organizations (NGOs and COs)—collectively referred to as voluntary organizations (VOs). Although the voluntary sector's role in rural development in Africa is widely acknowledged, its work in the continent's urban realm is scarcely understood, despite its increasing activity in this arena, and many scholars' contention that the sector is best suited for the role of meeting poor people's service needs and making urban planning policy more cognizant of their needs. Within the voluntary sector, there are many actors, including NGOs and COs. While the advocacy, intermediary, and community mobilizing role of NGOs is widely known, the role of COs is less appreciated because of the lack of sufficient information on their number, activities, and ability to contribute to development and poverty alleviation (Holmen and Jirstrom 1994). Using the case study of Nairobi City, Kenya, this research project (1) investigated the role of the voluntary sector (including COs) in urban service provision and planning—especially in the promotion of planning and building standards that are suitable to low-income areas); (2) sought to highlight the role of COs; and (3) analyzed several causes of VO effectiveness in these endeavors, including: funding and cost recovery, community composition and participation, service provision experience, use of technology, VO structure and leadership, organizational objectives, State support and cooperation with other VOs. The study's major findings are that the voluntary sector plays an important role in urban service provision and in the promotion of appropriate planning and building standards for low-income areas of Nairobi. Although voluntary organizations' service efforts are overwhelmed by the existing need for services, their contributions do ameliorate service needs in low-income areas. Moreover, even though NGOs are more visible in the literature, this study found that COs are crucial voluntary sector actors and that NGOs and COs are actually complementary, rather than competing, organizational forms. Thus, the most successful service provision initiatives are NGO-CO partnerships that utilize the strengths of each organizational type.
ai_rationale: Study of how the voluntary sector (NGOs/COs) fills institutional/administrative gaps in urban water and sanitation service provision for Nairobi slum residents.

title: Walkerton a risk management nightmare
abstract: While the eventual source of the infection may never be known, there is a suspicion that manure from large farming operations laced with a strain of E.coli 0157:H7 bacteria found its way into Walkerton's drinking water after a torrential downpour on may 12, 2000. According to preliminary press reports, a chlorinator in the water purification system in Walkerton was not working between May 14 and May 16, allowing untreated water to flow to the town. The Walkerton Public Utilities Commission received a fax from A & L Canada Laboratories, its private testing lab, on May 18, 2000, indicating that a water sample showed E.coli contamination. Unfortunately, neither the Ministry of the Environment nor the Public Health Office was notified. Government response, new laws, insurance coverage issues and risk management concerns are they pertain to this incident are discussed.
ai_rationale: Case analysis of the Walkerton E.coli drinking water contamination crisis, including notification/regulatory failures and resulting legal reform.

authors: Beall, Jo; Crankshaw, Owen; Parnell, Susan
title: Victims, villains and fixers: the urban environment and Johannesburg's poor
abstract: Urban water supply, sanitation, & electricity have been identified as basic needs by the postapartheid government & the Greater Johannesburg Metropolitan Council (GJMC). This article explores the relationship of Johannesburg's poor to the urban environment, &, in particular, these three key urban services. On the basis of survey data, case studies, textual analysis & in-depth interviews with policymakers & planners, it reviews how poorer citizens were, for a long time, seen as victims under apartheid urban planning. During the rent boycotts that characterized urban struggle politics during the era of late apartheid in Johannesburg, they were often represented as villains. This perception persisted well into the postapartheid period, where refusing to pay for services was seen as tantamount to a lack of patriotism. Today, Johannesburg's poorer citizens are increasingly being seen as fixers. The GJMC in its policy document, iGoli 2002, is committed to establishing the commercial viability of service delivery. Cost recovery is seen as important for solving the tension that exists between maintaining established service levels (in historically white areas) & extending services to new & historically underserviced (mainly black) areas. We conclude that there are opportunities to address urban poverty, inequality, & environmental management in an integrated way. However, these are predicated on the GJMC & its advisers understanding the ways in which pro-poor & social justice strategies interface with urban services & the urban environment. 11 Tables. Adapted from the source document.
ai_rationale: Survey

title: WORLD BANK: India, World Bank launch series on India's water resources management
abstract: India faces an increasingly urgent situation: its finite  and fragile water resources are stressed and depleting while demand  from various sectors ranging from agriculture to industry are growing  rapidly. Water is rapidly becoming a scarce resource in India yet  continues to be used inefficiently.India Water Resource Management: Initiating and Sustaining Water Sector  Reforms This report is a synthesis of a sector-wide program undertaken  in partnership between the Government of India and the Bank. The report  assesses the existing framework and mechanisms for water resource  allocation and management and focuses on service delivery in the water  sub-sectors--irrigation, urban water supply and sanitation, and rural  water supply and sanitation. It proposes a process for change to build  upon existing positive initiatives, strengthen management capabilities  and processes, and improve the quality of service delivery. It also  provides an action plan of fundamental reforms that are currently  needed in India in how water is captured, allocated between sectors,  delivered to users, and managed. A comprehensive approach is  recommended that simultaneously combines mechanisms in policy,  institutions, legal and regulatory framework, economic and financial  incentive framework and the strengthening data, technological and  information systems.Groundwater is an important source of drinking water and food security  for India's 1 billion inhabitants , supplies 80 percent of water for  domestic use in rural areas and perhaps 50 percent of water for urban  and industrial uses. Over the last three decades, the rapid expansion  in use of groundwater primarily for irrigation has contributed  significantly to agricultural and overall economic development in  India. This rapid development in groundwater, however, has had a price.  In many arid and hard-rock zones, increases in overdraft areas and  associated water-quality problems are emerging. Sustainability of the  resource base is thus critical for meeting an array of basic needs  -from health to economic development. Groundwater cannot be managed in  isolation of critical considerations such as : integration with surface  water; incorporation of water quality, pollution, environment, and  health issues; and a broad array of resource allocation, economic and  social concerns. User involvement is essential for effective  management. The report presents a reform agenda and action plan  concentrating on reorienting the approach to groundwater management,  creation of legal and regulatory mechanisms, reform of institutional  structures and operations and introduction of techniques and incentives  for sustainable groundwater management.
ai_rationale: World Bank sector-wide synthesis report assessing India's institutional

title: The State Civil Society Partnership in the Provision of Water and Sanitation for the Urban Poor: The Case of Kibera, Nairobi
abstract: This dissertation focuses on two main areas with regard to the provision of water and sanitation in informal settlements: First, it examines the weakening of the state in terms of its inability to provide these services to the poor, and the effects of this weakening on state-civil society relations. Second, it documents the activities of all actors involved in service provision with the aim of demonstrating the extent of change in service delivery strategies, and then places these changes within a theoretical context that captures the role of the respective agencies and groups. These issues are explored using the case of Kibera squatter settlement in Nairobi, Kenya. The study is based on survey data of 534 household heads in Kibera. Using the survey data, the study employs logistic regression analysis to examine the factors that influence accessibility to water supply and sanitation services in informal settlements. The survey data is supplemented by secondary data from documents published by the Kenyan government, and project reports from the Nairobi City Council and non-governmental organizations involved in the provision of water and sanitation. The study reveals that access chances to potable water are affected by cost to the user of the available water points. With regard to participation in water supply and sanitation initiatives, the reliability of the water sources was found to be an important determinant of the residents' willingness to be involved in communal water and sanitation projects. The study shows that in Nairobi, as in other Third World cities, the provision of water and sanitation is increasingly being organized through a mixture of public and private systems. It further demonstrates the importance of non-state actors in providing an effective link between the poor and state agencies by articulating the needs of the poor to the government.
ai_rationale: Survey-based logistic regression study of state-civil society partnerships shaping water and sanitation accessibility, cost, and reliability for households in Kibera, Nairobi's informal settlements.

title: Water, Power and Gender: Pressing Questions and Overlooked Interests in a Poor and Crowded Delta
abstract: Because of the prominence of water in production (primarily for irrigation) & in domestic use (drinking, washing, cooking), conflict over water & the effects of gender-influenced decisions about water have far-reaching consequences on human well-being, economic growth, & social change. At the same time, social conflicts & social change are shaped & mediated, often in unexpected ways, by the natural conditions in which water occurs. This paper examines some of the issues relating water & gender in the particular social & environmental conditions of Bangladesh. First, extraction of groundwater for irrigation has made many drinking water handpumps run dry. Second, this irrigation extraction has also been associated with the poisoning of at least 20 million people through the release of naturally occurring arsenic into the groundwater. Third, the paper examines some of the ways access to water has been changed by the rise of shrimp aquaculture for export. The literature has tended to focus on the implications of gender analysis for government policy, especially development projects & water resources management, & for women's organization. In this paper, we begin to sketch some questions that arise from a concern to understand the tripartite interaction of gender, water, & power in the broader context of social change.
ai_rationale: Analysis of how groundwater extraction for irrigation/aquaculture and government water-resource policy in Bangladesh have reduced drinking-water handpump access, with gender implications.

title: Public infrastructure and private costs: Water supply and time allocation of women in rural Pakistan
abstract: How the quality and quantity of infrastructure affect the time women allocate to their various activities is investigated. How variations in the water infrastructure's quality - at both the household and community levels - relate to differences in time allocated by rural women to market-oriented activities, water collection and leisure is discussed. The case study focuses on Pakistan, where a large proportion of the population lives in poverty and where there exists a significant gender gap in education as well as labor force participation. The results indicate that improvements in Pakistan's public water supply infrastructure, women increase the time that they allocate to income-generating activities.
ai_rationale: Case study of how quality/quantity of public water-supply infrastructure affects rural Pakistani women's time allocation between income-generating work and water collection.

title: Equity and access to basic services : Issues and options
abstract: Infrastructure and services are the most important factors determining the quality of environment of urban settlements. With the fast growth of urban population, there has been increasing need to expand the infrastructure and services at a rapid rate. Further, the slum population is growing twice as fast as the general rate of growth of the urban areas. Therefore, problems of providing services to the economically weaker sections assumed much importance. This paper analyses the present production and distribution strategies and their impact on the delivery of the economic and social services to the economically weaker sections of the society and raises issues in terms of pricing strategies, norms and standards, legal framework and the administrature machinery for planning and distribution.
ai_rationale: Analysis of pricing strategies, legal framework, and administrative machinery governing delivery of basic urban infrastructure/services (including water) to economically weaker sections.

title: Testing Community Empowerment Strategies in Zimbabwe: Examples from Nutrition Supplementation, and Water Supply and Sanitation Programmes
abstract: Provides a brief overview & examples of how communities were involved in feeding programs during years of drought in Zimbabwe & in the management of rural water supply & sanitation programs throughout the 1980s. The balance between political & technical demands in the implementation of these programs indicates that they started off with community interests at the center, but gradually gave way to the needs of the bureaucracy (both political & administrative). The main lesson to be learned from these programs is that information on entitlements & obligations (on the part of communities & external agencies) is a prerequisite for successful community development projects. Further, the extent of accountability to communities is directly proportional to progress made toward the devolution of power to democratic development structures, be they directly or indirectly elected. 2 Tables, 1 Figure, 10 References. Adapted from the source document.
ai_rationale: Case examples of community empowerment strategies in Zimbabwe's rural water supply and sanitation programmes, examining the balance between community interests and administrative/political bureaucracy.

title: Urban poverty in India: Issues and perspectives in development
abstract: The present paper examines the trends in rural and urban poverty, analyses the interstate variations and explains these in terms of socio-economic factors. It shows that rural poverty declines smoothly with economic development, which unfortunately is not the case with urban poverty. The availability of water supply, toilets and electricity, that are not explicitly incorporated in the official definition of poverty, has also been analysed at the state level as also across size class of urban settlements. It is argued that the small and medium towns have a weak and unstable economic base. As a consequence, most of these are not in a position to generate funds to provide civic services to all sections of population. These towns, particularly those located in less developed states, should, therefore, be the major concern of government policy. Further, overviewing the changing system of governance, it argues that the seventy-fourth Constitutional Amendment, has not succeeded in genuine empowerment of civic bodies. The power now seems to have shifted from the state governments to the financial institutions, international donors and credit rating agencies. Finally, the capacity of the government to generate employment directly through anti-poverty programmes would remain limited. The paper, therefore, recommends that the anti-poverty programmes should primarily be focussed on provision of basic amenities.
ai_rationale: Study of urban poverty in India examining availability of water supply and toilets alongside governance/decentralization (74th Constitutional Amendment) and municipal finance capacity.

title: Why women stay poor: An examination of urban poverty in India
abstract: In this paper the relationship of women to poverty in urban areas is explored and the need to understand the gender dimension of poverty in a specific cultural context is emphasised. In recent years there has been an increasing trend to incorporate the gender dimension in the analysis of poverty. The féminisation of poverty is a term used to describe the overwhelming representation of women among the poor. The present study examines the gender bias of poverty which underlies the social and economic subordination of women and the effects of gender on access to basic amenities such as education, health care and labour force participation. The 1996 World Bank publication, Poverty Reduction and the World Bank, identified three components to urban poverty: 1) provision of basic services such as water, sanitation, drainage and roads; 2) taking action on the top threats to health (lead, dust and microbial diseases); 3) making municipal finance more businesslike and inclusive. While these are commendable objectives, the problems of urban poverty for women can be examined in a qualitative way from the point view of how these goals are absorbed into the social and cultural surroundings of the urban poor. Why women are more vulnerable to poverty will be considered here and how the causes and experience of poverty differ by gender are determined, followed by some remarks on how to alleviate women's poverty.
ai_rationale: Discussion of gendered urban poverty in India, examining access to basic services (water, sanitation, drainage) within the World Bank poverty-reduction framework.

title: Housing poverty in urban India
abstract: In this paper an attempt has been made to understand the nature, extent and causes of housing poverty in India. Housing stock, new household formation, homelessness, type of structure, number of rooms and households, slums and squatter settlements, housing investment, housing affordability, ownership occupancy, water connection and toilets have been taken as indicators of housing poverty. The paper is based on secondary sources. It concludes that mainly critically poor, low income groups and low middle income groups are suffering from housing poverty. The main causes of housing poverty is existing socio-economic and political systems and unrealistic and insensitive attitude of ruling elite towards the growing needs of poor in growing cities. There is lack of political will rather than the resources. The need of hour is strong political will for comprehensive understanding of phenomenon and enhancement of human capabilities with public action and democratic government support.
ai_rationale: Secondary-data study of housing poverty in urban India using indicators including water connection and toilets, attributing causes to socio-economic/political systems and lack of political will.

authors: Bradshaw, York W; Schafer, Mark J
title: Urbanization and Development: The Emergence of International Nongovernmental Organizations amid Declining States
abstract: Tests the 1975-1990 impact of international nongovernmental organizations (INGOs) on three interrelated measures of Third World urbanization & development: overurbanization, economic growth, & access to safe water. The results show that INGOs slow overurbanization & promote economic & social development. It is argued that inclusion of NGOs in the literature is necessary & even compatible with several current theories of development. 4 Tables, 1 Appendix, 43 References. Adapted from the source document.
ai_rationale: Panel study testing INGO impact on Third World urbanization, growth, and access to safe water (1975-1990).

title: Watering the Garden of Tangier: Colonial Contestations in a Moroccan City
abstract: In the late 19th century, Tangier became the site of competing ideas about how to modernize the city. Foreign residents wanted to create new kinds of public services unknown in the traditional medina, while Moroccans resisted efforts to wrest away control of their municipality. This clash is explored through a discussion of the water system of Tangier and efforts to modernize it. Moroccans opposed innovation not only to thwart European political and economic interests, but also to preserve a system of values threatened by technologies beyond their control. 3 Figures, 36 References. Adapted from the source document.
ai_rationale: Historical case study of colonial contestation over water system control and modernization in Tangier.

title: Privatising Water in the Driest State: The Impacts on Employees and Industrial Relations of the Corporatisation and Outsourcing of Metropolitan Water and Sewerage Services in South Australia
abstract: The South Australian government's 1995 decision to corporatize & outsource its metropolitan water services to transnational corporations was the first privatization of a major water service system in Australia. The government's rationale for outsourcing included claimed cost savings delivered through a reduced workforce. Claims of increased efficiency & improved services lacked credibility following scandals in the contract process & a major sewerage treatment failure following outsourcing. These events fueled strong public opinion against outsourcing & chastened the industrial relations approach. This was less radical than movements taken by the federal & Victorian governments, both of which combined outsourcing with attempts to deunionize workers using new industrial relations legislation. Unions' participation in the public debate strengthened their bargaining position & they were able to reorganize in the new context. The companies reduced workforce numbers but negotiated employment conditions through collective bargaining. Water privatization remains a high-risk political strategy for governments. 1 Appendix, 59 References. Adapted from the source document.
ai_rationale: Study of the corporatization/outsourcing of metropolitan water and sewerage services in South Australia and resulting industrial relations and service-failure impacts.

title: The Impact of Public-Private Partnerships as an Approach to Social Delivery on Environmental Conservation and Protection
abstract: Following an overview of the development challenges facing the democratic government of postapartheid South Africa, its Reconstruction & Development Program is described, focusing on four main concerns: (1) poverty alleviation, (2) economic reconstruction, (3) human resource development, & (4) democratization. Estimates on the amount of infrastructure investment required to reach development goals are presented, revealing the unlikelihood of having these needs met by the government alone. A plan for the development of municipal service partnerships between the government & the private sector is outlined, & its implementation at the local provincial & national levels is described; an in-depth case study is provided of the Dolphin Coast Water Concession & its management of water & sanitation resources & services. A comment is offered by Diana Mitlin. 2 Tables. K. Hyatt Stewart
ai_rationale: Empirical case study of a South African water-and-sanitation concession (Dolphin Coast) delivered via a public-private municipal partnership, examining governance of service delivery.

title: Urban Economic Growth, Infrastructure and Poverty in India: Lessons from Visakhapatnam
abstract: Describes the rapid economic growth in Visakhapatnam, India, drawing on a case study (Kumar, 1998/99) & research on Indian slum improvement projects (Kumar; Rajan, Lalita; & Rajan, Vithal, 1996/97). How the city's further growth is constrained by inadequate investment in infrastructure -- especially for water & electricity -- is discussed, along with the political & institutional reasons for this. Presented are findings of participatory research on poverty & the many dimensions of poverty that are emphasized by urban poor groups, including inadequate incomes, lack of assets ("no shelter, no property, no gold"), lack of support (especially for widows, deserted women, & the handicapped), illness, & debt. The direct & indirect impacts on poverty of a Dept for International Development slum improvement project are discussed, showing which improvements low-income groups particularly appreciate. This demonstrates the importance of infrastructure & service provision to poverty reduction. 4 Tables, 2 Figures, 1 Box. Adapted from the source document.
ai_rationale: Case study of Visakhapatnam, India, examining how inadequate water infrastructure investment and institutional/political constraints affect urban poverty and service access.

title: An integrated approach to wastewater treatment: Deciding where, when, and how much to invest
abstract: In spite of the large sums invested in wastewater management systems in recent years (up to 1 percent of gross domestic product (GDP) in European countries), untreated discharges from municipal, industrial, and agricultural activities continue to contaminate waterways and coastal areas on all continents. Controlling water pollution is expensive. Even higher- income countries have a hard time mobilizing resources to expand the coverage of sound wastewater disposal, and to operate and maintain the new facilities. In developing countries, there is an even greater premium on ensuring that every dollar works harder. This is best done in a decentralized environment, with responsibility at the lowest appropriate level, stake-holder involvement, private participation in service delivery, and the use of market and regulatory signals. The challenge is how to reconcile this decentralization with a coherent framework for managing water resources across sectors, at the river basin level. This paper looks at the experience of four higher-income countries (France, Germany, Spain, and the United States) in managing wastewater at the river basin level. Each of them has gone through three stages: uncoordinated local management first, then a decentralized approach with a lead planning and facilitation agency to help set priorities at the river basin level, and more recently a move toward uniform disposal standards. The paper concludes that the first stage has led to inefficiencies, as well as gaps in coverage, and the third-stage 'blanket' approach gives poor value-for-money - a second-stage approach would be more effective for capital-scarce economies. Recent experiences in developing and transition countries are assessed against this framework. The paper then maps a process by which a 'stage two' approach could be implemented in a river basin: the role and design of a lead water resource agency, the planning and goals-setting process, and how stakeholders are involved. This is not meant to serve as a blueprint - the process would need tailoring to each country - but rather a useful checklist of issues to be addressed and possible ways to handle them. While the paper focuses on institutional arrangements, it also flags areas that call for complementary work: for instance, how the river agency might use markets (water trading) and price incentives (environmental taxes and grants) to convey agreed priorities to water users. Practitioners in government, donor agencies, and the private sector will find this paper a useful contribution to an urgent debate.
ai_rationale: Comparative institutional analysis of river-basin wastewater management decentralization stages and their effect on sanitation coverage in four countries.

title: Water for everybody?; [De l'eau pour tous?]
abstract: The experience that Lyonnaise des Eaux has acquired in its contracts in Argentina has shown up the problem of serving districts with low financial resources, under the general conditions of a contract which does not take into account the capacity to pay of the poorest populations. As this problem is also encountered in the contracts of La Paz, Manila, Jakarta, Casablanca etc., it was urgent to undertake a reflection on the subject. A project was financed in 1997. Before tackling the heart of the subject, it is useful to recall some basic ideas forming the basis of the reflection. One can observe a substantial increase in the number of cities with populations of more than a million: 157 in 1975, 320 in 2000. It is estimated that a large part of the people without access to drinking water or sanitation (1000 million and 2900 million respectively) live in underprivileged urban environments. In underprivileged districts, the technical impossibility (no roads or even any trace of them), the institutional impossibility (occupation of the land which is often illegal) and the financial impossibility (cost of a normal type of supply by a network with connections, relative to the population's capacity to pay) of providing in the short term a conventional water supply and sanitation service to the populations concerned constitute a considerable problem. The report proposes an approach wich best allows the situation of underprivileged districts to be dealt with. This approach may be summarized as follows: Development of appropriate contracts, Integration of the problem of underprivileged districts into the Master Plan as far upstream as possible, Implementation of transitory and progressive solutions.
ai_rationale: Examines institutional/financial/legal barriers to water/sanitation access in poor urban districts.

title: Urban water policy in Mexico: Municipalization and privatization of water services
abstract: Mexico's urbanization, development and democratization processes have demanded a transformation in the water supply and sanitation service, from a centralized, subsidy-dependent, and politically-mediated arrangement into a new profile. Policy questions include the traits of the new arrangement and how to implement them. The constitutional reform of article 115 in 1983 proposed municipalization, i.e. the transfer of water and sanitation services from federal to municipal control, as a new management arrangement. This broad urban services rearrangement, however, did not provide the necessary support to build the institutional capacity of municipalities. By 1988, only one third of the 31 Mexican states had municipalized the service. Efficiency indicators show that municipalization has not improved service. Since 1989, the National Water Commission (CNA) has been proposing a new strategy of autonomous, self-sufficient service, open to private participation. Legal reforms were made by most Mexican states to adopt this new profile. Statistics show that there has been progress in service coverage, revenue collection, and water control during the 1990s. Nonetheless, case-study research shows that CNA's campaign for water service efficiency also requires local democratic governance (legitimacy, transparency and accountability), civic participation, and bottom-up support. If these local requirements are missing, the restructuring of water services is likely to face user resistance and opposition. Mexicali is a good example of service restructuring with local support, while Hermosillo is a case in which lack of transparency and social participation have contributed to the failure of service restructuring. Thus, political pluralism and alternancia (the possibility of switching between political parties in government) appear to be necessary conditions of service restructuring. In addition, Aguascalientes and Cancun, the pioneer cases of private participation, have faced considerable obstacles due to the 1995 financial crisis. In both cases, the private contract was revised before it had been in effect for two years. Thus, local political conditions, social participation, and a stable economic context are critical elements for the success of the restructuring of urban water services.
ai_rationale: Study of municipalization and privatization legal/policy reforms and their effect on Mexican urban water service coverage.

title: The Role of Private Vending in Developing Country Water Service Delivery: The Case of Karachi, Pakistan
abstract: The private water vending industry in Karachi is an important source of water service delivery in Karachi, Pakistan. Water vending is largely a supplemental service to households with private water connections, due to limited service from the public utility. This research attempts to:i) Characterize the existing water supply situation in Karachi, with particular focus on the water vending industry;ii) Evaluate the extent to which water vending in Karachi affects households' water supply situation and generates excessive profits for vendors; andiii) Assess possible strategies for water sector reform in Karachi.The case of Karachi, where water vending coexists with a piped supply network, poses a challenge to policy makers in water supply planning. The study shows that the major clients of vended water in the city are those who have water connections, storage capacity, and the ability to buy water.The key findings of the study are:i) Karachi's water vending market may not be economically efficient. Although the vending market provides only 9% of the water consumed by city residents on a daily basis, it earns almost 50% of all revenues received from water.ii) Groundwater supplying households' wells and private hydrants is not recognized as a common property resource by the concerned public agencies. As a result, existing government policy fails to address the consequences of unregulated groundwater use by private individuals.iii) Surprisingly, a market for vended water exists even in a city where more than 3/4 of all households are served by piped water connections. When levels of the public utility's service are low - in this case an average of 3 hours of service each day - households are forced to turn to other sources to meet their water supply needs.In view of these findings, there appears to be a need for regulatory reforms. The study proposes the adoption of a dual strategy to solve the problem of rent seeking by hydrant owners in Karachi: regulation, and promotion of competition.
ai_rationale: Study of informal private water vending and regulatory/reform implications for water service delivery in Karachi.

title: INDIA: Demand for water charges on amended regulation stayed
abstract: THE Karnataka High Court has admitted Writ Petitions filed, challenging the validity of Notification No. CH/CAO-S/98- 99, dated 6.10.98 issued by the Bangalore Water Supply and Sewerage Board (BWSSB), which inter alia provides that consumers having water supply connections of size 20mm and above to their premises (excluding residential apartments) shall be charged for the minimum quantity specified against each size, or the actual consumption, whichever is higher.
ai_rationale: Court case report on a legal challenge to Bangalore Water Supply Board's water charge regulation for consumers.

title: Social Policies in Brazil: Decentralization in a Federal State
abstract: Analyzes the decentralization process of the Brazilian system of social protection, identifying its extension & variation, as well as the determining factors of its current state. Focus is on five social policies -- public health, education, sanitation, housing, & social welfare -- in the states of Rio Grande do Sul, Parana, Sao Paulo, Bahia, Pernambuco, & Ceara. The following factors' roles in determining the extension & the variation of decentralization are considered: (1) structural characteristics -- economic, fiscal, & administrative capabilities -- of local governments; (2) institutional characteristics -- constitutional rules, operational mechanisms of service delivery, & the legacy of earlier policies -- of the policies; & (3) variables related to political action -- state-society relations & intergovernmental relations. 5 Tables, 5 Graphs, 70 References. Adapted from the source document.
ai_rationale: Comparative Brazilian state study of decentralization determinants (structural

title: India: Improve incentives to urban water systems: IBRD
abstract: THE World Bank is in favour of improving the incentives to India's Urban Water Supply and Sanitation (UWSS) sector through "appropriate democratic governance, ownership and management structures and through appropriate financing systems".In a sector review on water resources management prepared by the Bank's rural development unit in its South Asia Region mission here in cooperation with the Ministry of Urban Affairs & Employment and UK Department for International Development (DFID), it said India's UWSS sector confronts a heap of problems and is currently bound up by a vicious circle of circumstances.Thus, it said, many UWSS providers are not financially viable and are unable to maintain services without extensive subsidies, while existing UWSS services fall woefully short of full coverage of the population and are often of "low quality due to insufficient funding of operation and management".
ai_rationale: News synthesis of a World Bank sector review on governance

title: An emerging logic of urban water management, Cochabamba, Bolivia
abstract: This paper examines the emergence of a new logic of water management in developing cities.  We argue that water provision is characterised by two largely disconnected circuits of water supply.
ai_rationale: Case study of the emergence of a new urban water management logic and disconnected water supply circuits in Cochabamba, Bolivia.

title: Risky business: An analysis of claimsmaking in the development of an Ontario drinking water objective for tritium
abstract: On December 22, 1994, the Minister of Environment and Energy for Ontario announced an interim Ontario Drinking Water Objective for tritium (a radioactive waste product released into drinking water supplies during nuclear power production) of 7,000 Bq/L.  The Minister's decision overrode the advice of his own advisory committee which had recommended a much lower level (100 Bq/L).
ai_rationale: Case study of the regulatory claims-making process behind Ontario's drinking water quality objective for tritium, including the Minister overriding the advisory committee's recommended standard.

title: Water supply, waste disposal, and the culture of privatism in the mid-nineteenth-century American City
abstract: Relatively few midcentury urbanites enjoyed access to centrally managed waterworks that provided running water through mains.  Water supply, waste disposal and the culture of privatism in the mid-nineteenth century American city are discussed.
ai_rationale: Historical study of mid-19th-century American cities showing how a culture of administrative privatism limited residents' access to centrally managed municipal waterworks.

authors: Van Vugt, Mark; Samuelson, Charles D
title: The Impact of Personal Metering in the Management of a Natural Resource Crisis: A Social Dilemma Analysis
abstract: A field study & scenario study entailing questionnaire responses from 80 residents of Hampshire, England, investigated the impact of a structural solution in the management of a natural resource dilemma that had affected the county in summer 1995: the effects of individual metering in a water shortage. Consistent with expectations, results revealed that conservation efforts were greater among metered (vs unmetered) participants when they perceived the water shortage as severe. Additional analyses suggested that the positive effects of metering could be partially explained by a greater concern with the collective costs of overconsumption during the drought. It is concluded that structural solutions such as metering may produce concomitant effects that extend beyond the outcome structure of the social dilemma. 5 Figures, 43 References. Adapted from the source document.
ai_rationale: Field/scenario study of the impact of individual water metering (a structural/regulatory tool) on household conservation behavior during a 1995 water shortage in Hampshire, England.

title: Promoting Clean Water in Nineteenth-Century Public Policy: Professors, Preachers, and Polliwogs in Kingston, Ontario
abstract: A case study of Kingston, Ontario, reveals that growing confidence in the response of science & statistics to the threat of epidemic disease supported the development & expansion of municipal water & sewer services in the late 19th century. Informed by science & statistics, professional city managers & sanitary experts sought solutions combining fiduciary responsibility with public service. Preliminary evidence also suggests that, in some cases, Protestant-inspired rhetoric contributed to this support for new sanitary measures. 1 Table, 1 Figure. Adapted from the source document.
ai_rationale: Historical case study of institutional/professional development of municipal water and sewer services in Kingston, Ontario.

title: Small-Scale Entrepreneurs in the Urban Water and Sanitation Market
abstract: Describes the importance of small-scale, private-sector or nongovernmental organization providers of water & sanitation in urban areas in Africa, Asia, & Latin America, illustrated by examples of -- contrary to conventional wisdom -- good-quality, low-cost services. Without these operations, large sections of the South's urban populations, including tens of millions of low-income households, would be worse off. Yet, these entities generally operate with no subsidy & have to recover their costs. Discussed here is how public policy can support (or at least not seriously constrain) small-scale entrepreneurs in water & sanitation provision, while ensuring checks on the quality & price of the services they provide. 3 Boxes, 15 References. Adapted from the source document.
ai_rationale: Discussion of small-scale private/NGO water and sanitation providers serving low-income urban households and the public policy needed to support them.

title: Excavation water harvesting in Sudano-Sahelian Nigeria: Problems and prospects
abstract: Excavation water resources in Sudano-Sahelian Nigeria were investigated through user and use surveys in some communities in Borno, Bauchi, Kano, Jigawa and Yobe states. It was found that water harvesting from these sources was a new experience in the study communities. Water from excavation reservoirs are used for various purposes in the communities with domestic, irrigation, commercial (e.g hawking and laundering), recreational and industrial (e.g brick making and food processing) and animal watering being the principal uses. Harvesting of excavation water has brought much relief relative prosperity and security to dependent communities through the extension of water supply in time and space. However, the harvesting of water from these newly found sources is fret with some conflicts. There exist two main types of conflicts: conflict between incompatible uses; and user conflicts. Conflicts between uses results from the fact that certain uses preclude others by rendering the resource unsuitable for other uses because quality is compromised. In-water animal watering and domestic uses are classic examples of incompatible uses found in the communities. User conflicts are caused by competition for access to resources, and sensitivity to uses that impair water quality and exclude other desirable uses.
