In 1889 and 1924, respectively, the cities abandoned municipal water and sewer networks for metropolitan systems which crossed county lines and were administered by semi-autonomous regional agencies. The new regional public works united each city with its suburban neighbors, creating new political units and permitting Boston and Oakland to overcome the environmental limits on their continued growth and prosperity. However, urban expansion and the centralization of power associated with regionalism also decreased voter oversight of public works and water resource policy, and spread the environmental costs of urbanization far beyond metropolitan boundaries.Regionalism succeeded because environmental crises precipitated a powerful consensus in favor of new public works construction, and because regional agencies balanced political reform with protections for municipal institutions. The new agencies concentrated power in the hands of a bureaucratic elite, but permitted elected officials to improve services without raising taxes. The popularity of regional public works allowed reformers to implement aspects of broader social and political agendas. Furthermore, the new services increased cities' access to water resources and, in so doing, permitted considerable urban growth in both Boston and Oakland. These similarities do not overshadow the very real differences between these communities, but rather highlight the significance of regionalism and of environmental crisis in urban history.This study addresses aspects of American politics and the environment not frequently invoked by current historiography. It combines resource allocation questions from environmental history with political history's attention to electoral process, government growth and reform ideology. This approach yields a perspective on political reform that highlights the unique contributions of public reactions to the urban environment and constituent demand for public services.
ai_rationale: Historical institutional case study of how Boston and Oakland created regional public works agencies to overcome contaminated drinking water and water shortages limiting municipal water/sewer service.

title: Impact of the 1986 Amendments to the Safe Drinking Water Act on the state of Mississippi
abstract: The 1986 Amendments to the Safe Drinking Water Act are complex regulations that could result in a significant economic impact on the public water systems (PWS) of Mississippi. Analyses for the contaminants will not affect the PWS since the Mississippi State Department of Health, Division of Water Supply (DWS) performs this service for $1.10 per service connection. No PWS is exceeding the MCL for any regulated volatile organic chemical, pesticide, organic chemical, or inorganic chemicals, except for lead and copper. Ninety-four PWS are out of compliance with the Lead and Copper Rule. Forty-nine of these PWS failed to monitor, 26 PWS and 19 PWS exceeded the action level for lead and copper, respectively. The Total Coliform Rule will have a dramatic impact and the Surface Water Treatment Rule will have no impact on the PWS. The DWS will not be able to continue its sampling, analytical, and technical services if increased funding and staffing are not made available.
ai_rationale: Analysis of Safe Drinking Water Act amendment impacts on public water system compliance in Mississippi.

title: Sanitary services and decision making in Houston, 1876-1945
abstract: In the late 19th century and early 20th century, city leaders in Houston had responded promptly to perceived community needs for a safe and plentiful water supply, an effective sewer system and practical solid waste disposal facilities, although services were not always delivered equitably.  By the 1940s, however, Houston's environmental infrastructure faltered, deficient in scale and kind to keep pace with the city's rapid expansion.
ai_rationale: Historical study of municipal decision-making on water supply and sewer service delivery (and its inequities) in Houston, 1876-1945.

title: Water Markets, Market Reform and the Urban Poor: Results from Jakarta, Indonesia
abstract: About 20% of the population of Jakarta, Indonesia, receive water from municipal water connections to their homes. Remaining supplies are private & include street vendors, standpipes, & wells. An expansion of the network of in-house connections is in progress, but will take several decades to complete. In the interim, various strategies have been advanced to deal with persistent problems of access to good water by the poor. Here, 1991 interview data collected from 291 residents in north Jakarta are used to examine the impacts of one such plan -- the Apr 1990 deregulation measure permitting private homes with water connections to resell municipal water. Findings show that the primary social benefits of deregulation are the money savings & increased consumption by former vendor & standpipe customers. 5 Tables, 1 Figure, 1 Appendix, 37 References. Adapted from the source document.
ai_rationale: Study of water-market deregulation and resale effects on poor households' access in Jakarta.

title: Management of Water Supply and Sanitation Projects in Maharashtra State, India
abstract: A field report shows the positive practical effects of teaching applied social sciences to technicians & students. As part of a course at Bradford U (England) on "Management of Water Supply & Sanitation in Rural Areas," 12 participants (mostly chief engineers) were divided into 3 groups that studied a water supply project, sanitation in drought-susceptible villages, & the financial sustainability of water supply projects in Maharashtra State, India. Participants learned that water consumption in rural villages was below recommended levels & that sanitation & environmental pollution threatened rural economies. Their recommendations were expansion of village water committees to cover sanitation & involvement of more local people, especially women & the poor, at the grass-roots level. E. Blackwell
ai_rationale: Field report on a training course studying rural water supply and sanitation project management, financial sustainability and community involvement in Maharashtra, India.

title: Household Demand for Improved Water and Sanitation in a Large Secondary City. Findings from a Study in Gujranwala, Pakistan
abstract: Assesses municipal service provision in Gujranwala, the fastest growing city in Pakistan. Data from 968 questionnaires document household responses to inadequate water & sanitation services. The demand for improved municipal services is estimated using the contingent valuation method. About 53% of the city's households are connected to the public piped water system, & about 40% are served by public sewer lines. Unconnected households are installing WCs, & unserved neighborhoods are discharging effluent into local ponds. These environmentally unsound & economically inefficient alternatives suggest that a large-scale extension of the public waterway system could result in net economic savings, & that attention to demand-side information about household priorities & preferences could provide valuable input in the planning process. 4 Tables, 1 Appendix. Adapted from the source document.
ai_rationale: Household survey of demand for improved municipal water/sanitation connections in Gujranwala, Pakistan, including connection rates.

title: Promoting Community Based Approaches to Social Infrastructure Provision in Urban Areas in Nigeria
abstract: Identifies inadequacies in the provision of social infrastructure (ie, schools, health care facilities, water, & sanitation) in urban areas of Nigeria, noting the traditions of self-help & community organization & changes over the precolonial to postcolonial periods. Case studies are given for an urban center from each of Nigeria's main regions: Lagos, Kaduna, & Umuahia. Possibilities for improving infrastructure & service provision & the institutional changes they imply are considered, & areas for further research suggested. 5 Figures. Adapted from the source document.
ai_rationale: Case studies of community-based social infrastructure provision, including water and sanitation, in Lagos, Kaduna, and Umuahia, Nigeria, with institutional analysis.

title: Problems in the Planning of Rural Water Supply Projects: Lessons from Nkayi District, Zimbabwe
abstract: Data from 5 months of fieldwork in Zimbabwe suggest that rural water supply projects need to widen their approach. Projects often fail to consider the multiple uses of water (eg, cleaning, watering small livestock), use of multiple water sources, the place of water management within the larger whole of rural resource management, previous use patterns, & past state provision of or interference with water. In Zimbabwe, women, children, & small animals are the main users of wells, & men & cattle the main users of boreholes. Thus, clean drinking water in wells does not mean that men will drink clean water exclusively. Water supplies were previously used to further government resettlement policies of moving blacks off European-held lands, making many suspicious when asked to volunteer for water source upkeep. Knowledge of such situations can help in the design & promotion of sustainable projects. 4 References. E. Blackwell
ai_rationale: Fieldwork study of rural water supply project planning in Nkayi, Zimbabwe, showing how past state resettlement policy and provision history shaped community trust and water source use.

authors: Hoque, Bilqis Amin; Hoque, Mohammed Mozzammel
title: Partnership in Rural Water Supply and Sanitation: A Case Study from Bangladesh
abstract: Presents results from a 2-year rural Water Supply & Sanitation (WSS) project in rural Bangladesh. Implemented by nongovernmental organizations (NGOs), the project was intended to provide low cost technology for water & sanitation, achieve better collaboration between agencies in water & sanitation services, & raise community consciousness of the importance of safe water use & hygiene. Handpumps, latrines, & hygiene education were provided to rural people through NGO partners. Data obtained during field visits reveal a lack of community participation, personal hygiene practices, & effective use & maintenance of the WSS provisions. However, the effectiveness of a multiagency approach in providing technologies to an unserved population in an efficient way, was demonstrated. Principal challenges to be addressed include the training of individuals & improvement of hygiene practices. Multiagency cooperation will be needed. 1 Table, 14 References. Adapted from the source document.
ai_rationale: Field study of an NGO-implemented rural water supply and sanitation partnership project in Bangladesh, examining multiagency effectiveness in reaching an unserved population.

title: Public Health and the Water Crisis in the Occupied Palestinian Territories
abstract: Statistical data indicate that, in contrast to Israeli settlers, Palestinians' access to adequate, clean water supplies is severely restricted by Israeli military authorities in the occupied Palestinian territories. Many West Bank & Gaza Strip communities have no piped water for domestic use, & available water supplies are often contaminated by infective microorganisms & chemical pollutants. As a result, the Palestinian population is at serious risk for exposure to high levels of salt, chemical toxins, & parasitic organisms that cause a variety of intestinal diseases. Children are most vulnerable, since malnutrition exacerbates the long-term effects of disease on growth, development, & health. AA
ai_rationale: Study of Palestinians' severely restricted access to adequate clean water under Israeli military authority in the occupied territories, and resulting health impacts.

title: Sudanese Refugees in Koboko: Environmental Health Interventions
abstract: Described is the process of developing springs from swampland & installing water collection chambers & tapstands to provide urgently needed water & sanitation for the large population of Sudanese refugees in Koboko (Uganda). The assistance of native women trained as spring technicians was essential to interpret actions of the refugees & educate them to use the system. Committees of both men & women were formed to maintain the tapstands efficiently, keep the area dry, & promote hygiene. V. Wagener
ai_rationale: Description of spring/tapstand water and sanitation infrastructure development with community committee management for Sudanese refugees in Uganda.

title: Implementing Urban Development Projects: A Search for Criteria for Success
abstract: Six possible constraints to successful implementation of urban plans & projects are identified: organizational issues, resource scarcity, lack of cultural understanding, technology, the potential exclusion of the target population from the planning & implementation process, & the political environment. Two examples of planning implementation are considered: (1) a squatter resettlement scheme implemented in Mirpur, Dhaka, Bangladesh, 1977-1990; & (2) a water development program in Tegucigalpa, Honduras. Whereas the Bangladesh project experienced serious implementation problems, the path to completion of the Honduran project appears to have been much smoother. An evaluation of the two projects in terms of the six implementation constraints identified is provided. Adapted from the source document.
ai_rationale: Comparative evaluation of implementation constraints including a water development program in Tegucigalpa, Honduras.

title: Rent‐extracting behavior by multiple agents in the provision of municipal water supply: A study of Jakarta, Indonesia
abstract: A framework is presented for the analysis of rent‐extracting behavior by multiple agents involved in the provision of municipal water supplies in Jakarta, Indonesia. It is shown that such behavior can dramatically affect the terms and conditions under which water service is offered to the public. A water supply system based on limited numbers of public taps, relatively few house connections, and water vendors can generate substantial monopoly rents that can be appropriated by both public and private agents. Most professionals involved with water supply projects in developing countries typically assume that the objective of municipal water authorities is to serve the public interest. In fact, agents involved in the water delivery system may pursue strategies designed for private gain, which can have important and pervasive implications for how a water system is actually designed and operated. Proposals to change the technical, engineering aspects of a water distribution system can thus threaten the interests of powerful groups. Effective public policy and donor involvement in the water sector must be based on an understanding of the structure of water markets and the political power supporting existing institutional arrangements. Copyright 1993 by the American Geophysical Union.
ai_rationale: Analyzes institutional rent-extracting behavior by multiple agents affecting terms and conditions of municipal water service provision in Jakarta.

title: A sanitation revolution in Bangladesh?
abstract: There is a possibility of full sanitation coverage in Bangladesh before the end of the decade. This may have effects on the donor's attitudes to low-cost sanitation programmes worldwide. The success of the sanitation programme has been a result of three factors: a successful advocacy programme has made sanitation coverage a high priority on the political agenda; an integrated approach to institutional responsibilities has forged partnerships between various institutions for promotion and social mobilization; and a flexible approach to appropriate sanitation technologies has made sanitary latrines affordable to people of all income levels. -from Author
ai_rationale: Examines sanitation coverage gains in Bangladesh tied to institutional/advocacy approach and affordable technology.

title: Water of life.
abstract: The Social Research Centre at the American University in Cairo, Egypt, trained 85 health promoters to teach women and children in the villages of Babil and Kafr Shanawan, Egypt, about households hygiene and water sanitation. Households instructed by health promoters had higher knowledge levels and practiced better behavior in areas of water storage, food preparation, latrine maintenance, and handwashing than those not receiving instruction. Researchers realized further improvement would not be possible without improving the village environment, so they also examined the water sanitation situation in the villages. In Babil, they noted that a standpipe needed to be repaired and a garbage collection system was needed. In Kafr Shanawan, the major problem was a high water table (1 m below the surface), but its other problems matched those of Babil. PVC handpumps were installed in Kafr Shanawan, resulting in increased access to potable water. Villagers wanted to learn how to maintain and repair the pumps. A women's group in Babil learned how to fix the standpipe. Administrative problems forestalled the garbage collection system after 3 months, however. The leading obstacles of improved sanitary conditions were a lack of communication between levels of government as well as between these levels and villages and unmanageable bureaucratic procedures. Villagers systematic doubt about the village of regional government agencies ever responding to villagers request for assistance resulted in apathy. Many villagers believed the government and not the villagers themselves was responsible for village sanitation, thereby becoming a major obstacle to community participation. Nevertheless, the villages did form committees on environmental issues. This health education model lays the groundwork for a partnership between decision makers, administrators, and villagers.
ai_rationale: Egyptian village handpump program increased water access; administrative/bureaucratic barriers examined.

title: The development of rural water supply in the province of Fayoum, Egypt
abstract: The paper provides a case study of rural water supply in Fayoum. First, the present state-of-affairs is described and analyzed with respect to production, consumption and coverage. A water balance is drawn up and the projected trends up to the year 2000 are indicated. Nearly full coverage has been achieved already but still more than 50% of the population is served by public standposts. Considerable demand for house connections is apparent. Based on the present trend it is expected that by the year 2000, 75% of the population could be served by private connections, provided sufficient production capacity becomes available. Secondly, the focus is on organization and finance with special attention to cost recovery. Estimates for present billing efficiency and the Unaccounted For Water (UFW) percentages are provided. With the perceived trend in the growth of house connections and decline of public taps there is ample potential to reduce UFW, provided an efficient billing and fee collection system is introduced and leakage is controlled. With the reduction of UFW by 'technical' measures half of the cost recovery target can be achieved. The other half has to come from tariff increases. Experience is drawn from the Netherlands-supported Fayoum Drinking Water and Sanitation Project (FADWS) which started in 1990.; The paper provides a case study of rural water supply in Fayoum. ai_rationale: Egypt case reports empirical house-connection coverage data tied to institutional/financial cost-recovery factors.

title: Water and bureaucracy in colonial Puebla de los Angeles
abstract: The allocation of water in the city of Puebla de los Angeles Mexico is examined.  The policies of the Ayuntamiento were at the root of problems of access to water in the city.  Petitions for direct access were used by the municipal government to provide for the development or maintenance of the municipal infrastructure.
ai_rationale: Historical study of colonial Puebla's municipal government (Ayuntamiento) policies underlying problems of urban water access.

authors: Choguill, Charles L; Franceys, Richard; Cotton, Andrew
title: Building Community Infrastructure in the 1990s: Progressive Improvement
abstract: The provision of safe drinking water & adequate sanitation in low-income neighborhoods of less developed countries is fundamental to meeting the basic needs of an urban population. There is growing concern that shifts of priority by international aid agencies might lead to less attention to local infrastructural issues making progressive improvement of water & sanitation by residents of such neighborhoods increasingly necessary. This progressive improvement can be accomplished if various levels of infrastructural provision are established. The primary level of service might be defined as the lowest level of improvement, eg, buidable land with positive drainage, access ways, communal water points, supervised temporary communal latrines, & solid waste disposal. As neighborhood incomes rise, improvements can be made to bring this infrastructure to intermediate level through technical advice & the use of demonstration units. Communal latrines would, at this stage, give way to the construction of on-lot pit latrines. Ultimately, infrastructural upgrading would lead, as incomes continue to rise, to the achievement of conventional facilities, which would be of equal quality to those enjoyed by higher income consumers. Central to this approach is the adoption of a demonstration/consolidation/expansion model that would be expected to lead to improved levels of service provision across the neighborhood. Variations in implementing the model are examined. AA
ai_rationale: Conceptual/empirical framework of progressive infrastructural upgrading for drinking water and sanitation in low-income urban neighborhoods.

authors: Mikkelsen, Britha; Yulianti, Yanti; Barre, Anton
title: Community Involvement in Water Supply in West Java
abstract: A description of the current project for supplying running water to 44 small towns serving as administrative centers of subdistricts in the province of West Java, Indonesia. The Danish-financed project involves managing, maintaining, & assessing public taps after determining amount & location of water supply needed. Affecting 400,000 people from widely varied socioeconomic & cultural backgrounds, details are provided of the project's design based on actual demand for water. Enhanced community participation is essential to the viability & long-term sustainability of the project. 2 Figures, 6 References. J. Sadler
ai_rationale: Description of a Danish-financed community-participation-based running water supply project for 44 small towns in West Java, Indonesia.

title: Meeting Women's Needs and Priorities for Water and Sanitation in Cities
abstract: Since women in developing countries are generally responsible for the provision of the family's water & sanitation, they are disproportionately affected by poor water infrastructure. Lack of access to clean water often underlies conditions of poverty & sickness in women & children, & consumes time that could be better spent in economic pursuits. These problems continue because social & cultural constraints limit women's participation in the planning & execution of water supply & sanitation projects, causing such projects to operate at less than optimal efficiency. It is recommended that to make these projects successful, women should have a major role in their design & implementation. Training suggestions are offered. 1 Table. M. Pflum
ai_rationale: Study of social/cultural constraints on women's participation in urban water supply and sanitation project planning, with recommendations for improving project design.

title: Water and Sanitation in SÃO Paulo, Brazil: Successful Strategies for Service Provision in Low-Income Communities
abstract: This thesis explores the role of community pressure in increasing water and sewer provision to previously-excluded squatter settlements and illegal subdivisions in Sao Paulo, Brazil between 1979 and 1991. User pressure increases agency responsiveness and accountability, but this is only possible if democratic guarantees allow excluded groups to mobilize, and permit reform-minded politicians and agency staff to overcome long-standing and entrenched resistance to service extension. Effective mobilizations are cyclical, decentralized, and do not necessarily develop into politicized movements. Periodic waves of mobilization show movement tenacity, rather than weakness and a retreat into nonengagement. Low-visibility community management activities during demobilized periods foster leadership continuity and a latent capacity for mobilization within the community. Thus, communities can rapidly re-mobilize, occasionally forming temporary district-level federations when the need arises.Constructive competition from small municipal agencies, combined with reform pressure from the state governor and ongoing community mobilizations have forced the larger specialized water and sewer agency in Sio Paulo to improve squatter settlement service. Small, multi-purpose municipal agencies, with staff committed to working with poor and at-risk residents, have pioneered service programs for squatter settlements in two periods over the past twelve years. The municipal agencies are well suited to small, detailed projects where they innovate new service approaches. In the first period, once the municipal agencies demonstrated that service was indeed possible, a small, low-status subgroup within the larger water and sewer agency applied these innovations on a citywide level, having a much larger impact. The agency subgroup successfully turned agency policies around by concentrating on one simple task -- water service -- and directing community pressure at resistant implementation staff, thus pushing them to adopt new service policies. Pressure on the water and sewer agency from the state governor gave the subgroup authority to act within the agency, but their ability to carry out reforms depended on ongoing community mobilizations.Community mobilizations were crucial in getting water and sewer services for previously-excluded communities, but were not sufficient by themselves to bring about institutional learning within the larger agency. Pressure from communities was channeled through the more receptive municipal agencies and agency subgroup, that in turn pressed the larger agency to improve service delivery. Thus, the pathways that community pressure takes to improving service delivery are circuitous. They reveal that small generalist agencies that are more sensitive to excluded communities' needs are better suited to developing service innovations, while larger, more specialized agencies can have a much greater impact once they begin to implement policy reforms. Yet these innovations and policy reforms could not occur without persistent pressure brought to bear through repeated waves of community mobilization.
ai_rationale: Historical thesis on community mobilization and agency accountability increasing water/sewer service extension to squatter settlements in São Paulo.

title: Politics, Class, and Gender in African Resource Management: The Case of Rural Kenya
abstract: The  key  resource  issues  in  Katheka  Sublocation in Machakos District  in  Kenya  are  soil  erosion  and  water availability.  Variables related  to  gender  and  class  are  critical to analysis of both of these issues.  Women are the key actors in resource use and management in Katheka.  In   soil   management,  they  have  achieved  notable  success.  In  water management,  however,  there  is  only a deteriorating situation.  Class and gender  meet  in  Katheka  over  the  politics  of resource access and use.  Women's groups, strong though they are in soil management, are fledgling in obtaining access to the political system.  Emerging in a system in which the boundaries  of  traditional  gender  relations  and  public  authority  are blurred,  these  groups do not see themselves as having a role in modifying the  system  of  resource  access  and  use to benefit the residents of the community.  Moreover,  they  are constrained by the broader class interests that bear down on their community.
ai_rationale: Study of how gender and class shape rural Kenyan women's access to the political system governing water resource management, linked to a deteriorating water availability situation in Katheka.

title: Possible Adverse Effects of Increasing Block Water Tariffs in Developing Countries
abstract: The use of an increasing block water tariff (IBT), a price structure in which a commodity is priced at a low initial rate up to a specified volume of use (block), then at a higher rate for additional blocks used, is widespread throughout developing countries.  Findings from a survey in Kumasi, Ghana, show that the IBT is not achieving its objective of helping the poor to obtain water at minimal cost.  Quite the contrary - the poor often pay higher average water prices than better-off households.  There are 2 reasons why this is so.  First, households in high-density housing conditions, which often share a single water connection, must pay more per unit under the IBT structure than households that share a connection with only a few others.  Second, many low-income families do not have private connections at all and purchase waters from neighbors, who thus become caught up in increasing block rates as well and probably pass them along to the buyer.
ai_rationale: Survey study in Kumasi, Ghana showing that increasing-block water tariff pricing regulation paradoxically raises effective water costs and worsens affordability for poor households.

title: The Dynamics of Community Development in Rural Areas: An Application of Practice Skills
abstract: A description of the experiences of student social workers who employed innovative strategies to assist the rural community of Makgeng, South Africa, to procure water. Information was obtained from the file entries of students, interaction with students during supervision, & community members. The urgent need for social work services in rural areas of South Africa is demonstrated through descriptions of deprivation, improper infrastructure, & perpetual economic recession. Modified AA
ai_rationale: Case study of social-work students assisting a rural South African community (Makgeng) to procure water amid poor infrastructure and economic constraints.

title: District Planning with Community Participation in Peru: The Work of the Institute of Local Democracy -- IPADEL
abstract: Case studies of two projects undertaken by Save the Children in the San Juan de Miraflores district of Lima, Peru, are presented. The first attempted to promote the involvement of low-income communities in decision making about the design of their district's development plan; the second worked with a low-income community in designing, implementing, & maintaining systems to improve water supply & provision for sanitation, washing, & the collection & disposal of household garbage. The projects reprsent an important step toward greater local democracy in Lima. 1 Map. Adapted from the source document.
ai_rationale: Case studies of Save the Children/IPADEL projects improving community participation in district planning and water supply/sanitation provision in a low-income Lima, Peru community.

title: Community Participation and Rural Water Supply Development in Sierra Leone
abstract: Community involvement in meeting costs for rural water development is examined in a study of the improved water wells program of the Plan International Rural Development Project in Makari-Gbanti Chiefdom, Northern Province, Sierra Leone. Improved wells were found to be least effective in meeting dry season water needs of villagers. Factors responsible for this include the ill-conceived nature of the community self-help development strategy, & the fact that villager motivation for meeting part of the cost of this program is largely determined by the benefits of an integrated package of services, of which water development is only a part. A case study of the village of Gbonombu, in which a successful water supply strategy was developed, demonstrates the effectiveness of community self-help in promoting development. 6 Tables, 24 References. Adapted from the source document.
ai_rationale: Case study of community self-help and cost-sharing effects on rural water well program effectiveness in Sierra Leone.

title: The provincial water supply in Thailand and the water decade
abstract: In order to comply with the International Drinking Water Supply and Sanitation Decade Plan (1981-1990), the Thai Government has set up a target that by the year 1990 not less than 95 percent of the Thai population, or more than 50 million persons, will be served with clean water, compared with 40 percent at the outset of the Decade. However, in 1985, due to several constraints, the Provincial Waterworks Authority (PWA) revised its own target to cover only about 70% by the end of 1990. In 1988 it was estimated that about 2.883 million people in PWA's service areas or about 58.0 percent can be served by PWA's systems. If the number of population in service areas increases by 2.5% per year, PWA has to increase the number of connections at the rate of 12.62% per year for the remaining two years of the Decade in order to meet the 70% coverage target in 1990. A budget of about 7,485 million baht (US $299 million) was allocated in FY 1980-89 for the expansion of water supply systems and services. It was estimated that the budget in 1990 should not be less than 1,950 million baht if the same target is to be accomplished. At any rate, there are still many constraints that could hamper the achievement, such as: - inadequate water resources, both in terms of quantity and quality due, to a great extent, to deforestation and pollution from factories and farming activities, etc. - inadequate manpower and equipment. - inadequate budget. - inadequate tariff, since the present tariff only covers operating expenditure but not future capital investments.; In order to comply with the International Drinking Water Supply and Santitation Decade Plan (1981-1990), the Thai Government has set up a target that by the year 1990 not less than 95 percent of the Thai population, or more than 50 million persons, will be served with clean water, compared with 40 percent at the outset of the Decade. However, in 1985, due to several constraints, the Provincial Waterworks Authority (PWA) revised its own target to cover only about 70% by the end of 1990. In 1988 it was estimated that about 2.883 million people in the PWA's service areas or about 58.0 percent can be served by PWA's systems. If the number of population in service areas increases by 2.5% per year, PWA has to increase the number of connections at the rate of 12.62% per year for the remaining two years of the Decade in order to meet the 70% coverage target in 1990. A budge of about 7,485 million baht (US $299 million) was allocated in FY 1980-89 for the expansion of water supply systems and services. It was estimated that the budget in 1990 should not be less than 1,950 million baht if the same target is to be accomplished. At any rate, there are still many constraints that could hamper the achievement, such as: inadequate water resources, both in terms of quantity and quality due, to a great extent, to deforestation and pollution from factories and farming activities, etc.; inadequate manpower and equipment; inadequate budget; inadequate tariff, since the present tariff only covers operating expenditure but not future capital investments.
ai_rationale: Thailand case reports empirical water supply coverage/connection data tied to institutional/budget constraints.

authors: Yang H.; Yiheng M.; Qiu X.; Zhang H.; Lin Q.; Guan J.; Clayton S.
title: A Multisectoral Approach to Primary Health Care in Fujian, China
abstract: The government of Yongan in Fujian province has developed a multisectoral primary health care program in the rural community of Dahu with the aim of reaching “Health for All” by 1993. In keeping with the spirit of the Alma Ata declaration and the tradition of local self-reliance in China, the program has involved the entire community and is financed almost exclusively at the local level. Community leaders were trained in the importance of primary health care so that they could serve as role models. The project includes school health education, domestic hygiene education, reconstruction of homes to separate the kitchen, toilet and animals pens, road construction to eliminate dust, environmental sanitation, occupational health, and the upgrading of health care facilities. A number of local ordinances regarding construction, zoning and smoking have also been instituted. The results of the project's first year of implementation in two villages indicate that construction of the new road is near completion, and access to clean water is almost universal. Gains are also reported in the percentage of the population receiving physical examinations, the number of health stations that now meet state standards, and the number of homes that are constructed according to the new guidelines. © 1991, Sage Publications. All rights reserved.
ai_rationale: China rural program reports near-universal water access outcome tied to local governance ordinances.

title: Operation and maintenance of water projects and services in Latin America
abstract: This paper concentrates on two aspects of the vast subject of ‘… water projects and services’. Even though the questions tackled may affect different water uses, this analysis is focused on operation and maintenance of water supply systems and the institutions that service them. The paper seeks to analyse some of the obstacles which impede the attainment of better performance in the operation and maintenance of water projects. It tackles the institutional problems and restrictions which must be overcome to speed up the adoption of operational patterns which will lead to a better use of available capacities. 1991 United Nations
ai_rationale: Analyzes institutional obstacles affecting operation/maintenance performance of water supply systems in Latin America.

title: Urban services in the National Cities of India: organization, financing, planning and delivery.
abstract: The research presented in this dissertation was undertaken to explain why the National Cities of India (Delhi, Calcutta, Madras and Bombay) are deficient in providing urban services and what can be done to improve service delivery.  The focus of the research was upon the organizational, financial, planning and management aspects of service delivery, rather than upon the technical and technological aspects, such as forecasting, service standards and infrastructure design.  Three urban services, electricity, environmental sanitation and roads, are examined through case studies.  Six main factors which contribute to service deficiencies are explored:  (i) the historical processes of urbanization; (ii) the historical patterns of urban growth; (iii) the historical organization of urban government for service delivery; (iv) the structure of urban finance; (v) the nature of urban planning; and (vi) the internal dynamics of service delivery agencies in planning, producing, operating and distributing urban services.  The research concludes that urban service deficiencies in the National Cities can be explained in terms of:  (i) the development policies pursued by colonial and post colonial governments, policies which saddled the cities with a poverty stricken population because they discouraged urban industrial development, causing the growth of marginal employment in the bazaar sector; (ii) the growth of the National Cities as accretions of differentiated serviced and unserviced areas and the accommodation of rural migrants through densification and the proliferation of unauthorized settlements, which together have resulted in intractable physical patterns which pose problems for service delivery; (iii) the creation in the colonial period and the perpetuation during the post colonial era, of a weak and spatially, sectorally and functionally fragmented system of urban government, incapable of delivering services on a co-ordinated and city wide basis; (iv) the weak structure of urban finance caused by institutional and admnistrative barriers to local resource mobilization and by the lack of appropriate mechanisms for transfers and institutional finance; (v) the absence of city wide urban planning during the colonial period and the inadequacies of urban planning during the post colonial period, inadequacies caused by the application of western theory, faulty assumptions, the inability to deal with the informal sector, lack of comprehensiveness and lack of concern for the built up areas of the city; and (vi) deficiencies in service delivery agencies in planning, producing, operating and distributing services, inadequacies caused by weaknesses in organization and management, pathologies of third world administration (such as corruption) and inequitable distribution.
ai_rationale: Dissertation examining organizational, financial and institutional causes of urban service (including sanitation) deficiencies in India's National Cities.

title: The Struggle against the Poisoning of Harlan County's Dayhoit: Fighting the Good Fight
abstract: In Feb 1989, state officials reported levels of vinyl chloride, trichloroethylene, PCBs, dichlorethene, lead, barium, & other chemicals in the well water of the community of Dayhoit, in Harlan County, to be considerably above federal EPA (Environmental Protection Agency) standards; this poisoning was caused by the nearby National Electric Coil plant. Residents were informed that while the state did not know the duration of their exposure to these toxics, their health was not likely to be adversely affected. The primary concern of most of the residents of Dayhoit was with the health of their children & themselves. Following their initial meetings with state & local officials, the citizens determined that the explanations to their most compelling questions were not forthcoming. They formed a citizens group whose membership included residents of the community, former workers, & other concerned citizens. The citizens group has had to confront seemingly indifferent county, state & federal governments plus the multinational corporation which owned the electric plant. Over the past two years, they have educated themselves about the deleterious consequences of multisyllabic poisonous chemicals, & discovered their personal fortitude to discern self-defined ends through cooperation, forged from grassroots activity. Proactive initiatives that they have implemented, including health tests & a community survey, are described.
ai_rationale: Case study of a Harlan County, Kentucky citizens' group confronting indifferent county/state/federal government and a corporation over toxic well-water poisoning.

title: Community Based Approaches in Water Supply and Sanitation Programme -- An Indian Experience
abstract: Global policies & strategies for the effective planning, implementation, & monitoring of water supply & sanitation programs in India resulting from the International Drinking Water Supply & Sanitation Decade, 1981-1990, are examined, drawing on case study data from Kerala state. Specifically, the extent to which social & economic factors were given equal weight & used to gain the commitment of the community is examined, including the implementation of socioeconomic units, a coordinating office that worked with the Kerala Water Authority (KWA), & strategies to promote the program, eg, community education/mobilization, intersectoral & intradepartmental collaboration, human resources/institutional development, & developing microlevel planning & implementation systems at the ward-level. The effectiveness of KWA's three-year experiment will be documented & disseminated for wider replication. Adapted from the source document.
ai_rationale: Case study of community-based approaches in a Kerala Water Authority water supply and sanitation program under India's International Drinking Water Supply and Sanitation Decade.

authors: Whittington, Dale; Lauria, Donald T; Mu, Xinming
title: A Study of Water Vending and Willingness to Pay for Water in Onitsha, Nigeria
abstract: As a means of assisting the government water authority to determine pricing for a new water supply system, a rapid reconnaissance survey was conducted in Onitsha, Nigeria, in 1987. At that time, the majority of the population obtained water from an elaborate & well-organized vending system run by the private sector, involving distributors with tanker trucks who purchased water from private boreholes. Interviews were conducted with vendors, tanker drivers, managers & attendants of boreholes, water distributors & retailers, & householders (total N = 416); the lack of a focused sample frame is noted. Results show an extraordinary willingness to pay: households were paying vendors more than twice the operation & maintenance costs of a piped distribution system -- during the dry season, almost 24 times as much. Of particular note for policy debates on whether the poor can afford water is the finding that they were paying the most, both in amount & % of income. Implications for water authority planning in developing countries are discussed, & the usefulness of this survey method is defended. 2 Tables, 9 Figures, 2 Appendixes, 13 References. Adapted from the source document.
ai_rationale: Survey of informal water-vending pricing, affordability and willingness to pay in Onitsha, Nigeria, informing utility planning.

title: Decentralizing Water Supply Services in Developing Countries: Factors Affecting the Success of Community Management
abstract: An exploration of factors that impact the ability of developing countries to provide their citizens with potable water, noting that 50+% of their rural populations still lack access to clean drinking water. It is suggested that breakdown or misuse of water supply systems can be traced to central government ministries or agencies that continue to give insufficient attention to community management with regard to water provision. Proposals to effect successful decentralized community management include: appropriate incentives to participate in community water systems management; development of appropriate skills & resources for such participation; institutionalization of effective processes for water system operation & maintenance; development of cooperative organizational relationships through which participation in planning & management can provide assistance; availability of efficient technology for water supply management; & a strengthened monitoring, feedback, & evaluation system to ensure effective management. 1 Table, 34 References. S. Millett
ai_rationale: Synthesis of factors affecting decentralized community management of water supply systems and access to clean drinking water in developing countries.

title: Water Supply Issues and Policy in Developing Countries
abstract: A review of the progress made in developing countries toward provision of clean water & adequate sanitation in cities & rural areas since 1970, with focus on the International Water Supply & Sanitation Decade, 1981-1990. Only indicative estimates are presented due to variation in data sources & wide differences in populations. Given the uncertainty regarding these & other factors, a systematic flexible approach for analysis & decision making concerning water issues is proposed. The key elements of the Integrated Water Resources Planning (IWRP) framework are economic evaluation of water projects & programs, optimization of water supply systems, water environmental & demand analysis, & policy instruments for water management. Effectiveness of IWRP is dependent on national objectives & a feasible financing plan, engineering & technical standards, an institutional framework for water supply, & proper maintenance & follow up in the field. Typical characteristics of institutional frameworks are illustrated, utilizing the examples of Cyprus, Egypt, Ghana, Haiti, Uruguay, Yemen, & Zaire, whose problems of finance, government interference, & lack of technical staff show that strategies for water supply & sanitation must be planned according to sound economic & environmental principles. 6 Tables, 1 Figure, 28 References. Adapted from the source document.
ai_rationale: Review of institutional frameworks for water supply and sanitation provision in developing countries during the Water Decade.

title: A review of the institutional arrangements and activities in the Philippine water supply sector
abstract: Toward the end of the 60's, one government agency was still in charge of providing the entire Philippine population with drinking water supply. After two decades, the task proved to be too gigantic for this agency, the National Waterworks and Sewerage Authority (NAWASA). Created in 1953, to serve the population then, the NAWASA constructed and operated waterworks systems in most provincial towns around the country. But as the population in these towns steadily grew, the NAWASA found it increasingly difficult to cope with the big demand for water for both people and industry. Furthermore, the waterworks systems could not be maintained nor expanded for lack of funds. And as if to compound matters, the waterworks personnel were poorly trained and thus could not provide the proper service to its consumers. In its bind to provide each Filipino household with easy access to safe, adequate and dependable water supplies, the Philipine government, by the early '70s, adopted very strong measures to improve the water supply situation in the country. Firstly, the centralized NAWASA was abolished to give way to two new agencies, the Metropolitan Waterworks and Sewerage System (MWSS), which was to take care of the needs of Metropolitan Manila. The other was the Local Water Utilities Administration (LWUA), which was to take charge of the water needs of provincial urban centers. Secondly, the new agencies' policies were coordinated by the then National Water Resources Council. Thirdly, the control of local water works systems in big provincial towns was transferred to autonomous and independent water districts. Fourthly, institutional development activities such as training in the fields of management, operation, maintenance and finance were conducted in planned water projects was encouraged. When the 1980's was declared by the United Nations asthe International Drinking Water Supply and Sanitation Decade, or simply the Water Decade, the Philippine government's efforts towards total water supply coverage were intensified. This meant giving more attention to the rural areas where potable water supply was not readily available. Established was the Rural Waterworks Development Corporation (RWDC) a government agency tasked with providing funds and technical assistance to Rural Waterworks and Sanitation Associations (RWSA). These RWSAs were formed to take charge of supplying water to rural communities. The role of the Department of Public Works and Highways, through its Project Management Office for Rural Water Supply (PMO-RWS) was highlighted in the rural water program further particularly in the building of facilities, in research and development and in the conduct of training programs. Institutional strengthening activities such as public information, education and training were indispensable to the success of the rural water supply program because water projects could only be implemented where a RWSA was organized to accept and maintain the facilities. By mid-1980s, additional changes were instituted in the sector in order to streamline the agencies involved in water supply development. Much efforts was wasted in overlapping functions and Water Decade accomplishments fell short of the targets. Thus, the RWDC was merged with the LWUA. Some of the functions of the NWRC was transferred to the DPWH and was re-named the National Water Resources Board. A new master plan was formulated that set more realistic goals for the sector which now include sanitation and sewerage, in addition to water supply. Institutional changes are necessary if the Philippines is to achieve the targets it has set for itself. Continued refinements and streamlining are needed to make the water agencies more efficient and effective in delivering this vital service. This is so because affordable safe and adquately supplied water for each Filipino, is the ultimate dream. As the Water Decade draws to a close, it would be well to know how the Philippines has coped, through the years, in making its dream a reality. Through this paper, the history and development of the water sector's institutions will be traced. The reasons behind the evolution of these sectors will also be analyzed. Lastly, the development activities that lead to institutional strength and stability will be enumerated.
ai_rationale: Reviews institutional evolution of Philippine water supply agencies affecting household access.

title: The Integrated Project in Ghana: its potentials for the 1990s.
abstract: The pilot Integrated Family Planning Nutrition and Parasite Control Project (IP) in Ghana is described in general and specifically for each of the 9 villages (Fetteh Kakraba, Osimpo, Tsotsoo, Ahintia, Aberful, Bontrase, Kwame Etteh, Awutu, Ojobi) in terms of major accomplishments, problems, population, occupation, educational institutes, impact on family planning, parasite infection, immunization, and members of the Steering Committee. The IP was developed by the International Planned Parenthood Federation (IPPF) in collaboration with the Japanese Organization for International Cooperation in Family Planning (JOICFP) in 1987. The aim is to improve the quality of life through family planning, control of parasitic infection, and to improve environmental sanitation, hygiene, and health. Modest but positive progress has been made including construction of a ventilated pit toilet in Fetteh Kakraba, Ahintia, and Kwame Etteh have refuse dumps in all communities, weeding around the rural water supply, and personal hygiene improvement. A nursing center and school meal project are operational at Aberful, Bontrase, and Ojobi. Weanimix is being used as a supplemental food for children. Bontrase women are producing gari (processed cassava) for income. Collaboration and cooperation as a strategy has been beneficial. Parasite management has increased community interest in improving health conditions. Family planning has been with effort made accessible to couples. The future need is how to sustain institutional arrangements to provide quality care, and to expand throughout Ghana. The example of one the community profiles--Fetteh Kakraba--demonstrates the improvement in the quality of life. A local Steering Committee was formed in July 1989. Misconceptions about family planning were dispelled through repeated home visits and meetings. Family practice rates improved from 8.3 to 31.25 in June 1990. Mothers learned how to prepare Weanimix; some is sole to generate income. Immunizations in conjunction with the Public Health immunization team at Winneba has achieved 87.03% coverage from 0. After construction of the pit toilet and a pipeborn water supply, the parasite infection rate has been reduced from 53.8 to 6.25%. A day care center for farming couples is needed.
ai_rationale: Ghana village study reports empirical health outcomes tied to institutional sustainability of water/sanitation access.

authors: Whittington, Dale; Briscoe, John; et al
title: Estimating the Willingness to Pay for Water Services in Developing Countries: A Case Study of the Use of Contingent Valuation Surveys in Southern Haiti
abstract: An area's water supplies and the water use practices in Haiti were studied using the contingent valuation method.  The results suggest that contingent valuation surveys are a feasible method for estimating individuals' willingness to pay for improved water services in rural Haiti.
ai_rationale: Contingent valuation survey estimating rural Haitian households' willingness to pay for improved water services, informing feasibility of water service pricing/provision policy.

title: Estimating the Willingness to Pay for Water Services in Deve
abstract: If rural water projects in developing countries are to be both sustainable and replicable, an improved planning methodology is required that includes a procedure for eliciting information on the value placed on different levels of services.  A key concept in such a methodology is that of willingness-to-pay (WTP).  In the contingent valuation method, the interviewer poses questions within the context of a hypothetical market.  A study was carried to determine if contingent valuation surveys could be used in developing countries to develop useful estimates of WTP for water services.  A contingent valuation survey was carried out in Laurent, a village in southern Haiti.  Source observation data were also collected.  The results suggest that it is possible to do a contingent valuation survey among a very poor, illiterate population and obtain reasonable, consistent answers.  There does not seem to be a major problem with either starting point or hypothetical bias.  The evidence with regard to strategic bias is less conclusive.
ai_rationale: Contingent-valuation survey study estimating rural households' willingness-to-pay for different levels of water service in Haiti, informing sustainable/replicable water-project planning methodology.

title: Women, Water Supply and Sanitation in Kenya
abstract: The need for a reliable supply of clean water & sanitation measures & facilities is a pressing one for most developing countries, which has been exacerbated by rapid population growth & the increased economic marginalization of the people. The role of women as carriers of water, managers, family health educators, & motivators & agents of change must be taken advantage of in the struggle for water supply & sanitation. Focus here is on women's role in this effort in Kenya. It is suggested that factors inhibiting the participation of women include poor planning & implemention, vague objectives in regard to community participation, & lack of training. 14 Tables, 11 References. Adapted from the source document.
ai_rationale: Study of factors (poor planning, vague objectives, lack of training) inhibiting women's participation in water supply and sanitation delivery in Kenya.

title: Community Self-Financing of Water Supply and Sanitation: What Are the Promises and Pitfalls?
abstract: The debt crisis in developing nations during the 1980s, & shrinking donor resources, made it evident that free provision of water supply & sanitation (WS&S) is impossible. Here, operational implications & potential outcomes of attempts to recover system-development costs from beneficiary communities are considered. It is argued that the demand of self-financing should be moderated by an evaluation of a community's ability to pay. The impact of cost recovery on system sustainability & on the creation of community-level management skills is examined, & alternative approaches to cost recovery -- including community-based resource mobilization -- are suggested. 18 References. Adapted from the source document.
ai_rationale: Discussion of community self-financing/cost-recovery policy effects on water supply and sanitation sustainability in developing countries.

authors: Arlosoroff S.; Roche R.; Wright F.
title: Economic Considerations for Low-Cost, Groundwater-Based Rural Water Supply
abstract: An estimated 1,800 million rural people will have to be provided with improved water supplies in the 15 years to the end of this century if developing countries are to approach the coverage targets of the International Drinking Water Supply and Sanitation Decade (IDWSSD). Accelerated progress is hampered by financial, technical and institutional resource constraints faced by many developing countries. The problem is also aggravated by the growing number of completed projects which are broken down and abandoned, or functioning well below their potential capacity. The Community Water Supply Project (formerly the Rural Water Supply Handpumps Project) was initiated to address these problems and work towards sustainable, replicable rural water supply programs. As part of this work, the Project has devised a simple, analytical tool, based on traditional cost/benefit analysis, that can be used to evaluate rural water supply projects. © 1989.
ai_rationale: Discusses institutional/financial constraints on rural water supply coverage and an evaluation tool.

title: Urban service delivery system and federal government bureaucracy: A structural analysis of spatial distribution of water supply in a suburban community of Metropolitan Lagos
abstract: This study identifies the prevailing scarcity of urban public services and the conceptual relations among service delivery, patronage, bureaucratic activities and structural factors in the Lagos Metropolitan region. It examines the extent to which clientelism, bureaucratic decision rules and structural theoretical models explain water service delivery patterns in Festival Town (Festac), a suburb of Lagos, Nigeria.The unprecedented pace of growth of the Lagos Metropolis since the mid-twentieth century gave rise to the spectacular spatial expansion of the continuous built up region. Urban industrial and governmental institutions have not kept pace with the population growth rate of Lagos. This demographic trend also continues to tax the urban service delivery system. The federal government policy proscription entailed the planning and creation of a new town, Festival Town (Festac), as a response to addressing the urban public service problem in the Greater Lagos.Festac is well serviced with modern urban infrastructural facilities for the delivery of water supply and water related services. In recent years, however, the local residents of Festac have been faced with a similar problem in water supply which is not different from that experienced by urban residents in other parts of Lagos. The painstaking efforts that detailed a pre-planned, designed and carefully considered development of a new urban community have not succeeded in creating a regularly functioning delivery of water supply and water related services. Various analytical tools were utilyzed in conducting the study.The study concludes that the central factors in the prevailing scarcity of water supply in Festac are technology and infrastructural dependence and dwindling federal state revenues, all of which exacerbate the internal production of essential urban public services and thereby making delivery problematic. The findings presented in this study demonstrate the significance of the specific articulation expressed in the link between the Nigerian export sector, the fiscal capacity of the federal state and public service financing.This study recommends that if the Nigerian public service delivery system is to overcome its contemporary problems, policies should be adopted which largely depend on existing internal resources.
ai_rationale: Structural analysis of bureaucratic/clientelist factors shaping spatial water supply delivery patterns in suburban Lagos.

title: Environmental upgrading and intra-urban migration in Calcutta
abstract: Approximately a third of the population of Calcutta live in slums and an estimated 43% live below the poverty level. This work examines the connections between three types of slums or low income settlements within the metropolitan area and investigates how recent attempts at improving one type, the Calcutta bustees, has affected the urban poor. Bustees are rented rooms in legal, traditionally designed, single storey buildings within the city. Since 1971 a large scale improvement programme has been implemented by the Calcutta Metropolitan Development Authority with the objectives of improving the health and sanitation, as well as the employment prospects, of bustee dwellers. However the bustees occupy valuable urban land in a city of severe shortage. Intra-urban migration, created by the natural increase of bustee tenants, is exacerbated by increasing land prices. Rent control exists but rather than offering protection it appears to be driving the real cost of obtaining accommodation underground; demands for large key money payments and evictions of sitting tenants have been reported. Some bustee landlords are rebuilding their properties into expensive, middle class apartment blocks. This has meant that those who were targeted for help have actually moved out of the area, often to settlements with far worse facilities than the bustees. Some moved to suburban slums far away from their work, while others became illegal squatters in the city close to job opportunities. Poor people are therefore moving out of the city to peripheral, legal, rented slums where there is space - but no employment, infrastructure, or services. As they seek accommodation in the suburbs, rents there are beginning to rise sharply. Suburban residents are suffering from the `domino effect' of rising costs. They are priced out of the area and join the illegal squatter settlements back in the city. This study questions the appropriateness of area based investment strategies for the long term benefit of the urban poor.
ai_rationale: Case study of a slum sanitation/health improvement programme and displacement effects on Calcutta's urban poor.

title: Cultivating Hot Peppers and Water Crisis in India's Desert
abstract: An analysis of the politics of groundwater extraction & use in a Ru region of India's Rajasthan desert. The most common agricultural crops produced are locally consumed food grains, cereals, pulses, & oil seeds. The local cash crop, chili peppers, however, is the newly emergent product; it consumes many times more water than all the locally consumed crops combined, at a time when water levels are falling. It is hypothesized that access to & appropriation of natural resources (in this case, water) result in the production of cash crops, on the one hand, & transform the relations of production to suit the emergent needs of capitalist farming, on the other. A theoretical question is posed: whether groundwater depletion is affected/influenced by caste, class, & access to political power. Taking a historical perspective, first examined are local & regional ecological problems: the degradation of the water catchment & body system by the mining industry; the deforestation of the Aravali mountains & watershed by the state forestry department; & the intensive extraction of Ru water resources for Ur/industrial consumption. The recent Ru drought is seen as a result of the local struggle over access & control of a historically common property resource, water. The impact of the water crisis is described: poor-peasant farming & animal husbandry are disappearing, & women are experiencing an increased workload in supplying water for the household; the configuration of the local economy & culture is being transformed; young men are being forced to migrate elsewhere for wage-labor; women (with their infants) are taking up wage-labor work with "famine relief" projects; & men are taking jobs are wage-laborers with local mines & the cash-crop chili farms. The local water crisis is ecological, economic, & cultural. These findings are based on ethnographic, oral historical, & comparative historical research, with particular emphasis on interviews with poor peasants, rich farmers, social workers, & state officials.
ai_rationale: Study of how cash-crop (chili pepper) groundwater extraction and mining/forestry governance in Rajasthan increased household water-supply workload for women amid desert water crisis.

title: Public reform for private gain? The case of investments in sanitary infrastructure: Germany, 1880-1887
abstract: The issue of comparative progress in sanitary reform is examined using the conditions of Germany, 1880-87, as a case study.  The case of sanitary infrastructure yielded rapid investments and unusual success for Germany.
ai_rationale: Historical case study of German administrative/public reform (1880-87) driving investment in sanitary infrastructure.

title: Goal Multiplicity in the Implementation Setting: Subtle Impacts and the Case of Wastewater Treatment Privatization
abstract: Conceptualization of policy goal as a source of tension between the top-down & bottom-up perspectives of implementation research is examined through analysis of questionnaire data on public wastewater treatment programs in five privatized cities & five matched locales. Preliminary analysis suggests that privatization of treatment facilities yielded better results than other alternatives when evaluated in terms of removal of pollutants from wastewater & recycling of clean effluent, two measures of success gauged by the standard top-down research design, which omits evaluation of other policy goals, eg, improved technical capacity at the local level, federal encouragement of innovative technology, affirmative action & equal employment opportunity, & local autonomy & accountability. A more bottom-up research approach emphasizing goal multiplicity may provide a clearer overall picture of program success. 25 References. D. Generoli
ai_rationale: Comparative questionnaire study of wastewater treatment privatization's effects on pollutant removal performance across five privatized U.S. cities and matched public locales.

title: Evaluating Water and Sanitation Projects: Lessons from Imo State, Nigeria
abstract: The Imo State Drinking Water Supply & Sanitation Project was a pilot intervention designed to improve health & hygiene in poor rural Nigerian communities through low-cost technology & appropriate educational support. An evaluation of the project's health impact is presented using longitudinal & cross-sectional survey data collected from 850 households in 3 intervention villages & 420 households in 2 control villages over 3.5 years covering the pre-, peri-, & postintervention periods. The main findings are summarized, & policy implications for the planning, implementation, & evaluation of water & sanitation projects are discussed. 19 References. Modified HA
ai_rationale: Longitudinal evaluation of a water/sanitation pilot project's health impact in rural Imo State, Nigeria, with policy implications.

title: Same Game, Different Players: Problems in Urban Public Utility Regulation, 1850-1987
abstract: Factors that have historically confronted efforts to protect public interests with respect to provision of public utility services through fixed & networked distribution facilities in major cities in the US are investigated, drawing on both theoretical explorations by institutionally oriented economists & case studies of historical experiences in water works & cable TV. In both industries, cities & private firms have often found themselves embroiled in contentious two-party bargaining relationships. Even if specified in initial franchises, the ability of cities to enforce requirements regarded as burdensome by private water works & electric utility firms has generally proven very limited in the context of these relationships. The greater importance of the role played by government ownership in water works than in cable TV thus far is attributed to both lesser market discipline on private water works firms & to the greater importance of the public goods demanded by cities of water works. Implications for the future evolution of public policy in the cable TV industry are considered. Modified AA
ai_rationale: Historical-institutional analysis of urban public utility (water works) regulation and city-firm bargaining in the US, 1850-1987.

title: Paying for and Getting Water in Hyderabad City
abstract: Despite four years of great water shortage & an outbreak of cholera in 1987, the 3 million inhabitants of Hyderabad City, India, have managed to cope with a theoretically draconian & egalitarian rationing system, & the water supply system has managed to continue. Possible reasons for this survival are explored in terms of the development of a sophisticated internal water market that reallocated public water toward those with greater effective demand (largely wealthier citizens who can afford private storage). It is argued that such a system avoids many of the technical problems of egalitarian rationing. It is concluded that the urban water shortages facing Hyderabad & other cities in India & other rapidly urbanizing countries arise because national political systems prevent a similar Pareto-efficient allocation of scarce water on a regional scale. Modified HA
ai_rationale: Study of Hyderabad water rationing system and internal water market allocation under political constraints.

authors: Arlosoroff S.; Tschannerl G.; Grey D.; Journey W.; Karp A.; Langenegger O.; Roche R.
title: Executive summary—Community water supply: The handpump option
abstract: An estimated 1,800 million people need improved water supplies in the fifteen years to the end of the century, if developing countries are to reach the target of full coverage. The first half of the International Drinking Water Supply and Sanitation Decade (1981–1990) has seen increases in the percentages of the rural population with access to safe water supplies, but only in Asia has the pace been quick enough to envisage a target of essentiahy full coverage by the end of the century (ten years later than the original Decade goals). In Africa, present progress rates would leave half of the rural population still without safe water in the year 2000, while in Latin America, it may be ten years into the next century before full coverage is achieved unless progress improves dramatically. Accelerated progress is hampered by financial and technical resource constraints faced by many developing countries, and the problem is aggravated by the growing number of completed projects which are broken down and abandoned, or functioning much below capacity. Attempts to increase the pace of providing improved community water supplies have often been frustrated because the technology used has proved impossible to sustain in village conditions. To make a lasting impact on the urgent needs, community water supply (CWS) strategies must be based on sustainable and replicable programs, and must take account of the pace at which resource constraints can be overcome. Human resource development programs take time to produce results, and institutional changes can only be accomplished gradually. © Taylor & Francis Group, LLC.
ai_rationale: Reports empirical rural water supply coverage progress under Decade tied to institutional/human resource factors.

title: Institutional Aspects of Water Supply and Sanitation in Asia
abstract: The world has enough water to meet the basic human needs for potable water, so the problem of lack of access to safe drinking water is not technical but institutional. The various institutional shortcomings that limit the ability of the developing countries of Asia to supplying potable water and adequate sanitation are reviewed, and some recommendations for alleviating the institutional difficulties are explored. 1988 United Nations
ai_rationale: UN review argues lack of safe water access in Asia is institutional, not technical, with recommendations.

title: Notes from the Underground: On the Nineteenth-Century Urban Water Economy
abstract: Increasing population density in nineteenth-century cities disturbed the equilibrium between micro-organisms & their human hosts as used water flowed back in the supply channels carrying disease agents. Poverty & filth were believed to be the cause of the resultant cholera epidemics, but they seemed impervious to reform. Only when the causal chain was understood could a feasible program of sanitary reform be advanced. This nevertheless provoked dilemmas of collective action, which were overcome because city areas became socially more homogeneous, & dwellings in the wealthier neighborhoods were connected to a common water supply & sewerage network. By the time the city was saturated with these networks, the remaining poorer areas were compulsorily connected, & water supply & sewerage became public goods.
ai_rationale: Historical study of how 19th-century sanitary reform led wealthy areas to connect first and poorer areas to be compulsorily connected to common water supply and sewerage networks.

title: French-Speaking Africa: Toward a Transfer of Water Management to Villagers
abstract: Given the context of the economic crisis of the 1980s, most African countries have had to review their water management policies. To reduce the cost of water projects, render their management more efficient, & increase their social & economic returns, new approaches involving participation by villagers have been initiated. A case study of a project undertaken in Togo, in cooperation with Canada, provides an example of new village water policies. Some of the technical, organizational, & social problems, & the conditions needed for the success of these new approaches are pointed out. 1 Figure, 16 References. HA
ai_rationale: Case study of decentralizing water management to villagers in Togo (French-speaking Africa), examining technical, organizational and social conditions for successful participatory water management.

title: Public-private partnership in water supply and sanitation in sub-saharan Africa
abstract: Purely public water supply systems are characterized by high costs, insufficient supplies and chronic deficits that are covered by central government transfers. The private water supply programme in Abidjan has not met its coverage targets either, but the system has remained financially solvent and fostered a rapid growth in capacity through the informal sector. The material reviewed here and the experience of developing country water systems in general support several conclusions. (1) Water vending is common in developing countries, which suggests that charging for water is not culturally unacceptable. Demand for wastewater services is low, but surcharges could be imposed on water usage to cover some sanitation costs. (2) Incentives are critical to sound management of water supply and sanitation services. They are typically part of the structure of private firms, but are rare in publicly run systems. (3) The private sector's role in the provision of water supply and sanitation can be extensive. Regulation of private activity and quality control by public authorities is essential to maintain competition and ensure proper and fair operation. (4) Public efforts to supply water can be supplemented by a government-regulated, parallel system to increase the amount of water available. Normally these systems involve trucked water, but private sales outlets with pipe infrastructure should be encouraged where feasible. (5) Even where the public sector decides to control and operate the water supply and sanitation system, some partnership with the private sector is possible through contracting out specific tasks such as billing, metering, maintenance of various components or tracking water losses. Finally, the supply of water is an ideal activity for a public-private partnership.
