Both sectors have comparative advantages that are best applied in conjunction with the other. © 1987 Oxford University Press.
ai_rationale: Analyzes public-private partnership models and coverage outcomes for water supply/sanitation provision in sub-Saharan Africa.

title: REFORMING THE URBAN ENVIRONMENT: SANITATION, HOUSING, AND GOVERNMENT INTERVENTION IN GERMANY, 1870-1910
abstract: European and American cities grappled with severe housing and sanitation problems during the rapid urban growth after 1850. They responded with innovations in government intervention--massive investments in sewers and waterworks and the regulation of housing and land use--that are today institutionalized in comprehensive urban planning. Breaking new ground in the economic analysis of urban history, the three essays of this dissertation examine the economic roots of these developments in Germany before 1910. The study of housing markets draws on a new microdata set of household characteristics and housing consumption to analyze the economic determinants of housing and sanitation problems. The study of the sanitation revolution uses a new set of data from over 100 cities to explain the diffusion of central water supply.The first and second essays apply the hedonic model of housing markets to examine the allocation of supply and the demands of households in a sample of several hundred tenants and owners from the 1889 Basel housing census manuscripts. They conclude that segmentation of housing markets along class lines raised the supply price of housing to the poor. Household demand for access to the city's center and sanitation were most responsive, while the demand for space was relatively unresponsive to differences in incomes. The rural origins and older housing traditions of households--where employer and employee lived under the same roof--are quite important in accounting for high housing densities, while income explains little.The final essay develops and estimates a model of city decision-making based on the median voter framework to explain the diffusion of the first major innovation of the sanitation revolution: waterworks technology. Using a comprehensive cross-sectional data set of cities in Rhenish Prussia, statistical estimation of the model reveals that the rising income of the median voter for town assemblies exerts much more influence on the spread of sanitation technologies than does evidence of incipient government bureacracies or of urban environmental deterioration.
ai_rationale: Economic-history dissertation on government intervention (sewers, housing/land-use regulation) and its effects on sanitation access in Germany, 1870-1910.

title: Short-run water supply allocation under uncertainty: Markets and market failure
abstract: Market allocation of water supplies raises a fundamental economic question: will the market work? There are a number of reasons to have doubts. First, water authorities regard supply reliability as the paramount concern of water management and demonstrate a marked preference for operating systems "reliably" rather than "efficiently". Second, legal and institutional restrictions also inhibit the free exchange of water supplies. Finally, trade among municipal water authorities is likely to be trade among the few so that market power may influence the terms of trade.The study proceeds from a theoretical analysis of water markets to an empirical analysis of market exchange between two cities. The theoretical analysis derives conditions for Pareto optimal exchange from a model of bilateral free trade. Once this benchmark is established, additional constraints are imposed on the model to incorporate conditions of market failure. The primary contribution of this work is the development of a stochastic water supply allocation model capable of analyzing contractual, legal and market power effects on market efficiency and supply reliability.The empirical analysis demonstrates the welfare consequences of departures from the Pareto optimal allocation of water resources for a case study in Cyprus. Using both optimization and simulation techniques, welfare and reliability measures are developed for the alternative allocations implied by the analytic models.The results of this work suggest that the simple view of the efficient markets is inadequate to fully understand the nature of the water transfers problem. The economic gains from market transfers of supplies may be relatively small. However, from a management perspective, the impact of water transfers on system reliability can be very significant providing strong support for some form of cooperation among water authorities.This work is important for several reasons. Municipal water supply is moving toward greater regional integration. The market problems addressed in this study are characteristic of situations that could emerge if regional integration of municipal water systems develops on the basis of market exchange. Market failure and uncertainty have received little attention in previous work on water markets. Policy actions that would promote market exchange cannot disregard the perceived value of system reliability.
ai_rationale: Theoretical and empirical study of legal/institutional restrictions on water market exchange and supply reliability between municipal water authorities in Cyprus.

title: U.S. to Issue Rules On Farm Workers' Sanitary Facilities
abstract: The Labor Department said it plans to issue rules soon to improve sanitation facilities for farm workers, but will still seek a rehearing of the court order requiring the action.Federal regulations guaranteeing farm workers access to drinking water, hand-washing and toilet facilities could come as early as next month. The 14-year battle over such rules culminated last month, when a federal appeals court here ordered the department to issue a field-sanitation standard and end a "disgraceful chapter of legal neglect."Labor Secretary William Brock said yesterday that a national standard was needed because not enough states have adopted effective regulations on their own. In October 1985, Mr. Brock gave the states 18 months to improve farm worker sanitation facilities before he would decide whether to issue federal rules. That action reversed an earlier department decision against issuing a national standard.
ai_rationale: News account of US Labor Department regulatory battle over farm worker sanitation facility (drinking water, toilets) standards.

title: The 20th century comes to the farm
abstract: Studies done for the Occupational Safety and Health Administration (OSHA) show that only one-fourth of the country's growers provide sanitary facilities.  [...]more than half the farm workers have no drinking water on the job, more than one-third no access to toilets, and one-fifth no place to wash up.
ai_rationale: News on an OSHA study finding widespread lack of sanitary facilities (drinking water, toilets) for US farm workers.

authors: Agthe, Donald E; Billings, R Bruce
title: Equity, Price Elasticity, and Household Income Under Increasing Block Rates for Water
abstract: In order to examine the relationships between household income levels and residential water use, individual household survey data from Tucson, Arizona, are combined with monthly water use data for these same households.  The objectives are to examine individual response to the existing block rate pricing structure and to provide policy conclusions on potential improvements in this rate structure.  A simultaneous equation model of demand is estimated for households within each income group in order to determine the price elasticity of demand for each income group.  The demand models indicate that, under the existing increasing block rate pricing schedules, higher income households use more water and have lower elasticities of demand.  Therefore, a uniform proportional rate increase will lead to a larger percentage drop in water use among low-income households than among high-income households.  Given the assumption of declining marginal utility of water use, this result calls for a policy of substantially steeper block rates to improve interpersonal equity in water pricing.
ai_rationale: Empirical demand-model analysis of how increasing block-rate water pricing structures in Tucson, Arizona affect price elasticity and equity of water affordability across household income groups.

title: The International Drinking Water Supply and Sanitation Decade: Review of regional and global data
abstract: During 1981 data were collected from countries on the status of water supply and sanitation services to determine the situation that existed on 31 December 1980 at the commencement of the International Drinking Water Supply and Sanitation Decade (IDWSSD). The information collected, which consisted of general demographic, economic, and health statistics and data on levels of service coverage and plans and targets for 1990, institutional infrastructure, human resources development, costs and sectoral investment, constraints and Decade approaches, was analysed and used to produce the baseline figures from which Decade progress could be assessed. A similar survey was carried out during 1984 to ascertain the status of water supply and sanitation services as at 31 December 1983, after three years of Decade implementation. This publication includes summaries of some of the data by WHO Region, together with comparisons of results on a global basis (global review) and some tentative conclusions.
ai_rationale: Global/regional review of water supply and sanitation service coverage data at the outset of the International Drinking Water Supply and Sanitation Decade.

title: Water and hygiene: The case of North Carolina farmworkers
abstract: This study uses a linear regression model to examine the determinants of reported personal hygiene practices of children in 87 migrant and seasonal farmworker families in eastern North Carolina. The results suggest that by ensuring that families have water piped into multiple taps in the house, handwashing is substantially increased and that by having access to heated water and showers, bathing of children, too, may be substantially increased. It is concluded that if hygiene practices of farmworkers are to be improved, enforcement of existing State and Federal legislation will have to be improved and amendments to this legislation enacted.
ai_rationale: North Carolina study ties legislative enforcement and piped water access to farmworker hygiene outcomes.

title: Two Approaches to the Improvement of Low-Income Urban Areas -- Madras and Orangi
abstract: Although slums or squatter settlements have long been a major Ur problem in India & Pakistan, substantial public improvement has been made in only two such settlements. However, these projects -- in Madras, India, & in Orangi-Karachi, Pakistan -- differ in their orientation & the extent of their success. The emphasis of the Orangi Pilot Project (OPP) has been on self-management by the residents, which has proven to be a viable approach to improvement in low-income Ur areas. The Madras Slum Improvement Programme (SIP) is managed by public agencies, & has not been fully successful because the local community has not been effectively involved. The OPP approach is successful because it has developed local organizations & motivated residents to form local units of 20-30 households each. The Madras SIP would be more successful if the local community were involved in its planning, implementation, & maintenance. Modified AA
ai_rationale: Comparative study of self-managed (Orangi) versus publicly-managed (Madras) low-income urban slum improvement approaches, including sanitation infrastructure.

title: Will New Leadership Unlock OSHA's Resources?
abstract: Secretary of Labor William E.  Brock has been interviewing candidates for the top leadership position at the Occupational Safety and Health Administration (OSHA).  A number of candidates have been interviewed, but no front runner has emerged.  Whoever gets the nod from Brock will be subject to a White House security clearance and Senate confirmation prior to assuming control.  The new OSHA chief will not lack for an agenda.  The agency is under pressure from the courts and Congress to resolve a number of problems, including: 1.  setting field sanitation standards for agricultural workers, 2.  moving on the hazard communication standard, which involves extending coverage to workers outside the manufacturing sector, reducing restriction on disclosing trade secret protection of substances, and extending access to information about hazardous chemicals to workers and union representatives, 3.  setting final benzene standards, 4.  developing a new formaldehyde standard, and 5.  reexamining a short-term exposure limit for ethylene oxide.  Meanwhile, acting secretary Patrick L.  Tyson will face some significant challenges in implementing a plan of action for OSHA.
ai_rationale: News on OSHA regulatory agenda including field sanitation standards for agricultural workers' water/toilet access.

title: Monopoly Pricing as a Consumer Exaction in the Public Utility Sector: Monopoly Welfare Loss and Regulation in the Municipal Water Industry
abstract: The many studies of deadweight welfare loss due to monopoly power have largely ignored the public utility sector.  A study is undertaken to measure the deadweight welfare loss in the municipally-owned water industry.  The study includes tests of the effectiveness of state regulation in reducing welfare loss since the rate structures of municipalities in 5 states are subject to regulatory review at the state level, while in the remaining states the municipals are locally regulated by city councils or water commissions.  For the residential customer class, the useable formula for the welfare loss triangle depends upon the divergence between price and long-run marginal cost and the price elasticity of demand, with only price being directly observable.  The statistical methodology presented provides unique estimates of marginal cost and elasticity for each utility.  Cross-section data for the various samples are obtained from the 1965 American Water Works Association's Survey of Operating Data.  The results show that the welfare loss, as a percentage of the annual water bill of the residential customer class, is 9% to 10% for locally-regulated water utilities and 5% to 6% for state-regulated utilities.
ai_rationale: Econometric study estimating deadweight welfare loss from monopoly pricing and effectiveness of state regulation in the US municipal water industry.

authors: Olaseha, I O; Namanja, Gracian Bazilious
title: Focusing on Women for Water and Sanitation: The Case of Mapo Community in Ibadan, Nigeria
abstract: A description of an early 1980s health education project in the Mapo community (Ibadan, Nigeria). A needs assessment study based on unstructured interviews with 100 Rs indicated that an adequate, clean water supply was the community's most pressing health need. Accordingly, an educational program directed toward Fs, who traditionally fetch & maintain water supplies, was implemented, including health talks, water purification demonstrations, & workshops for health care providers. Participants demonstrated behavioral changes & satisfaction with the project, but water infection levels did not drop immediately. 4 Tables, 7 References. J. Taylor
ai_rationale: Health-education project addressing inadequate clean water supply as the most pressing need in the Mapo community, Ibadan, Nigeria, with a gendered focus on water fetching.

authors: Mumme, Stephen P; Ingram, Helen M
title: Community Values in Southwest Water Management
abstract: The applicability of the policy framework labeled the new resource economics to Western water management is challenged, particularly as applied to two examples examined here: the Papago Tribe in south-central Ariz, & Hispanic villages along the Upper Rio Grande River. Contrary to the assumptions of new resource economics, water is regarded by these communities not just as an economic commodity but as a special resource closely related to community values. It is concluded that should policy prescriptions of the new resource economics framework be adopted, community control over resources & the maintenance of traditional values would be eroded. The political system, for all its shortcomings, serves these communities better than pure market allocation of water. 3 Tables, 28 References. HA
ai_rationale: Study of Papago Tribe/Hispanic village community control over water resources versus new resource economics policy framework.

authors: Francis, Joe D; Jussaume, Raymond A, Jr
title: Community Water Systems: A Typology
abstract: The phrase "information society" reflects the growing interconnectedness of all segments of society. As mass media, business, & interpersonal communications among all reaches of society have become more numerous, the traditional distinctions between Ru & Ur society have become less meaningful. Coupled with this pervasiveness of information transferral has been the influence of reverse migration trends of the past decade. Consequently, in many spheres of life, Ru & Ur societies are becoming more like one another. Perhaps nowhere else is this melding more obvious than in the demand for community services. These developmental processes are examined through an investigation of one central, critical, pervasive local service -- community water supply (CWS). Factor analysis was used to uncover the main dimensions of attributes that characterize Ru CWS systems, including a typology. Special emphasis is given to understanding how ownership patterns of CWS systems relate to the development, use, & larger service goals (or purposes) of the community. The analysis concludes with a theoretical interpretation of the results in terms of general community infrastructure & the consequences for residents in terms of who pays for, & who benefits from, the creation & modification of CWS services. Specifically, the case of Ru CWS systems & services is used as an example of how Ru society is becoming increasingly interwoven with other aspects of US society in this day & age of extensive communication & information transferral.
ai_rationale: Typology study of rural community water supply (CWS) systems, their ownership patterns, and implications for who pays for and benefits from service.

title: Obstacles to Full Community Participation in Water Supply Programmes
abstract: Despite agreement in principle on the need for community involvement in water supply programs, the current practice of water agencies creates obstacles to such participation. Several types of programs are noted where participation is readily attained, & some ways of expanding involvement are outlined. W. H. Stoddard.
ai_rationale: Discussion of obstacles that water agency practices create for full community participation in water supply programmes.

authors: Berk, Richard A; Cooley, Thomas F; LaCivita, C J; Parker, Stanley; Sredl, Kathy; Brewer, Marilynn
title: Reducing Consumption in Periods of Acute Scarcity: The Case of Water
abstract: An important recent development in US society is a growing awareness of resource limitations. Various mechanisms have been proposed for dealing with them. Social psychology suggests that resources in common use can be conserved through such mechanisms as identification with a group suffering such shortages, moral commitment to group welfare, belief in the capacity of personal efforts to solve collective problems, belief that the personal cost of conservation is low, & belief that others will also take part in conservation. Microeconomics suggests that the use of a price system can also bring about conservation. These approaches are evaluated through data from the Calif coast communities of Goleta, Montecito, Summerland, & Carpinteria for the years 1970-1977, aggregated by month & water district. Analysis of the data shows effective results from both social & moral pressures & price changes in bringing about conservation. 6 Tables. W. H. Stoddard.
ai_rationale: Analysis of social/moral pressure and price-system mechanisms for reducing water consumption during acute scarcity in California coastal communities, 1970-1977.

title: Water Supply Constraints on Nigeria's Economic Development: The Example of Anambra State
abstract: Water supply is one of the basic infrastructures of a developed society. The water problems typical of Nigeria are illustrated through the case of Anambra State. Official statistics on water supply are examined. The estimated basic water requirement is 14 gallons per person per day; the average Ur water supply falls short by an average of 2 gallons per person per day. Limited water supply is an important factor in poor public health & high infant mortality, which in turn cause significant economic problems. State water supply is inadequate to provide a base for industrial development. Water supply problems also limit other aspects of social functioning. The problems are due not so much to inadequate technical ability as to funding problems; legal limitation of water charges to less than 50% of the estimated rate needed to pay full costs makes it impossible for the water boards & water corporations to gain sufficient funding. Some opinions for improvement of the situation are noted. 8 Tables, 1 Figure. W. H. Stoddard.
ai_rationale: Study of Nigerian (Anambra State) water supply shortfalls linked to legal rate-charge limitations constraining water board funding.

title: Water Conservation Policy Making in Local Government during Drought
abstract: Focus is on water conservation policy-making processes in 12 Iowa communities during the 1977 drought. The sample includes 3 Ur, 2 metropolitan, & 8 Ru communities. Their water resources vary. Data were gathered by in-depth personal interviews with local policy makers. Water conservation policy makers varied from community to community. Included were mayors, councilmen, personnel of public water works, members of water boards, etc. The following aspects are analyzed & discussed: (1) how the water conservation policies were made at the local government level, (2) whether or not types of water conservation policy-making processes made differences in actual policy decisions made & in their rationales, & (3) whether or not types of policies made resulted in differences in objective & subjective measures of effectiveness, the policy makers' equity evaluations, & the degree of citizen cooperation & reasons for it as perceived by the policy makers.
ai_rationale: Interview study of local government water-conservation policy-making processes, effectiveness and equity across 12 Iowa communities during the 1977 drought.

title: Water Dependency and Urban Poverty
abstract: Discussed is the inadequacy of Ur Third Word water systems; problems stem in part from demographic pressures, but more importantly from land speculation & inequities in the design of large-scale water & sewerage projects, in which the needs of Ur squatters & slum dwellers are usually excluded. Government agencies, overburdened by work in preferred sectors, are generally not equipped for the nonroutine establishment of a standpipe in poorer neighborhoods. This situation means that the poor must buy polluted water by the tin at exorbitant prices. Water sources accessible to the peri-Ur poor are often polluted by waste water drainage from the central city. Thus, the incidence of water-borne diseases is greatest among those who can least afford it. Attention is only beginning to be paid to the social effects of extant water supply systems; ongoing analysis focuses on the social economy of tariffs, water charges incidence, & investment patterns in terms of satisfying the needs of the majority. HA.
ai_rationale: Analysis of inadequate water/sewerage systems, tariffs and exclusion of urban squatters/slum dwellers in developing-country cities.

authors: Islam, Nurul; Huq, Aminul; Murshid, K A S; Hossain, Monowar
title: Water and Sanitation in Bangladesh
abstract: In Ru Bangladesh, the water suppy fluctuates between abundance & scarcity. This rhythmical oscillation means that, with the highest density of Ru population in the world, Bangladesh faces acute problems of water quality & sanitation-related diseases as well as of sufficiency. Reviewed is a UNICEF-assisted national campaign to provide potable water to the Ru population, which comprises 93% of Bangladesh's people. Evidence shows that this country will be one of the few in the Third World to reach 1980 goals set by the UN for the Water Decade. 4 Tables, 1 Figure. HA.
ai_rationale: Review of a UNICEF-assisted national rural water supply campaign in Bangladesh addressing water quality, sanitation disease and coverage against UN Water Decade goals.

authors: Mora Ramirez, Jaime; Salazar Duque, Alfredo
title: A Community-Initiated Water Supply Project in Colombia
abstract: Analyzed is the experience of a Colombian village, Juanambu, which participated in a government-sponsored water supply & sanitation program. Colombia's National Instit of Health has viewed community participation as a key element in this project, with important planning & implementation responsibilities delegated to regional & local levels -- with regard to financing as well as in construction of water systems. Estimates from 1977 suggest that 43% of Ru Colombians had potable water, 20% from individual house connections & 23% through public fountains. HA.
ai_rationale: Case study of a government-sponsored, community-participatory water supply and sanitation program in a Colombian village.

authors: Jones, Bryan D; Greenberg, Saadia R; Kaufman, Clifford; Drew, Joseph
title: Service Delivery Rules and the Distribution of Local Government Services: Three Detroit Bureaucracies
abstract: Theorized is that the distribution of municipal services to definable demographic groups is influenced by the valuation of services & the efficiency of the producing organization. Service delivery data are assembled from 3 Detroit bureaucracies: the Environmental Enforcement Division of the Environmental Protection & Maintenance Dept, the Sanitation Division of the same Dept, & the Dept of Parks & Recreation. Supplemental data are taken from the US Census. The strategy is to elaborate on the political & economic approaches & then to "trace the distributional impacts of service rules in the 3 bureaucracies." Routine service delivery rules influence service distribution & each set of rules produces different service distribution patterns. 9 Tables, 3 Figures. D. Neville.
ai_rationale: Empirical study of service delivery rules' distributional impact on sanitation (and other) services across three Detroit bureaucracies.

title: Colonias in the Lower Rio Grande Valley of South Texas: A Summary Report. Lyndon B. Johnson School of Public Affairs, Policy Research Report, Number 18
abstract: The Lower Rio Grande Valley of South Texas consists of three counties: Cameron, Hidalgo, and Willacy. Poverty pervades in the Valley, especially in the colonias ("a poor, rural unincorporated community with 20 or more dwelling units, where home ownership is the rule"). Colonia residents are almost exclusively Mexican Americans. Contributing to the problems of colonia residents is the physical and legal isolation of the colonias. The colonias are physically isolated from urban areas where the residents might obtain health care, education, low-cost food, and other necessities. Since the colonias are not part of towns and cities, they cannot benefit from those governmental units' taxes, nor from the Federal and state programs administered by towns and cities. Colonias are also faced with water-related problems, i.e., access to clean drinking water and sanitary sewage disposal. A 1975-76 Policy Research Project examined the water-related problems of the colonias. This report gives a brief overview of the demographic and economic characteristics of the Valley, presents an overview of the Valley's water resources, examines the current water supply and sewage disposal systems of the colonias, considers the cost estimates for provision of water and sewage systems of the colonias, explores the institutional alternatives for water and sewage treatment, and examines the current situation of land-use management in Texas and in the Valley. Appended is a discussion of the colonias as rural housing. (NQ)
ai_rationale: Policy research report on how the legal/institutional isolation of unincorporated colonias in South Texas (excluded from municipal governance and funding) shapes their access to clean drinking water and sanitary sewage.

title: An Analysis of the Social Impacts of the Availability and Provisions of Water in Rural Kentucky
abstract: Based on information from a comprehensive survey of the 418 Ru water supply systems in Ky, data are compiled on the proportion of the Ru population unserved by public water supplies, & the quality of water in their wells, cisterns, etc. Also, analyzed are the financial & physical characteristics of public water supply systems. Several significant social impacts of the current situation in Ru Ky are revealed. Among these are: the presence of industrial customers in a system raises the residential water rate 20 -- 50%; the development of new water systems in Ky usually means the extension of existing systems rather than water resources development projects, thereby placing increasing pressure on the resource base; water systems which buy water from another system tend to charge their customers more than customers in the "selling" system must pay resulting in periphery systems making up the losses of the central system producing water, & the apparent lack of any economies of scale in the relationship between operating costs & size of population served. Interpretation of these findings is pessimistic in view of the needs for Ru water system development: switching from poorer quality individual systems may only substitute a different set of problems for Ru residents. Institutional modifications may be in order in the arrangements for providing public water service in Ru areas.
ai_rationale: Survey-based study of the proportion of rural Kentucky population unserved by public water supplies and the financial/institutional characteristics of rural water systems.

title: Effect of Rural Industrialization on Residential Water Costs in Kentucky
abstract: Based on information from a comprehensive survey of over 400 Ru water supply systems in Ky, data from existing sources & a mail survey are compiled on the proportion of the Ru population unserved by public water supplies, & the quality of water in the systems serving the Ru population. Also, analyzed are the financial & physical characteristics of the public water supply systems. Numerous significant social & environmental impacts are documented. One of the most important for studies of the effects of industrialization on Ru communities is the finding that residential customer water rates are 20% to 50% higher when industrial & commercial customers are also supported. The reasons for this higher rate structure are examined, & the findings are related to similar studies in the literature. Findings support the contentions of the growing number of critics of industrialization as the primary strategy in Ru development.
ai_rationale: Survey study of how rural industrialization raises residential water rates and documents the unserved population in rural Kentucky water supply systems.

title: Chief Joseph Dam Community Impact Report
abstract: In 1973, the Corps of Engineers announced that funds were available to add 11 hydropower units to an existing hydroelectric dam at Bridgeport, Wash. Most nearby communities had a population of about 1,000 people or less. During construction of the original dam & 16 hydropower units in the early 1950's, local communities suffered hardships in not having enough public facilities to handle the influx of construction workers. Local citizens & governmental officials were fearful of the anticipated wave of new construction workers into the area. The study was a planning tool which (1) identified population impact problems for each community within commuting distance, (2) provided guidelines to selected communities to deal with the problems, & (3) identified potential sources of assistance. The study projected total population associated with construction activities. Community public facilities & services within commuting distance were inventoried & population service capacity determined. Evaluation developed current standards for the use of water supply systems, sewage disposal systems, schools, police protection, fire protection, & medical facilities & services. Result provided degree of present use of excess or deficient capacity to provide for increased population. Difficult areas of evaluation were (A) determination of size of public facility or service as standards vary, & (B) allocation of construction related population to several communities. The evaluation provided base conditions with projections of possible impacts. The report has been & is currently used by local planners & government officials in requesting governmental funding for public utilities & schools. Follow-up studies are discussed.
ai_rationale: Community impact planning study evaluating water-supply, sewage-disposal and other public-facility capacity for communities near the Chief Joseph Dam construction.

title: Self-Help in Rural Mexico: Santa Maria's Well
abstract: A successful effort of village self-help in Ru Mexico is described, & the implications of this kind of activity for Ru development are considered. The village, Santa Maria Aquiahuac de Ocotlan, was settled in 1950, &, having no services at its inception, one of the first priorities was to get an assured supply of water. The water situation when the village was first settled is decribed, as are the first & second phases of the digging of the well, the organizational problems that developed between phases, & the methods used to overcome the obstacles. The same spirit of self-help that resulted in the successful digging of the well which became accessible to the entire village, carried over to other community projects, such as the building of the school, the hiring of a teacher, road construction, installation of electricity, & the organization of a rabbit reproduction center. G. Simpson.
ai_rationale: Case study of Mexican village self-help organizing to secure a community water well and supply.

title: The Challenge of Africa's Water Development
abstract: Although Africa boasts of immense water resources, & some of the greatest modern water-related energy feats were performed there (eg, Aswan Dam), the battle against natural calamities such as draught is nowhere near being won. A UN study showed that only 73% of the Ur & 19% of the Ru African population had access to safe water supply. The slow rate of growth in the extension of access guarantees that unless some radical solution is soon found, the numbers of Africans lacking access will continue to grow. Another disparity is between the 3.5% annual population increase & the slower 2.5% food production increase. The anomaly is that the food shortage could be eliminated if existing resources were properly utliized. It is encouraging that a tradition of regional cooperation is taking shape among the newly independent African nations. That gives some hope that Africa will not only resolve its water development difficulties by the time it reaches a critical point at the end of this century, but that its experience may be helpful to Asia & Latin America. S. Karganovic.
ai_rationale: Discussion of Africa's water development challenges including access statistics and regional cooperation policy.

authors: Blase, Melvin G; GREEN, PARMAN R; Matson, Arthur
title: SELECTED IMPACTS OF PUBLIC WATER SUPPLY DISTRICTS ON FIRMS, HOUSEHOLDS AND COMMUNITIES
abstract: WATER & SEWAGE UTILITY SERVICES HAVE REMAINED DEFICIENT IN RU AREAS. THESE DEFICIENCIES HAVE CONSTITUTED SIGNIFICANT OBSTACLES TO THE DEVELOPMENT OF RU COMMUNITIES. CHANGES IN 2 COMMUNITIES SUBSEQUENT TO THE INITIATION OF PUBLIC WATER SUPPLY DISTRICTS (PWSD'S) ARE IDENTIFIED & DOCUMENTED. THESE COMMUNITIES ILLUSTRATE CHARACTERISTICS OF RU & RU-UR US. BARTON COUNTY PWSD NO. 1, IN MO, WAS SELECTED FOR STUDY. IN THE ANALYSIS, THE FOCUS WAS ON POPULATION MOVEMENTS, HOUSEHOLD FACILITIES, & LAND VALUES. THE LACK OF ADEQUATE WATER PRIOR TO THE FORMATION OF THE PWSD IS FOUND TO HAVE BEEN A CONSTRAINT TO POPULATION GROWTH IN THE DISTRICTS. WHEN THE PWSD WAS BUILT, THE VALUE OF LAND PER ACRE INCREASED. THIS PLACED THE ABSOLUTE DOLLAR ADVANTAGE WITH FARMERS. THE WATER DISTRICT WAS ALSO A KEY FACTOR IN IMPROVEMENTS MADE IN THE HOMES. PUBLIC WATER SUPPLY DISTRICTS HAVE A MEASURABLE IMPACT ON COMMUNITIES, FIRMS, & HOUSEHOLDS. A SECONDARY EFFECT IS TO INCREASE THE COST OF OTHER PUBLIC SERVICES. RU-UR FRINGE AREAS WILL EXPERIENCE MORE RAPID URBANIZATION TRENDS AS A CONSEQUENCE OF PWSD DEVELOPMENT. MORE COMPREHENSIVE PLANNING PRIOR TO FORMATION OF ADDITIONAL DISTRICTS & FURTHER INVESTIGATIONS OF THEIR EXPOST IMPACTS ARE NEEDED. MODIFIED HA.
ai_rationale: Study of the impacts of establishing public water supply districts on rural households, firms and communities in Missouri, addressing prior water/sewage deficiencies as a constraint on rural development.

title: MIGRATORY LABOR IN COLORADO. PROGRESS REPORT
abstract: DEVELOPMENTS, FROM 1950 THROUGH 1960, ARE TRACED CONCERNING MIGRATORY LABOR IN COLORADO IN THE AREAS OF EMPLOYMENT, WAGE RATES, MINIMUM WAGE LEGISLATION, EMPLOYMENT OF MEXICAN NATIONALS, EDUCATION, HEALTH, HOUSING, SANITATION, WELFARE, UNEMPLOYMENT COMPENSATION, WORKMEN'S COMPENSATION COVERAGE, AND THE LICENSING AND REGULATION OF LABOR CONTRACTORS AND CREW LEADERS. FUNDING AND ENFORCEMENT OF REGULATIONS ARE THE MAJOR OBSTACLES TO FULFILLMENT OF GOALS FOR IMPROVING THE LIVING, TRAVELING, AND WORKING CONDITIONS OF THE MIGRANT. INTERSTATE PROGRAMS HAVE TO BE WORKED OUT BEFORE THE PROGRAM WITHIN A STATE CAN FUNCTION AT ITS BEST. FIELD STUDIES AND REGIONAL MEETINGS ARE PLANNED TO PROVIDE ADDITIONAL INFORMATION TOWARD SOLUTION OF PROBLEMS INVOLVED. IT WAS RECOMMENDED THAT THE PRESENT SUMMER SCHOOL PROGRAM FOR MIGRANT CHILDREN BE EXPANDED, THAT FINANCING CONTINUE TO BE DRAWN FROM THE CONTINGENCY FUND OF THE PUBLIC SCHOOL FOUNDATION, THAT STATUTES WHICH AUTHORIZED THE STATE BOARD OF HEALTH TO PERFORM SPECIFIC FUNCTIONS AND PROMULGATE RULES AND REGULATIONS, ESPECIALLY WITH RESPECT TO LABOR CAMPS AND SANITATION, BE REVISED TO GIVE ADEQUATE REGULATORY AND ENFORCEMENT POWERS, AND THAT THE EMPLOYMENT OF MEXICAN NATIONALS BE STUDIED FURTHER, WITH GREATER EFFORT DIRECTED AT EMPLOYING DOMESTIC INTERSTATE AND INTRASTATE MIGRANTS WHENEVER POSSIBLE. LEGISLATIVE DEVELOPMENTS ARE APPENDED, BILL BY BILL. TABLES SHOW WAGES PAID, AND WELFARE EXPENDITURES.
ai_rationale: Government progress report tracking sanitation, health and regulatory enforcement conditions for migrant farm labor in Colorado, 1950-1960.

title: THIRSTY INDIANS, INTRODUCTION OF WELLS AMONG PEOPLE OF AN ARID REGION
abstract: A report of the Papagos Indians, who inhabit an arid region in North America. They suffered constantly from a scarcity of water and were forced to move from season to season to follow the scant available water. Wells were brought in by whites, either in connection with mining or cattle rearing; whites later departed leaving the wells. Wells were also constructed by the IB, usually at centers of pop. There was one example of opposition to the construction of a well by a tribal spokesman, but the government went ahead. The very necessity of a supply of water forced the capitulation of the spokesman and his faction. The bare necessities of living forced technological change upon the Papagos and with this came changes in their living habits and in other aspects of the culture. W. Linton.
ai_rationale: Historical ethnographic account of government/Indian Bureau well construction resolving chronic water scarcity among the Papagos, including community response to institutional provision.

authors: Fobi Kontor M.; Núñez Collado J.R.; Brown A.
title: Bridging the Gap in Urban Water Accessibility: Exploring the Barriers to Equity in Water Access in Ghana
abstract: Access to clean water is recognised by the United Nations as a fundamental human right. However, in urban Ghana, significant disparities exist in access to clean water, particularly in poor communities. This chapter analyses the persistent inequalities in urban water accessibility in Greater Accra to understand the barriers hindering equitable water provision. We do this by examining four interconnected aspects: colonial legacies that shape fragmented water infrastructure, contemporary infrastructural deficits, commodification and privatisation of water services, and fragmented governance and regulatory mechanisms. Using these dimensions as analytical lenses, we demonstrate how historical patterns of urban planning and water infrastructure development under colonial rule established spatial inequalities that persist today. Contemporary infrastructure gaps and poor water governance further deepen these disparities, particularly in low-income and informal urban communities. These areas often rely on costly informal water sources such as tankers and sachets/bottled water. Privatisation efforts promoted under neoliberal policies and commodification practices have further exacerbated these inequities by prioritising profit over equitable distribution. By unpacking these interconnected factors, the chapter calls for a new paradigm of urban water governance, one that explicitly prioritises equity, reclaims water as a social and ecological good, and foregrounds the voices and agency of marginalised communities. This lays the foundation for advancing sustainable water management to drive resilient urban waterscapes. © The Author(s), under exclusive license to Springer Nature Switzerland AG 2026.
ai_rationale: Chapter analyzing Ghana urban water access inequities via governance/privatization lenses, but empirical method unclear from abstract.

authors: Chirwa E.; Mwalwanda A.; Soko M.; Mbakaya B.C.
title: Effectiveness of emergency WASH strategies in disaster-prone areas of Africa: a systematic review
abstract: Gap analyses conducted in emergency water, sanitation, and hygiene (WASH) interventions have pinpointed essential obstacles to the effective implementation of sanitation in disaster scenarios. This systematic review aimed to gather and consolidate evidence on the effectiveness of emergency sanitation strategies in areas that experience disasters. We systematically searched for articles in the ReliefWeb, International Organization for Migration (IOM), World Health Organization (WHO), United Nations Office for the Coordination of Humanitarian Affairs (OCHA), Google Scholar, PubMed, Directory of Open Access Journals (DOAJ), BASE (Bielefeld Academic Search Engine), Web of Science, Scopus, Cochrane Library, Hinari, Medline, and African Index Medicus databases, guided by the best practice developed by the PROSPERO and COCHRANE for systematic search and selection of articles. Search strings were applied across these databases. In addition, a PRISMA flow diagram was used to elaborate on the number of articles retrieved, retained, excluded, and the reasons for every action. Studies that evaluated emergency sanitation strategies in disaster areas of Africa, which were interventional in nature, were included in this review. A mixed-methods appraisal tool was used to appraise studies. Six articles met the eligibility criteria. Of the six articles, only three reported the challenges faced during the implementation of emergency sanitation interventions during an emergency, particularly in response to cholera outbreaks. The findings from all the studies have not directly specified the sanitation strategies suitable for a specific type of disaster. However, the nature of the emergency context (e.g., displaced populations, poor water quality, makeshift facilities) allows us to infer suitability for specific disaster types. One study found that 87% of the drinking water sources tested were contaminated with fecal matter, which was likely a major contributor to the continued cholera outbreak. However, emergency sanitation measures introduced in response showed a positive impact (water testing and treatment, chlorine sprayers, waste incineration, water storage tanks, and health promotion), reflected by a downward trend in cholera cases, as was seen in the epidemic curve. This systematic review emphasizes that while emergency sanitation measures in Africa have considerable potential to lessen disease spread during disasters, their effectiveness is frequently hampered by contextual, logistical, behavioral, and infrastructural challenges. The success of these measures is closely linked to prompt execution, cultural relevance, fair distribution of resources, and ongoing community involvement. © 2026 The Authors.
ai_rationale: Systematic review of emergency WASH intervention effectiveness; unclear whether a legal/administrative/governance factor is examined as exposure.

authors: Ogata R.; Matsumoto S.; Otsuka T.; Hattori Y.; Kitawaki H.
title: Influence of customer satisfaction and perceived water service quality on urban water supply management: A systematic review
abstract: Previous studies have found relationships among customer satisfaction, the management of water utilities, and users' willingness to pay (WTP) for improved water service quality. However, these studies have captured only part of the water supply situation in each country. This study, through a systematic literature review of 62 studies published since 2010, aimed to clarify the measures taken for the effective management of water utilities, focusing on improvements in water supply service quality and customer satisfaction. A search of relevant databases using keywords such as “Water AND Consumer,” “Water AND Customer,” and “Water AND Willingness to Pay” originally yielded 4131 articles for the sample period of 2010 to June 2023. The systematic literature review of the finally selected 62 studies showed that water service improvement generally had a positive impact on WTP. Countries or service areas with lower water supply service quality showed a higher WTP than countries or service areas in which services were already at a certain level. A number of studies indicated a significant correlation between customer satisfaction and water supply services. However, the factors that customers valued varied by the water supply conditions and needs in each country. Some studies suggested that customers evaluated water supply services based on their past experiences with reliability. Others showed that improving customer satisfaction may enhance management of water utility. As recommendations for policymaking, water utilities should conduct regular surveys to evaluate customers' satisfaction with water services, focusing on customers’ priorities, WTP, and trust in the water utility. © 2026 The Authors
ai_rationale: Systematic review linking customer satisfaction/WTP to water utility management; legal/administrative exposure and population unclear from abstract.

title: From the Paramos to the City: Environmental History, Water Sources, and More-Than-Human Governance for the City of Quito, Ecuador; [Dos páramos à cidade: história ambiental, fontes de água e governança mais que humana para a cidade de Quito, Equador]; [De los páramos a la urbe: historia ambiental, fuentes de agua y gobernanza más que humana para la ciudad de Quito, Ecuador]
abstract: Objective/context: This paper presents a historiographical review to characterize Quito’s expansionist water policy, tracing its origins from the colonial and republican periods to the development of the expansionist model of municipal hydraulics (1950-1975). It then identifies a turning point influenced by dominant trends in welfare programs and conservation efforts. Finally, it outlines a third phase of this model: Integrated Water Resources Management (iwrm) (1990-2000), culminating in a new form of environmental governance for the city of Quito, Ecuador (2000-present). Methodology: Based on a historiographical analysis of drinking water services and environmental policies in Quito, this study highlights the different stages of hydraulic expansionism and draws on specialized literature on environmental conservation in Ecuador. It explores conflicts within public water policies and their effects on contemporary water management. Originality: While historical overviews of urban water in Quito exist, they tend to focus only on the early dynamics of the city’s modernization, based on a simplified view of technology. This article first addresses this deficiency by highlighting later phases of the urban water system as correlates of different moments in the expansionist model and, second, by exploring the connection between technology and the environment. Conclusions: We examine the role of the Water Protection Fund (ronas, for its acronym in Spanish) in Quito’s environmental and infrastructural transformation, arguing that this fund is innovative not only because it connects water conservation with environmental protection but also because, through its work, it provides input for a more-than-human environmental history. © 2026, Universidad de los Andes, Colombia. All rights reserved.
ai_rationale: Historiographical review of Quito's water policy evolution and governance; unclear if it reports an identifiable empirical access outcome.

authors: Rojas C.; Riascos-Ochoa J.; Clerici N.; Longo-Sánchez M.C.
title: Integrating local perceptions and Bayesian belief networks into model ecosystem services multifunctionality in the Colombian Andes
abstract: Access to water in rural watersheds is affected by land-use changes and limited integration of governance factors into ecosystem service (ES) analysis. This study implemented a participatory spatial Bayesian belief network (BBN) for the practical application of ES multifunctionality in Rural water supply systems (RWSS) to enhance their role in watershed planning and governance. The framework applies indicators of ES supply and demand (derived from the InVEST and ARIES models), socioeconomic data (demographic and multidimensional poverty), and local perceptions collected through interviews. Two BBN models were developed: Model 1 used quantitative biophysical and socioeconomic indicators. Model 2: Incorporating governance and perception variables from a local community perspective. Probabilistic spatial inference and uncertainty analysis were implemented to map multifunctionality and to identify priority zones for governance. The results showed that incorporating local perceptions increased the probability of highly multifunctional areas by approximately 10%, particularly in the upper sub-watersheds characterized by strong local participation. The uncertainty analysis identified transitional agricultural–urban zones as areas that require additional data collection and participatory validation. The participatory BBN framework successfully integrated socio-ecological and governance dimensions, facilitating the identification of ES multifunctionality zones that align ecological integrity with community priorities. A spatial BBN is a flexible methodology for data-scarce Andean regions that supports watershed management plans. This approach contributes to a method that links stakeholder perceptions to spatial decision-making and benefits achievement to Sustainable Development Goals (SDG), SDG 6 (Clean Water and Sanitation), and SDG 15 (Life on Land) by advancing adaptive, inclusive, and evidence-based watershed planning. © The Author(s) 2026.
ai_rationale: Participatory Bayesian model of rural water-supply governance and ecosystem-service multifunctionality; outcome is a multifunctionality index, not clearly an access/connection metric.

title: A systems thinking approach to operationalizing integrated water resources management in Ethiopia through leverage points and feedback loops
abstract: Operationalizing Integrated Water Resources Management (IWRM) in climate-vulnerable and water-insecure contexts is constrained by complex interactions among hydrological variability, infrastructural deficits, institutional capacity, and socioeconomic conditions. This study applies an integrated semi-quantitative systems framework to identify leverage points and dominant feedback loops that shape IWRM implementation in Ethiopia. This approach combines causal loop diagramming, eigenvector centrality, MICMAC influence-dependency analysis, and structural loop gain assessment to examine how the system structure governs behavior. Six leverage points, household income level, access to reliable water supply, governance effectiveness, economic water scarcity, food availability and access, and irrigation coverage, emerge as critical system connectors and strategic intervention nodes relevant to SDG 6.5 implementation. The results indicate that IWRM performance is driven by isolated sectoral action rather than by reinforcing feedback linking water access, livelihoods, food availability, and economic water scarcity, thus amplifying vulnerability to rainfall variability, limited storage capacity, and chronic underinvestment. The balancing feedback between governance effectiveness and infrastructure investment suggests a potential regulatory pathway to stabilize system performance, though its influence is constrained by institutional fragmentation and financial constraints. By explicitly linking system behavior to DG 6.5.1 (degree of IWRM implementation), this study demonstrates that effective IWRM operationalization requires coordinated interventions that simultaneously strengthen water infrastructure, governance capacity, and livelihood resilience. The proposed framework complements SDG monitoring by revealing the structural constraints and feedback mechanisms that must be addressed to achieve integrated, equitable, and climate-resilient water management in Ethiopia and other similar water-insecure countries. © The Author(s) 2026.
ai_rationale: Systems-dynamics modeling of IWRM leverage points including governance and water access in Ethiopia; primary data source/population unclear from abstract.

authors: Pandey S.; Acharya S.; Bhandari S.; Running K.
title: Effectiveness and equity of local climate adaptation: Evidence from a comparative LAPA case study in rural Nepal
abstract: Like other countries, Nepal’s National Adaptation Program of Action (NAPA) institutionalized the Local Adaptation Plan of Action (LAPA) to translate national climate priorities into locally grounded, pro-poor adaptation strategies. Despite its international recognition as a participatory model, systematic evidence of its distributive effectiveness remains limited. This study evaluates LAPA outcomes using the Livelihood Vulnerability Index (LVI) to compare vulnerability levels between LAPA-implemented and non-implemented communities and across caste groups (Brahmin and Dalit). Based on face-to-face surveys with 80 households, we constructed LVI scores across nine components: socio-demographic profile, livelihood strategies, social networks, food, water, health, infrastructure, natural disasters, and climate variability. Results show that the LAPA-implemented community exhibits slightly higher overall vulnerability than the non-implemented community, challenging assumptions that localized adaptation planning automatically reduces vulnerability. While some targeted gains are evident in adaptation-related infrastructure, including water, these improvements were partial and unevenly distributed, and did not reduce overall vulnerability. Dalit households remain disproportionately vulnerable, particularly in socio-demographic conditions and social networks, critical determinants of adaptive capacity. Of 38 implemented activities, most focused on drinking water supply and commercially oriented livelihood diversification, with minimal attention to strengthening social capital or addressing structural inequalities. Interventions disproportionately benefited relatively better-off households with irrigated land and greater risk-bearing capacity. These findings suggest that technocratic, infrastructure-driven adaptation planning may fail to confront entrenched social hierarchies that shape vulnerability. Enhancing LAPA’s effectiveness requires embedding equity-sensitive targeting, strengthening social capital, and integrating social justice considerations into adaptation design and implementation. Without addressing underlying socio-political drivers of vulnerability, decentralized adaptation risks reinforcing existing inequalities rather than reducing them. © The Author(s) 2026.
ai_rationale: Household survey evaluating a climate-adaptation program's uneven drinking-water infrastructure gains by caste; water is one of several vulnerability domains.

authors: Leite J.; Carmo C.; Correia G.
title: Enhancing Efficiency in Urban Water Services: Applying the Balanced Scorecard to the Portuguese Municipal Company AEP
abstract: This study explores how the Balanced Scorecard (BSC) can enhance strategic management practices aimed at minimizing treated water losses in a municipal water utility. Although operational efficiency has shown improvement, unbilled treated water remained notably high in 2020, exceeding 17% during distribution. This ongoing inefficiency underscores the importance of systematic, theory-informed approaches for sustainable performance enhancement. A mixed-methods design was employed, combining qualitative insights with quantitative data derived from financial statements and managerial forecasting tools. These inputs were synthesized into a strategic map aligned with the four BSC perspectives, enabling the effective translation of strategy into measurable objectives. Findings indicate that implementing the BSC strengthened organizational alignment, refined planning processes, and enhanced performance assessment. The framework also clarified the connections between financial outcomes and non-financial performance drivers. Particular attention was given to the learning and growth perspective, highlighting the crucial role of employee engagement in addressing inefficiencies. This focus supports improvements in internal processes, such as technological modernization and infrastructure upgrades, which contribute to stronger customer relationships and increased awareness of efficient water use. Overall, the study confirms the BSC as a valuable tool for strategic governance and evidence-based decision-making in the water utility sector. © 2026. Joaquim LEITE, Cecília CARMO and Gastão CORREIA.
ai_rationale: Case study applying Balanced Scorecard governance tool to a water utility's non-revenue water; unclear link to household access/connection outcome.

authors: Sinharoy S.S.; Xia D.; Patrick M.; McManus S.; Chipungu J.; Reddy Y.M.; Ahmed T.; Mink T.; Pan Y.; Bhan T.; Conrad A.; Caruso B.A.
title: The Agency, Resources, and Institutional Structures for Sanitation-related Empowerment (ARISE) scales: Psychometric evaluation across eight cities in Asia and Africa
abstract: A well-established need exists for reliable and valid measures of empowerment across sectors, including in water, sanitation, and hygiene (WASH). To address this need, we followed a multi-phased, theory-informed approach to develop the Agency, Resources, and Institutional Structures for Sanitation-related Empowerment (ARISE) scales, a set of 16 distinct yet inter-related scales, each of which measures a different sub-domain of women’s empowerment related to urban sanitation in low- and middle-income country settings. Here we present the third of three phases, which was focused on refining and further evaluating the ARISE scales. The objective of the current phase of work was to evaluate the reliability, validity, and measurement properties of the ARISE scales using cross-sectional data collected between August 2021 and June 2022 from a total of 5,586 women across eight cities in Asia and Africa: Meherpur (N = 720) and Saidpur (N = 730), Bangladesh; Narsapur (N = 721), Tiruchirappalli (N = 563), and Warangal (N = 704), India; Dakar, Senegal (N = 720); Kampala, Uganda (N = 713); and Lusaka, Zambia (N = 715). We evaluated the psychometric properties of the scales, including by using factor analytic methods to assess structural validity and measurement invariance across country settings and over time; calculating coefficients of internal consistency (composite reliability) and test-retest reliability; and using generalized linear regression, nonparametric Spearman rank correlations, t-tests, and ANOVA to test for construct, known groups, and criterion validity. We demonstrate that the ARISE scales can measure most sub-constructs of sanitation-related empowerment in a reliable and valid way, to generate data for better prioritization, design, implementation, and evaluation of strategies to improve women’s empowerment in the context of urban sanitation at the program and policy level. We also describe how these scales can contribute to our understanding of empowerment as a universal concept and process that can be quantitatively measured across contexts and populations using rigorous psychometric methods. © 2026 Sinharoy et al. This is an open access article distributed under the terms of the Creative Commons Attribution License, which permits unrestricted use, distribution, and reproduction in any medium, provided the original author and source are credited.
ai_rationale: Psychometric validation of sanitation-empowerment scales across 8 cities; primarily a measurement-development study, not a reported access outcome.

authors: Brum M.; Pathiraja V.; Haddadi M.; Saraswath L.; Kurmi O.; Rathnayake N.; Eleje G.U.; Mbwele B.; Ikwuka D.C.; Mitra P.K.; Nguyen N.T.; Wijamuni N.; Benetti-Pinto C.; Tweneboah-Koduah F.; Martyn-Dickens C.; Mintah-Afful N.; Kemp H.F.; Shi J.Q.; Elneil S.; Phiri P.; Delanerolle G.
title: Brazil's national menstrual health program–Progress, gaps, and pathways to equity: A concept note (PLATO WP1)
abstract: Brazil recently implemented a national menstrual health program within its public health system (Sistema Único de Saúde [SUS]), representing a significant policy shift toward recognizing menstrual dignity as a public health and human rights issue. The distribution of menstrual products has expanded rapidly; however, this alone is insufficient to address the structural inequalities affecting menstrual health. The aim of the present study was to analyze the implementation of the menstrual health program in Brazil, identify existing inequalities and operational barriers, and propose a research and data framework capable of strengthening monitoring, policymaking, and global collaboration. The study is part of the PLATO project (Work Package 1), integrating public health, gender equality, and implementation science. A narrative analysis was conducted using government and legal documents, demographic and WASH data, and international literature on menstrual equity. Despite strong legislation and intersectoral governance, substantial gaps remain in access, digital inclusion, infrastructure, and participation of marginalized groups. Brazil lacks standardized indicators, interoperable data systems, and monitoring strategies to assess real outcomes. A logic model and equity-centered research architecture are proposed to address these gaps by integrating product provision, WASH, data systems, community participation, and global integration. Brazil has made fundamental progress in menstrual health policy. However, achieving menstrual dignity requires moving beyond product distribution to integrated data collection, infrastructure, equity monitoring, and participatory governance. This framework offers a model applicable to Brazil and other low- and middle-income countries. © 2026 International Federation of Gynecology and Obstetrics.
ai_rationale: Concept note analyzing Brazil's menstrual-health legislation and WASH access gaps; narrative policy analysis, empirical basis unclear.

authors: Kpodzro S.; Cronk R.; Lineberger H.; Lansing L.; Anderson D.M.
title: Implementation and adaptation of WASH FIT in healthcare facilities: A systematic scoping review
abstract: Environmental health services are important for patient safety and strong health systems, yet access in many countries is poor. To address this, the World Health Organization (WHO) and the United Nations Children’s Fund (UNICEF) developed the Water and Sanitation for Health Facility Improvement Tool (WASH FIT) to drive improvements. While widely used, there is no systematic documentation of how WASH FIT has been adapted across contexts and the implications of these adaptations. We conducted a systematic scoping review to assess WASH FIT implementation contexts and processes, adaptations, and good practices for implementation. We included peer reviewed and grey literature that described the implementation and/or adaptation of WASH FIT in at least one healthcare facility in a low- or middle-income country. Our search yielded 20 studies; few reported details on healthcare facility contexts. Adaptation was widespread, with nearly all studies deviating from the five-step WASH FIT cycle as designed in the WHO/UNICEF manual. Many studies conducted only one facility assessment and one or no rounds of improvement. Good practices for implementation included adequate resourcing, government leadership, and providing WASH FIT teams with sufficient training and autonomy. Low-quality reporting and a high degree of adaptation make it challenging to determine how and why WASH FIT achieves change. We hypothesize that healthcare facility-level action by WASH FIT teams to assess conditions and implement improvements has some effect. However, advocacy that uses WASH FIT indicators to highlight deficiencies and promotion of WASH FIT by WHO and UNICEF to pressure government action may be equally or more powerful drivers of change. More rigorous evidence to understand how and why WASH FIT works is essential to improve its performance and inform scale-up. © 2026 The Author(s).
ai_rationale: Systematic scoping review of a WASH improvement tool in healthcare facilities; population is healthcare facilities rather than households/communities.

authors: Gaudry A.; Colon M.; Baron C.
title: REVISITING: Off-grid, the New Water Supply Solution
abstract: Drawing on recent research, policy reports, and interviews, this chapter explores what the term "off-grid" – originally borrowed from the energy sector – means in the water sector. Off-grid water solutions encompass a wide range of arrangements, many of which have long existed to serve populations whose needs are unmet by water utilities. What has changed over the past decade, however, is the shift in perspective: once viewed as temporary fixes until network expansion, off-grid solutions are now increasingly seen as a desirable and sustainable option for achieving SDG 6.1 (universal access to safe and affordable drinking water). This chapter critically examines the expectations placed on off-grid solutions and reviews the challenges that must be overcome to position them as a viable alternative to centralised piped water supply. A key question emerges: How should public authorities adapt the governance and regulation of complex, fragmented water supply systems in order to ensure equity, continuity, quality, and protection of water resources? © 2026 selection and editorial matter, François Molle and Sylvain Barone.
ai_rationale: Book chapter on off-grid water governance and regulation; empirical basis (interviews) unclear relative to conceptual discussion.

authors: Vogelmann E.S.; Prevedello J.; Tiruneh G.A.
title: Drinking Water Quality Regulations: A Contrast Between Germany and Latin America
abstract: This article investigates the differences among drinking water quality standards adopted in Latin American countries, Mexico, Cuba, and the European Union, considering the growing challenge of ensuring safe drinking water in a context marked by environmental pressures, climate change, and the occurrence of emerging contaminants. The study aims to compare regulatory limits, identify normative inconsistencies, and assess the extent to which these divergences may compromise public health protection. To achieve this objective, the research employs a comparative documentary analysis, examining legislation, technical parameters, and water quality management instruments currently in force in the regions evaluated. The investigation analyzes microbiological indicators, priority chemical substances, operational parameters, and the presence or absence of risk-based approaches. The results show that the European Union, particularly Germany, adopts more stringent standards and updates its technical references more frequently, whereas several Latin American countries maintain more permissive limits, regulatory gaps regarding emerging toxins, and lower integration of water safety plans. These findings indicate that the observed differences stem not only from technical choices but also reflect structural inequalities related to institutional capacity, availability of financial resources, governance mechanisms, and continuity of public policies. The study concludes that regulatory harmonization across regions requires progressive strategies that strengthen institutions, expand investments in sanitation, promote international cooperation, and systematically incorporate risk assessments, thereby ensuring more protective and effective standards for the quality of drinking water intended for human consumption. © 2026 The Author(s). Environmental Quality Management published by Wiley Periodicals LLC.
ai_rationale: Comparative legal/regulatory analysis of drinking-water quality standards; outcome is regulatory stringency, not clearly an access/connection/affordability metric.

authors: Zaman M.N.U.; Sai A.; Yamauchi T.
title: Knowledge, economic, and WASH challenges affecting menstrual health and hygiene among nursing students in Bangladesh using a mixed-methods approach
abstract: Menstrual health and hygiene (MHH) remain stigmatized and neglected in low- and middle-income countries such as Bangladesh due to cultural taboos, poor infrastructure, and limited education. This study examines how knowledge, socioeconomic background, and WASH facilities are associated with key MHH indicators. A convergent mixed-methods design was applied between December 2024 and January 2025, combining a survey of 370 students from seven public nursing institutions with six focus group discussions involving 21 female and 21 male students for gendered understanding. Quantitative data were analyzed using descriptive statistics and multivariable logistic regression, while qualitative data were examined through thematic analysis. Quantitative results showed that adequate access to menstrual products was associated with higher odds among students enrolled in the B.Sc. in Nursing program (AOR = 6.91, 95% CI 2.44–19.55, p < 0.05), as well as among students whose mothers had secondary education (AOR = 4.82, 95% CI 1.52–15.28, p < 0.05). Adequate WASH facilities were also associated with higher odds among students in the B.Sc. in Midwifery (Post Basic) program (AOR = 2.87, 95% CI 1.28–6.43, p < 0.05) and those whose mothers had higher secondary education (AOR = 6.19, 95% CI 1.47–26.00, p < 0.05). Qualitative findings revealed limited menstrual knowledge prior to menarche, embarrassment in purchasing products, unmanaged menstrual pain, and inadequate privacy and disposal facilities within campuses. Male students reported minimal formal exposure to menstrual education but demonstrated increased awareness of menstrual pain, privacy needs, and disposal challenges after engaging in shared academic and residential environments. This study is novel in integrating male student perspectives with institutional WASH constraints in nursing education, positioning menstruation as both a gendered and systems-level issue. The findings support actionable recommendations for gender-inclusive MHH curricula, minimum WASH standards in educational institutions, and policy alignment between nursing education, sanitation infrastructure, and menstrual waste management to promote menstrual dignity and equitable health training. © The Author(s) 2026.
ai_rationale: Mixed-methods survey of WASH-facility association with menstrual hygiene among nursing students; population/exposure framing is individual-level rather than clearly institutional/legal.

authors: Kumar S.; Mishra S.; Kumar A.
title: Deciphering the Water Accessibility in Urban Neighbourhoods: A Case of Water Supply in Delhi
abstract: The growing population brings along an increased demand for infrastructure and services in our cities; hence, city managers will never stop working to meet that demand. Water shortage is one of the main bottlenecks to urbanization, together with other fundamental societal needs. The Urban Local Body (ULB) or Municipal Corporation in an urban region takes responsibility to provide safe drinking water and availability of water supply for all domestic, commercial, and industrial purposes, as per the 12th Schedule of the Indian Constitution. According to Sustainable Development Goals, 2030, especially SDG-6, all sections of society should have access to and management of water and sanitation services. This research will evaluate the water accessibility in urban neighbourhoods of Delhi and will also assess the role of Urban Local Body and other agencies in it. © The Author(s), under exclusive license to Springer Nature Singapore Pte Ltd. 2026.
ai_rationale: Study of urban water accessibility and municipal-body governance role in Delhi; methodology described in future/proposal tense, empirical completion unclear.

title: The Effect of Water Access on Female Health, Nutrition and Economic Empowerment—A Case Study of Kaudihar Block, Prayagraj, India
abstract: Access to clean water significantly impacts female health, nutrition, and economic empowerment, particularly in rural areas. The study examines the manifold effects of water accessibility on the lives of women in Kaudihar Block, Prayagraj, India. Using a mixed-methods approach, data were collected through household surveys, interviews, and focus group discussions with local women. The findings reveal that inadequate access to water exacerbates health issues such as waterborne diseases and increases the physical burden on women, adversely affecting maternal health. Nutritional outcomes are compromised, as limited water availability restricts household food preparation and kitchen gardening. Economically, the time spent enticing water reduces opportunities for women to engage in income-generating activities, hindering their financial independence. Generally, water scarcity reinforces gender inequalities by limiting women’s mobility and participation in decision-making processes. Even though existing government interventions, significant gaps remain in infrastructure, maintenance, and policy implementation. This study underscores the urgent need for gender-sensitive policies and community-driven initiatives to improve water access. Recommendations include implementing sustainable water management systems, launching awareness campaigns, and involving women in local water governance. By addressing these issues, the study contributes to the broader discourse on achieving sustainable development goals related to health, gender equality, and water and sanitation. © The Author(s), under exclusive license to Springer Nature Singapore Pte Ltd. 2026.
ai_rationale: Mixed-methods study of water access effects on women's health/economic outcomes; policy-implementation gaps noted but outcome is broader welfare, not directly access/connection/affordability.

authors: Chen C.-Y.; Cai Y.-S.; Hung Y.-J.; You G.J.-Y.
title: Institutional conflicts of interest in regional water management: a case study of the water supply in the Taipei metropolitan area
abstract: Institutional conflicts of interest constrain regional water management in metropolitan systems supplied by multiple reservoirs and operated by separate utilities. Such conflicts arise when decentralized utilities pursue cost-minimizing strategies that diverge from system-wide reliability and social welfare objectives. This study examines these dynamics in the Taipei metropolitan water supply system, where two reservoirs with contrasting hydrological reliability are physically connected through a cross-basin water transfer infrastructure intended to rebalance regional allocation. A deterministic scenario-based analysis using the Water Evaluation and Planning (WEAP) model is conducted under varying hydrological stress regimes to evaluate alternative allocation priorities and pricing structures. The analysis links hydrological conditions, infrastructure operation, and utility-level financial incentives to system-level social loss. Results indicate that pricing and transfer-payment adjustments can align institutional incentives with socially preferred outcomes when scarcity is localized and overall system reliability is maintained. However, when severe drought affects the historically more reliable subsystem, pricing mechanisms alone become insufficient to prevent socially suboptimal allocation. These findings demonstrate that physical integration without incentive alignment does not guarantee effective coordination and clarify the conditions under which pricing instruments can mitigate institutional conflict in regional water systems. © The Author(s) 2026.
ai_rationale: Scenario-based hydrological/institutional modeling of utility conflicts of interest in Taipei's water supply; simulation-based rather than clear empirical population data.

authors: Izah S.C.; Jacob D.E.; Alum E.U.; Fayiah M.
title: Water Safety in Sub-Saharan Africa
abstract: Water safety is a critical public health and development challenge in Sub-Saharan Africa, where millions lack reliable access to safe drinking water. This chapter examines the status, determinants, and impacts of water safety in the region, focusing on the quality and availability of water sources, contamination risks, and the associated burden of waterborne diseases. Drawing on empirical studies and regional data, it highlights key threats including microbial pathogens, chemical pollutants, inadequate infrastructure, climate variability, urbanization, and displacement. Case studies from countries such as Rwanda, Ghana, Nigeria, and the Horn of Africa illustrate both progress and persistent barriers to water safety. The chapter reviews relevant policy frameworks, such as the WHO Water Safety Plans and regional commitments to Sustainable Development Goal 6, and evaluates community-based and technological interventions aimed at improving water quality. Institutional capacity gaps, fragmented governance, and limited data systems are identified as core obstacles to sustained improvement. The chapter concludes with actionable recommendations focused on strengthening water governance, scaling up investment in infrastructure and hygiene education, and promoting multisectoral collaboration for sustainable, equitable water access. © The Author(s), under exclusive license to Springer Nature Switzerland AG 2026.
