ai_rationale: Empirical access-measurement study in Bangkok slums mentioning government policy role but with weak governance-factor analysis.

title: Irrigation systems as multiple-use commons: Water use in Kirindi Oya, Sri Lanka
abstract: Irrigation systems are recognized as common pool resources supplying water for agricultural production, but their role in supplying water for other uses is often overlooked. The importance of non-agricultural uses of irrigation water in livelihood strategies has implications for irrigation management and water rights, especially as increasing scarcity challenges existing water allocation mechanisms. This paper examines the multiple uses of water in the Kirindi Oya irrigation system in Sri Lanka, who the users are, and implications for water rights and management policies. There are important residential, gender, and class differences among the water users. People use irrigation system water not only for field crops, but also for fishing, homestead gardens, and livestock. Even within irrigated farming households, men have more control over paddy crops in the main fields, whereas homestead gardens are women's domain. Because the irrigation system provides water for birds and animals, even wildlife and non-resident environmental groups can be considered stakeholders. Current policies emphasize user involvement in both irrigation and domestic water supply. While government agencies have had primary responsibility, institutions such as Farmers' Organizations are being promoted. These have the potential to serve as user platforms for negotiating water allocation among irrigated farmers. However, the user organizations reflect the sectoral responsibility of the government agencies. Their membership and structure do not take into account the multiple uses or users of water. Developing platforms that accommodate different user groups remains a major challenge for improving the overall productivity, as well as equity, of water use. [PUBLICATION ABSTRACT]
ai_rationale: Study of multiple-use irrigation commons in Kirindi Oya, Sri Lanka, covering water rights/allocation institutions; primarily an irrigation/agricultural water study but notes domestic water supply policy involvement too.

authors: Nyong, A O; Kanaroglou, P S
title: Domestic water use in rural semiarid Africa: A case study of Katarko village in northeastern Nigeria
abstract: Katarko village in the Sahel region of northeastern Nigeria relies entirely on natural sources of water such as rainfall and ground water. The latter is potentially the only constant source of water.
ai_rationale: Very short case description of domestic water use in a semiarid Nigerian village; abstract too thin to assess legal/administrative exposure or study design.

title: Reforming China's institutional environment for urban infrastructure provision
abstract: Rapid urbanisation in the reform period has resulted in a very high demand for basic urban infrastructure in China. Improving its provision by the public sector is a challenge as problems persist in the form of unmet demand, deficiencies in cost recovery and inadequate maintenance.
ai_rationale: Study of institutional/regulatory reform for China's 'basic urban infrastructure' provision, unmet demand and cost recovery, but does not specify whether water/sanitation is included among the infrastructure examined.

authors: Lockie, Stewart; Momtaz, Salim; Taylor, Bruce
title: Meaning and the Construction of Social Impacts: Water Infrastructure Development in Australia's Gladstone/Calliope Region
abstract: Demonstrates social impact assessment (SIA), with a particular focus on underlying social constructions & conflicts & meanings attached to change processes, in an analysis of water infrastructure development in the Gladstone/Calliope region in central Queensland, Australia. Water development proposals in the region are reviewed, & the positive & negative impacts for the local community, as identified by an independent SIA, are addressed. The SIA implicates technocratic rationality, which empowers the government & developers while failing to address subjective & cultural dimensions of change. SIAs also tend to obscure the politics of decision making, thus marginalizing smaller groups. It is suggested that a more dynamic approach be adopted for SIAs to include frameworks that assess cultural & psychological impacts as well as the meanings associated with change for "communities of common interest.". 17 References. T. Noland
ai_rationale: Social impact assessment of water infrastructure development in an Australian region, discussing governance and community impacts, but abstract does not specify concrete access/connection/affordability outcomes.

title: Return of the Citizen: The Unstable Territories of Citizenship in Latin America
abstract: Citizen's rights are seen as the area most favored by contemporary social struggles, & one with frontiers in a constant state of flux. Differences between intellectual traditions & historical experiences in Europe & Latin America are discussed. The importance placed on the state-civil society antithesis in the debate in Latin America is emphasized, & some of its limitations regarding systems of citizenship are pointed out. Development of water services is taken as an empirical example. 72 References. Adapted from the source document.
ai_rationale: Comparative essay on citizenship rights in Latin America that uses development of water services as an empirical example, but the extent of substantive water-service analysis is unclear from the abstract.

title: Working group AGHTM. Drinking water service pipes; [Groupe de travail AGHTM. Les branchements d'eau potable]
abstract: Service pipes technology is seldom surveyed in technical papers and the AGHTM 'water supply' committee thought it could be useful to publish a feature of 'TSM' on that topic. The paper brings extensive information on legal, administrative and regulation aspects and studies functional points. The principal families of service pipes and fire connections are reviewed, as well as the installation and rehabilitation techniques. The survey shows that service pipes technology is complex and the range of applied solutions wide. Some indications are provided so that, in a given context, the appropriate technical choice can be made.
ai_rationale: Reviews legal/regulatory/technical aspects of drinking-water service pipe connections; empirical design unclear.

title: Decentralisation, rural development and local government performance: A case study of rural municipalities in north-east Brazil
abstract: Rural areas suffer from a combination of disadvantages: settlements are often remote and spatially dispersed; people rely on agriculture for most of their income, yet investments in agriculture are inherently risky and subject to periodic, catastrophic failure; and rural local governments and communities are rarely able to mobilise sufficient local resources to cover the costs of providing a full range of basic public goods and services, such as roads, water supply, primary schools and health clinics. Worse still, central governments in many countries have proved successful in concentrating power and resources in urban areas, where the political pay-off is typically higher. The resultant high rates of rural poverty and low levels of service delivery have provided a major challenge to policy-makers and researchers alike in their quest to find better solutions for rural people. Recognising the specific difficulties of rural areas, governments, local organisations and international aid agencies have developed specific policies that target resources at rural areas. But rural development programmes themselves have been dogged by problems, and despite the allocation of substantial resources, levels of rural poverty continue to remain high. New development initiatives that involve decentralising certain responsibilities to local governments, and promote the use of more participatory approaches to involve rural people directly, in designing, implementing and monitoring their own development programmes, have shown some signs of success. Results from rural development programmes in north-east Brazil suggest that, if appropriately empowered, local municipal governments can be effective at delivering the goods and services their citizens demand. We are, however, also concerned to measure how effective local governments are in fulfilling their service-delivery responsibilities. Despite the growing importance ascribed to non-economic factors, such as institutional capacity, civil society and political representation, formal economic models rarely include quantitative measures of these social factors, nor are they typically included as variables in econometric analyses. We construct an econometric model that does explicitly include quantitatively-based social indicators that permit the model to be tested, with data from 41 municipalities in north-east Brazil. Construction of the model indicates that it is feasible to utilise an econometric approach to derive insights about local government performance. Results from ordinary least squares regressions demonstrate some strong relationships between different social, institutional and political factors, and the attempts of municipal governments to deliver an adequate level of goods and services, in a cost-effective manner.
ai_rationale: Case study of decentralisation and local government performance in rural Brazil mentioning water supply among basic services delivered; unclear whether water access is specifically analyzed as an outcome.

title: Cultural responses to water shortage among Palestinians in Jordan: The water crisis and its impact on child health
abstract: Jordan is facing a serious problem with regard to its water supply.  This problem has implications for the distribution of childhood diarrhea.
ai_rationale: Brief note on cultural responses to water shortage and child health impact among Palestinians in Jordan; abstract too thin to identify a legal/administrative exposure or study design.

title: Informal rules! Using institutional economics to understand service provision in Turkey's spontaneous settlements
abstract: Turkey 's spontaneous settlements (gecekondus) house half the urban population and face infrastructure deficiencies that reduce quality of life and economic productivity while increasing the vulnerability of the urban poor.  This article reports on research that used the new institutional economics to examine the formal and informal institutional frameworks for infrastructure provision in gecekondus.  In theory, formal rules should create incentives that produce behaviour.
ai_rationale: Institutional-economics study of formal/informal infrastructure provision in Turkey's informal gecekondu settlements is highly relevant but the abstract is truncated before specifying whether water/sanitation is covered or what was found.

title: Perceptions on Healthy: Water and Sanitation Problems in Nigeria. A Comparative Study of Rural Small Town and Urban Shantytown
abstract: Presents some preliminary findings from an ongoing comparative study of household environmental health problems in urban & rural settings in Nigeria & their impact on human well-being. The importance of safe water supply & sanitation are described in-depth. It is suggested that more emphasis should be laid on local knowledge when conceptualizing a health risk, particularly as new healing methods are defined to promote the living standard of local people. The theoretical frame of the study is based on Mary Douglas's theory concerning risk acceptability in different societies, with emphasis on the sociological formulation of norms, beliefs, patterns, & practices of everyday life within a community. The discussion of culture & risk is based on an ecosocial approach to the reproduction of everyday life. Fieldwork has been conducted in a small town & village in Ile-Ife (Osun State) & in an urban shantytown in Lagos (Lagos State), including 29 focus group discussions, 37 in-depth interviews, & participatory observations of participatory rural appraisal practices.
ai_rationale: Comparative ethnographic study of household water-supply and sanitation problem perceptions in Nigerian rural small-town vs urban shantytown settings; water/sanitation topic is central but the institutional/legal exposure is not explicit (focus is risk perception/local knowledge).

title: BRAZIL: WATER TREATMENT EQUIPMENT MARKET (1); [2]
abstract: The first federal regulation on water resources was created in Brazil in 1935. When 70% of Brazil's population lived in rural areas. The industrialization  process, which started in the 1930's and dramatically increased as of the 1950's attracted most of the rural population to the cities.   Stabilizing by the mid 1980's, with approximately 75% of the Brazilian's population in urban areas. The Brazilian Association of Sanitary Engineering (ABES) reports that the per capita water consumption increased 10 times in Brazil since the beginning of the century; doubled in the last 20 years and is likely to double again in the next 20 years. In contrast, the supply of water in cubic meters per habitant per year decreased three times between 1950 and 1996. A 1994 ABES  a study on the sanitation (water and sewage) market in Brazil indicates that:The Brazilian water treatment sector is dominated by State and municipally-owned sanitation companies. The 27 State-owned companies cover in most of the cases almost the entire area of the State. Of the 6,500 municipalities existing in Brazil, about 5,200 are served by State-owned companies. The water treatment and distribution services in the remaining 1,300 municipalities are provided by municipally-owned companies. ABES reports that in 1992, 79.9 million Brazilians were served by State-owned water treatment companies. In 1995, the number of citizens served by State-owned sanitation companies grew by 6% to reach  84.6 million people, an increase of 4.7 million. During the same period, however, according to the Brazilian Institute for Geography and Statistics (IBGE), the urban population in Brazil grew by 7.1 million. This trend indicates that municipal water treatment companies may be increasing their participation in the market and that an increased percentage of the population does not have access to those services.Most of the trade sources report that a major impediment to the speedy implementation of concession projects is the lack of financing resources. While BNDES' financial participation in this market is important, it is not sufficient to cover all the financial needs of the sector. Brazilian construction and engineering companies are eagerly looking for foreign partners with expertise in financial engineering and knowledge of alternative financing sources. The private Brazilian Association of Public Water and Sewage Treatment Services Concessionaires - ABCON, reported that the key to participation in the Brazilian concession of water and sewage treatment service is finance engineering expertise. ABCON is the sole private association in Brazil that gathers approximately 50 construction and engineering companies that are already participating in the concession of water and treatment services. Some of its members such as Cavo Construtora, Carioca Christiani-Nielsen Engenharia, REK Construtora are already concessionaires of water and sewage treatment services.
ai_rationale: Market report on Brazil's water treatment sector history and state/municipal utility coverage statistics; study design not clearly identifiable.

title: A Study of the Interest Structure in Conflicting Regions by the Use of Water Resources
abstract: Explains regional interest structures involved in water-use conflicts in South Korea, & advocates institutional changes designed to promote efficient water use & dispute resolution. Analysis of conflicts regarding specific dam projects from technological, institutional, & sociological perspectives relies on the concepts of social dilemmas & barriers. It is concluded that removal of the structural dilemma that exists between advantaged & disadvantaged regions depends on minimizing water-related socioeconomic inequality by changing pay-off structures. Ways to institutionalize the entire conflict-resolution process are suggested. 3 Tables, 1 Figure, 44 References. Adapted from the source document.
ai_rationale: Analysis of regional interest structures and institutional dispute-resolution in South Korean water-use conflicts over dam projects; unclear if outcome is household service access.

title: Negotiating development charges in Ontario: Average cost versus marginal cost pricing of services
abstract: A study determines how the interplay of stakeholders in a larger economic and political context influences the design of development charge regimes in particular jurisdictions.
ai_rationale: Study of stakeholder influence on municipal development-charge pricing regimes in Ontario, which often fund water/sewer infrastructure, but the abstract does not specify which services or confirm a water/sanitation access outcome.

title: Water: From Basic Need to Commodity: A Discussion on Gender and Water Rights in the Context of Irrigation
abstract: With growing water scarcity & programs to increase the efficiency of water allocation & delivery, the allocation of water rights is critical. Here, the implications of changing water policies for women's water rights & access to water in irrigation systems are examined, drawing on examples from irrigation projects in Nepal & Sri Lanka. Although women often have informal means & mechanisms to obtain & secure access to water, often there is no recognition of women's specific water needs, especially for production, as opposed to domestic consumption. Current policies to privatize & devolve management of irrigation need to increase responsiveness to specific women's water needs & interests if they are to address efficiency as well as equity concerns. 45 References. Adapted from the source document.
ai_rationale: Study of gender and water rights in Nepal/Sri Lanka irrigation systems, distinguishing domestic consumption from production needs; primarily irrigation-focused.

title: Privatizing Africa's infrastructure - Promise and challenge
abstract: Africa's infrastructure - comprising electricity, gas, telecommunications, water supply and transport - trails the world, in both extent and quality. Poor infrastructure is a major obstacle to the region's economic growth, and adversely affects the living standards of its people. It has important impacts on health, education, and the capacity for effective governance as well as on the ability of industries to compete in international markets. Despite the importance of these sectors, investments in Africa's infrastructure have too often been squandered. Service provision has been entrusted to state-owned monopolies tasked with multiple, poorly defined and often conflicting objectives, and facing weak or perverse incentives for efficiency. Investment decisions are often driven primarily by political considerations. Tariff policies typically benefit only the more affluent in society who have access to service, and even when tariffs are reasonable, collection has been weak. Failure to cover costs through tariffs leads to insufficient funds for investment, which is left to already over-burdened public budgets. Within enterprises, management is often appointed more on the basis of political loyalty than competence, and excessive staff are often employed to benefit favored groups. The poorest suffer the most from these policies, since they lack access to any services at all, or must bear the high costs of self-provision or supply from the informal sector.
ai_rationale: Discusses African infrastructure governance/tariffs and access disparities but multi-sector narrative, design unclear.

title: Urbanization: the challenge for the next century.
abstract: This article summarizes a new 1996-97 report from the World Resources Institute, the UN Environmental Program, the UN Development Program, and the World Bank, which describes a future with increased levels of urbanization that were reshaping the physical and social environment. Urbanization increased economic growth and environmental degradation. By the year 2000, 50% of the world population will live in urban areas. Cities are the center of economic activity. Consumption is the highest in cities. Cities produce the most pollution and waste. Three issues are particularly crucial to survival: the water supply, sanitation, and water resource management. Neglect of these and other environmental issues is likely to have important consequences in both developing and developed countries. The greatest growth in urban areas is occurring in developing countries. Cities in developing countries have huge populations living in poverty. The poor in either rural or urban areas are confronted with lack of access to clean water, to sanitation, and to housing. There is overcrowding and exposure to industrial wastes and air pollution. There is a need for policy reform, stronger institutions, and enlightened political leadership. Cities need to improve their environment and to strengthen local government and implement poverty reduction programs. Reform of urban policies must be accompanied by effective urban governance. Community-based approaches are essential. Broad-based support is needed for changes in strategies and practices and for attainment of a more sustainable environment.
ai_rationale: Global urbanization report links access to water/sanitation with governance need, but narrative, no identifiable design.

title: Washington news
abstract: The Environmental Protection Agency has launched 2 major initiatives on state revolving funds.  One deals with the new funds established under the Safe Drinking Water Act amendments passed by Congress in 1996 to help public systems finance the cost of drinking water infrastructure, and the other with funding under the SRF provisions of the Clean Water Act, the long-standing vehicle for helping finance construction of wastewater treatment plants.  The agency has issued an interim guidance on SDWA revolving funds, for which the new law provides nearly $10 billion through fiscal year 2003, with an initial amount of $1.3 billion for fiscal 1996.  In connection with the Clean Water Act, EPA has sent to state environmental agency directors its final SRF Funding Framework - Policy and Guidance, that is described as a year-long dialogue between EPA and its state partners to clarify the possible use of SRF funds.
ai_rationale: News item on EPA's launch of state revolving fund programs to help finance drinking water and wastewater infrastructure under SDWA/CWA; directly relevant to service investment/affordability but is a brief administrative news report without empirical study design.

title: Water Policies in Europe
abstract: Traces France's public water policy from 19th-century economic development to current European integration. The French guidelines are compared to those of other European countries, highlighting the nation's progressive policies to protect potable water supplies for cities against natural & industrial hazards & to protect the surrounding environment. Current French policies serve as an effective model for Europe because they include private participation in managing & distributing the drinking water supply. 51 References. Adapted from the source document.
ai_rationale: Descriptive historical overview of French public drinking-water policy including private-sector participation; topically relevant but no clear empirical study design evident from the abstract.

title: Will open market and deregulation come to water and wastewater
abstract: Dramatic change is occurring in the public utilities industries.  It can be called the return to the open market.  Every day the media contains stories of open access, transportation of customer-owned energy, choice in providers, competition, incentive rate-making, performance based regulation, price cap rate-making, benchmark/profit sharing rate-making and even deregulation.  The revolution has hit gas, telecommunications, transportation and, most recently, electricity.  It is driven by statute, by regulatory action, and by utility initiative.  Competition in the water and wastewater industry is extensive and continues to grow in various forms.  There may be competition between different investor-owned systems or between investor-owned systems and municipal-owned systems to serve a particular area.  There may be competition to regionalize.  There may be competition to privatize and there may be competition with alternative, non-traditional providers.
ai_rationale: Trade commentary on deregulation and open-market competition trends in the US water and wastewater utility industry; directly on-topic regarding regulatory/institutional change but reads as an industry overview rather than an empirical study with identifiable population and outcome data.

title: Evolving water policy in the Bangkok Metropolitan Region
abstract: The study focuses on the problems of allocation in Thailand where the alternative of introducing a comprehensive water-pricing system has become a controversial issue. Governed by the regime of open access, the Thai water allocation system has failed to cope with newly surfacing demands and necessities. The system has yet to overcome old perceptions and habits. The case studied is the Bangkok Metropolitan Region (BMR), the area of greatest social-economic changes and most acute water allocation conflicts in Thailand. Proposals to shift water allocation decisions from the government to the market by way of water-pricing have not been well received by the government as a result of political uncertainty. While the government is in favour of increased centralization to improve its administrative control, the academic circles are calling for institutional reforms which would include specifications of property rights to water.As a contribution to the area of Thai water management, this study examines water resource issues in relation to the water demand profile of the BMR, the issue of property rights and water allocation, the historical development within Thai political economy, the trends that shape possible changes within the policy arena and how these changes can positively affect water allocation systems in Thailand in terms of pricing. The study is based on reviews of relevant theory, interviews and analysis of both published and unpublished data on the BMR.Water issues in the BMR revolve around problems of water shortage, groundwater over-extraction, and deteriorating water quality. The demand profile indicates that the existing water allocation system is not able to sufficiently accommodate the BMR's water demand, neither in quantity nor in spatial distribution. The state's centralized administrative control has failed to provide an efficient and equitable system for water allocation. Solutions currently being proposed follow one of three alternatives: increase state centralization to correct administrative errors, conserve and revive traditional systems, or introduce market-based tools such as a water-pricing.The study suggests that there needs to be a shift in government policy to develop a mechanism whereby water allocation and management recognize the significance of local community inputs as represented by interest groups.
ai_rationale: Dissertation on water allocation and pricing policy reform in Bangkok Metropolitan Region; unclear whether focus is specifically household service access versus general resource allocation.

title: Reviews -- Covering Ground: Communal Water Management and the State in the Peruvian Highlands by David W. Guillet
abstract: Review.
ai_rationale: Book review ('Review.' only, no content) of 'Covering Ground: Communal Water Management and the State in the Peruvian Highlands'; topic (communal water governance) highly relevant but no assessable content provided.

title: Water poverty and social policy: A review of issues for research
abstract: Huby suggests how social policy research can address the difficulties an increasing number of people face in England and Wales in paying for water services.  Research needs to look at the economic, environmental and political considerations underlying increasing costs.
ai_rationale: Commentary outlining a research agenda on water affordability ('water poverty') and social policy in England/Wales; squarely on-topic but framed as a review/agenda-setting piece rather than presenting its own empirical findings.

title: The frontier problem in incipient groundwater management regimes in Balochistan (Pakistan)
abstract: A study investigated how resource management regimes in Balochistan Pakistan evolve or fail to evolve.  The definition of access rights and the lack of knowledge on the limits of resources are key problems.
ai_rationale: Brief study of evolving groundwater access-rights regimes in Balochistan, Pakistan; abstract too thin to confirm household-service relevance or design.

title: The Role of Indigenous People in Sustainable Development
abstract: Discusses several common themes facing the Indian Nations of the Mni Sose Coalition, which includes 22 Indian nations located in the Missouri River Basin. Among the themes discussed are the relative underdevelopment of infrastructure; difficulties produced by the Pick-Sloan project, a system of river dams that has destroyed indigenous economies & communities; & conflicts over river management. While the Indian Nations of the region possess extensive land & water rights, land & water have thus far been developed by various agencies of the US government for the benefit of others. It is argued that without an adequate environmental infrastructure, tribal efforts to take control of their situation have been ineffective. It is suggested that the approach of the federal government to the Indian Nations must change dramatically while the environmental infrastructure is developed in such a way that the River Basin can become a source of sustainability for the Indian populations that live there. D. M. Smith
ai_rationale: Discussion of Indian Nations' land and water rights, federal water-resource development, and environmental infrastructure in the Missouri River Basin; legal/governance relevance unclear whether it addresses household service access specifically.

title: Public Attitudes toward Environmental Problems and Environmental Protection: The Case of Taegu City
abstract: The public attitudes of Taegu City (South Korea) residents toward the environment were examined through a survey of 861 adults. Respondents demonstrated substantial environmental concern, particularly to quality of drinking water. The experience of the phenol water contamination in 1991 had a significant impact on environmental concerns. Social bases -- eg, class & age -- had trickle-up & trickle-down effects on environmental concerns & were mediated by values toward the relationship between development & environment & between people & nature. Social reform orientations & political discontent had both direct & indirect impacts on environmental concern. Environmental attitudes were often inconsistent, contradictory, & even premature, likely a result of widespread discontent with government & industry measures of environmental protections & lack of systematic & institutional opportunities for environmental education. 20 Tables, 30 References. Adapted from the source document.
ai_rationale: Survey of Taegu City residents' environmental attitudes, focused on drinking water quality concern following a regulatory contamination incident, but the outcome measured is attitudes rather than access.

title: Improving Human Welfare through Appropriate Technology: Government Responsibility, Citizen Duty or Customer Choice
abstract: Explores recent attempts to improve the effectiveness of environmental health programs & projects by reference to the International Drinking Water Supply & Sanitation Decade (1980-1990) & beyond. Reference is made to how water & sanitation as technical interventions have drawn on the natural sciences, notably concepts of race & sex, & the social sciences, including culture & gender, for their authority & legitimacy. The Water Decade sought to challenge the powerful & enduring high tech image of development on which much Western environmental & social transformations have been based. Beginning as a critique of modernism with a commitment to basic needs as human rights, it was driven by a recognition that sophisticated technology could not satisfy human health needs. Alternative technologies would, by contrast, cater for a more extensive & varied market & would promote participatory approaches to service delivery. During the course of the decade, sections of the aid community began to redefine basic needs as commodities involving the efficient marketing & delivery of a product with minimal state intervention. Also examined is the changing role of the expert & the links being forged among large donors, nongovernmental organizations, & the private sector. The significance of this reformulated progressivism for the development debate is then considered, notably in relation to concepts of citizenship, consumer choice, & the role of the state. 88 References. Adapted from the source document.
ai_rationale: Historical/critical essay on governance paradigms (state, market, NGO) during the International Drinking Water Supply and Sanitation Decade; empirical basis for claims unclear from abstract.

title: Soil sensitivity and wastewater management: Implications for rural landscape planning
abstract: This study examines on-site wastewater disposal systems management as a rural landscape planning issue, with the Rural Municipality of Springfield in Manitoba as its Study Area.The applied methodology includes a review of relevant literature and field tests. Three percolation testing procedures were conducted on selected soils of five sites in Springfield, to determine the sensitivity of the soils and to evaluate the proposed Manitoba percolation testing procedure prior to its inclusion in the Manitoba Regulation 95/88R. The results were subjected to quantitative and mapping analysis. The management of on-site wastewater disposal systems in the Province of Manitoba was then evaluated.One of the study's key findings is that the majority of Springfield's soils pose significant limitations to the conventional wastewater disposal system. The implication is that such installed systems in Springfield have a high potential for malfunctioning or failure, resulting in a high risk of environmental degradation from failed systems. The study also determines that the proposed Manitoba percolation testing procedure is an acceptable tool for evaluating the soil sensitivity of a proposed site for an on-site sewage disposal system.Three major recommendations of the study include: (a) the use of systems that 'fit' the environment, i.e. systems that can adapt to the requirements of the particular environment; (b) thorough site evaluation before installing on-site sewage disposal systems, including the use of percolation testing where the soil is suspect; and (c) educating homeowners about the need for proper installation, operation and maintenance of on-site systems.The study also examines how on-site wastewater disposal management practices impact on rural landscape planning from the regional to local levels, and how such practices assist landscape planners to create sustainable environments of the highest quality in rural areas.
ai_rationale: Study evaluating a Manitoba regulatory soil percolation testing procedure for on-site rural wastewater disposal systems; primarily technical, regulatory link unclear.

title: The design of a water quality management system for nigerian rivers
abstract: There is an intricate relationship between water quantity and quality, development, human health and welfare, and aquatic life.  Water availabilty is, however, variable in location and time.  The increase in human populations and various anthropogenic activities have exerted significant impacts on the quantity and quality of freshwater resources.  Nigeria is a rapidly developing country with a population of 88.5 million.  About 70% of the rural population has no access to potable water.  There are no data on access to sanitation facilities.  The pace of industrial development in Nigeria has been without adequate environmental considerations.  The need was, consequently, identified to assess water resources in Nigeria, determine the causes and sources of water pollution, and design a water quality management system for Nigerian rivers.  Before such a system could be designed, it was necessary to study in depth the administrative, operational and legislative framework of an existing functional organisation.  The National Rivers Authority, in the north west region of England, was chosen as such a model.  The research started with a detailed survey of literature on water pollution, its nature, sources, types, modes of propagation, effects, means of detection, enumeration and control.  A thorough assessment of the functions and institutional framework of the National Rivers Authority which enable it to manage river water quality in the north west of England was carried out.  A comparative assessment was made, of water resources and the current status and practice of water quality management in Nigeria.  The research culminated in the design of a water quality management system for Nigerian rivers.  The design took into consideration the political and cultural orientations, and the level of industrialisation of the country.  Recommendations were made, which if adopted, will ensure the sustainable use of rivers in Nigeria.
ai_rationale: Dissertation designing an administrative and legislative water quality management system for Nigerian rivers

title: Accessing Water Channeling Power: Class, Gender, and Caste Inequalities in India's Desert
abstract: An investigation of why social groups have unequal access to natural resources & unequal risk through their participation in state-of-the-art sustainable development, & whether these social-political processes are related to processes of ecological degradation. A case study is presented of one of the world's largest irrigation projects, the Indira Gandhi Canal in India's Thar desert, financed by the World Bank. It is argued that the state's expansion into the desert, & its control over its natural resources, worsens class, caste, & gender relations. The literature on the Third World capitalist-developmental state considers questions of risk, access, & inequality, but fails to understand the role of nature as dynamic, instead reducing & reifying it as site & input for production. Here, it is suggested that water, as well as other natural resources & processes, should not solely be analyzed as inputs, but as critical variables interacting with cultural, political, & economic forces on the local, regional, & global levels. Nature is socially embedded & production relations & village life have ecological-historical & naturalized elements. From this perspective, the state's control over natural resources has its manifold disempowering effects on nonelite communities & their access to, & control over, production on the desert's common lands, pastures, & forests. Typically, the commons were managed by low-caste, poor communities, & the desert's water resources managed by women before the construction of the Indira Gandhi Canal. It is concluded that sustainable development practices do two things best: sustain social inequalities & develop ecological crises.
ai_rationale: Case study of the World Bank-financed Indira Gandhi Canal irrigation project's disempowering effects on class/caste/gender access to desert water resources, including domestic water previously managed by women; largely an irrigation/commons study with some domestic-water relevance.

title: Indian Water Settlements: The Prerequisites of Successful Negotiation
abstract: Since the late 1970s, the federal government has been negotiating, rather than litigating, conflicts over Indian water claims. According to the literature on dispute resolution, successful negotiations are usually characterized by a specific set of conditions -- alternative strategies, funding for implementation, participation, consensual negotiation, & procedures agreement. It is concluded that negotiations over Indian water rights are not characterized by conditions usually found in fair negotiations. 57 References. Adapted from the source document.
ai_rationale: Reviews conditions for successful negotiated settlement of US Indian water rights claims; legal/institutional analysis of tribal water rights, but access-outcome specificity is unclear.

title: From crisis to recovery: the difficult progress of African public utilities - Cameroon, Niger and Senegal; [De la crise a l'assainissement: le difficile cheminement des services publics africains (Cameroun, Niger et Senegal)]
abstract: This study is devoted to a diagnosis of the crisis and policy reform of public utilities (water, transportation, electric power) for three sub-Saharan countries: Cameroon, Niger, Senegal. The main conclusion we draw is that some fundamental issues remain concerning the way these enterprises are managed, the influence of the macroeconomic framework or the institutional relationship with governments. -English summary
ai_rationale: Diagnosis of utility crisis/institutional relationships across 3 countries but water bundled with other utilities.

title: A Multifaceted Approach to Health Education: A Case Study from Rural Egypt
abstract: Draws on qualitative & quantitative survey data to describe & evaluate an environmental health education project, focusing on water & sanitation issues, in 2 Egyptian villages in the Nile delta. Various hygiene education strategies carried out by health unit staff, teachers, graduate volunteers, & local village leaders are compared. The project is multifaceted in that it: looks at health education in relation to specific health interventions; identifies the full context of relevant local behavior; & collaborates with local people, especially women, in the design & implementation of the program. Based on the experience gained during this project, a broad-based model for health education is presented. 2 Tables, 17 References. Adapted from the source document.
ai_rationale: Mixed-methods evaluation of a rural Egyptian water/sanitation health-education program; outcome centers on education model rather than access.

title: Women and Water in Rural Maharashtra
abstract: The relationship between environmental issues & the status of women in developing countries is explored through examination of the causes & effects of a water shortage in Maharashtra, India. In general, the division of labor along gender lines, accompanied by the low status accorded "women's work," causes women to benefit least from economic development while suffering most from its ecological consequences. In Maharashtra, increasingly intensive farming may actually be contributing to the drought, but, because crop production is considered more important than women's work, most of the available water goes to the farmers. The result is that water for drinking & household uses is extremely difficult for the women to obtain. Further, in times of drought, many men desert their villages in search of work in the cash economy, leaving women alone to tend to subsistence farms as well as large families. It is suggested that ecological problems are likely to increase women's awareness of their oppression as a group. Water shortages may lead to increased activism as women fight for equal access to scarce resources. K. Pizer
ai_rationale: Case study of women's difficulty obtaining domestic water due to agricultural water priority in rural Maharashtra; exposure is resource allocation rather than explicit legal/institutional factor.

title: The Organisation and Management of Urban Local Authorities in Zimbabwe
abstract: Findings obtained in a case study of Bulawayo are used to examine the organization & management of urban local authorities in Zimbabwe, focusing on center-local trends, financial adequacy & autonomy, & provision of urban services. It is concluded that: urban local government in Zimbabwe has a relatively large degree of autonomy, both in organizational & financial terms; local revenue-raising capacity is relatively high, although capital expenditure has been declining; & the level of services provision is very high, both in terms of accessibility & reliability. 6 Tables. Adapted from the source document.
ai_rationale: Case study of Zimbabwean urban local authority organization/finance and urban service accessibility/reliability (Bulawayo); services not specifically identified as water/sanitation.

title: International Drinking Water Supply and Sanitation Decade and beyond
abstract: The International Drinking Water Supply and Sanitation Decade ends in 1990. Though the Decade has not achieved its numerical objective of universal access to water and sanitation, it has been quite successful in creating awareness about the sector and in developing workable strategies and models which enhance sector sustainability. The disparity in coverage between urban and rural areas, the wide differential between the provision of water supply facilities and those for sanitation, the active and meaningful involvement of women in the management of water and sanitation programmes, and effective means of accelerating coverage in a sustainable manner, are all issues for which effective answers must be found during the 1990s. If the sector were to perform in the 1990s, similar to its performance during the 1980s, a significant proportion of developing countries' population will yet be unserved by the year 2000. Thus, the strategies of the 1990s must be such that their combined effect will make and enormous difference with respect to sector performance. A more management-oriented sector, based on frequent and systematic monitoring at country and global level, with a functional and effective institutionalized entity for global advocacy, should form the corner-stone of the thrust for the 1990s.
ai_rationale: Decade review cites access/coverage disparities and institutional factors but lacks identifiable study design.

title: Rhetoric and Reality: Privatisation and the Water Environment
abstract: Proposals to privatize the water industry in GB are critically examined, focusing on the difficulties a private water company would face in developing a river management system. Interdependencies in the network of water resources, & the management structure that currently handles water allocation, regulation, & protection are described. It is argued that the government's proposals are a triumph of ideology over the needs of consumers. While European experience shows that private ownership is not incompatible with consumer interest, the regulatory system proposed to accompany privatization offers no assurance that consumer interests will be protected & promises to increase bureaucratic costs. 3 Tables, 2 Figures. A. Waters
ai_rationale: Critical policy analysis of proposed UK water industry privatization and its regulatory/consumer implications, though largely prospective/analytical rather than presenting outcome data.

title: Assessing Preferences in Cost-Benefit Analysis: Reflections on Rural Water Supply Evaluation in Haiti
abstract: An area of cost-benefit methodology that has come under increasing philosophical scrutiny in recent years is examined: the appropriate treatment of individuals' preferences. Some of the difficulties involved in assessing preferences are illustrated in the context of a concrete example: the evaluation of a Ru water supply project in southern Haiti. Four problems in the application of cost-benefit principles are discussed: (1) how to count the social value of private water taps connected to homes if they are preferred for prestige reasons, (2) how to assess husbands' preferences concerning the time savings by wives who previously carried water from more distant sources, (3) how to count preferences based on a R's desire to support general community welfare, & (4) how to evaluate a water project when people's preferences may change after the new water system is installed. Reasons are given as to why some preferences should be included in such evaluations & others ignored. 1 Table. HA
ai_rationale: Methodological discussion of assessing preferences in cost-benefit evaluation of a rural Haiti water supply project; unclear legal/institutional exposure.

authors: Dezelic, Nada; Zebec, Mirna; Kern, Josipa; Pantic, Zeljko
title: Health and Ecological Aspects of Life in the Villages of the Croatian Hinterland
abstract: A study was conducted of a typical rural Yugoslav village in Croatia -- the community of Belec in Hrvatsko Zagorje -- seeking to determine the extent to which development of housing, water supply, & waste disposal facilities follow general economic development. It was found that of the houses built for incoming workers, only 30% had indoor toilets, thus lowering the overall hygiene standards for the region. Since poor human waste disposal directly affects health, immediate measures are needed -- first to educate the population in regard to personal hygiene, & then to improve housing conditions. 11 Tables, 1 Figure, 11 References. Modified HA
ai_rationale: Study of housing, water supply, and waste disposal facility development in a Croatian village; unclear legal/institutional exposure.

title: Political Economy and the Environment of Appalachia: The Case of Yellow Creek
abstract: Appalachia is experiencing severe problems with maintaining clean, safe water supplies. The political economy of Appalachia, as seen through the Yellow Creek controversy, places itself in opposition to a sound & responsible management of these water sources, as well as to the total environment. Yellow Creek is a fourteen-mile-long stream in Bell County, Ky, with a population of about 1,200 residents along its banks. In illustrating the case as typical of Appalachia, a brief historical account & political overview of the region provide a framework for core-periphery theory. Analysis then shifts to a brief explanation of the environmental concerns of the case. Out of these concerns has emerged a well-organized citizens' movement. Thus, the case provides an excellent example of the affinity of government agencies with business interests.
ai_rationale: Case study of Appalachian political economy (Yellow Creek) and government-business affinity affecting clean/safe water-supply management, with citizen mobilization; governance-relevant but outcome measure of access is not explicit.

title: "Top-Down Planning": Analysis of Obstacles to Community Development in an Economically Poor Region of the Southwestern United States
abstract: The process of developing a plan for management of water from the Rio Grande River in the Espanola Valley, NM, is examined. The major parties in the controversy surrounding this project were: (1) the Bureau of Reclamation, (2) the State Engineer's Office, (3) the tribal councils of San Juan & Santa Clara Pueblos, (4) the chicano communities, & (5) the city of Espanola. The effect of these participants on events prior to, during, & after a government-sponsored social impact assessment are analyzed. Numerous negative effects of the management plan are noted, including the probability of a major reduction in water available to local farmers. The activities surrounding this project are an example of "top-down planning," without any regard for local grassroots participation. P. Montgomery.
ai_rationale: Case study of top-down federal/state water management planning for the Rio Grande in New Mexico reducing water available to local Pueblo and Chicano farmers, though focus is agricultural/community rather than clearly household service.

authors: Shapiro, David L; Shelton, Robert B
title: The Application of an Agency Decision-Making Model
abstract: A number of bureaucratic decision-making models have appeared recently in the literature. Generally, these models have focused on identifying one argument in agency managers' utility functions, eg, agency size or budget, or wealth of managers. A generalized statement of these models is developed & is applied to the price of water by water resource agencies. The model is applied to the contemporary concern with environmental quality, & its implications for congressional decision making are traced. 4 Figures. Modified HA.
ai_rationale: Develops a bureaucratic agency decision-making model applied to how water resource agencies set water prices, which is directly relevant to affordability/governance, but the abstract does not make clear whether this is an empirical study or a purely theoretical/econometric exercise.

title: 1,400 GOVERNMENTS
abstract: Subtitled, 'The Political Economy of the New York Metropolitan Region,' this volume discusses in 5 Chpts the 1,400 gov'al units in the NY Metropolitan Region (NYMR). (1) The Political Economy of a Metropolitan Area - covers the expanding role of gov'al activities in regional econ affairs & the corollary that many econ decisions become pol'al. (2) Pressures onthe Public Sector - examines a sample of 64 medium-size New Jersey municipalities close to the center of the NYMR. Factor analysis indicates the following factors most related to gov'al spending: community size, industrialization, housing density, age of pop, low-income prevalence, residential affluence & land reserve. (3) Responses of the Local Governments - indicates that in the NYMR local gov's have responded to the Ur pressures by 1 of 3 strategies: (a) pol'al moves to avoid effects of metropolitan growth, (b) use of public power to modify the environmental circumstances, & (c) appeals to higher levels of gov for help in sustaining local burdens. Illustrations of varying strategies of adjustment are given as NY City, the NY suburbs & the New Jersey suburbs. (4) The World of Metropolitan Giants - examines the large units of gov (regional enterprises) & the way in which they deal with transportation, water supply & physical development. (5) The Political. Economy of the Future - indicates that 'the most signif fact is that 2 diff types of pol'al systems rule the public sector today - the local gov's & the regional enterprises,' & suggests that while informal & private concern with & arrangements for metropolitan-wide functions may grow, a metropolitan gov is not likely to result. Appendices & an index. S. F. Fava.
ai_rationale: Political-economy monograph on 1,400 governmental units in the New York metropolitan region, including a chapter on how 'regional enterprises' handle transportation, water supply and physical development amid governmental fragmentation.

title: URBAN AND SUBURBAN NASHVILLE A CASE STUDY IN METROPOLITANISM
abstract: Nashville, in Tennessee, provides an interesting case study of an area in the first stages of metropolitanism. Whilst its problems are not comparable to those of larger cities, they provide a headache for the authorities because of the absence of a unified gov for the area & the various maladjustments between the Ur & subUr areas. The systems of sewerage disposal, police protection, fire protection, water supply, public health, hospitals & educ & welfare all lack unified control. There are the usual financial difficulties caused by the city providing free services to the county & vice versa, the duplicate expenditures of both & the multiplicity of authorites to which the suburbanites have to pay for their services. These problems were studied by the Community Services Commission in 1951 whose main recommendations were: annexation of subUr Nashville, establishment of county responsibility for county-wide functions, provision in the Tenn constitution for city & county home rule & the redistricting of Davidson County. (IPSA).
ai_rationale: 1951 Community Services Commission case study of fragmented, non-unified local government in Nashville hindering coordinated provision of water supply and sewerage disposal among other municipal services; water/sanitation mentioned as part of a broader multi-service governance study.

title: COVERAGE DOUBLED ON SANITARY RULES
abstract: WASHINGTON, Dec. 2--The number of people protected by sanitation regulations meeting the standards of the Public Health Service of the Federal Security Agency, has increased in the last five years from 40,000,000 to 82,000,000 persons.
ai_rationale: Brief historical news item reporting the population count covered by expanded US sanitation regulations; on-topic but too thin on population/methodology detail to be confident.
